Sports.title: Battle of boxing's most unlikeable stars: Conor Benn takes on troubled Ryan Garcia after burning Eddie Hearn with $10MILLION payday in his sights - but here's why Briton's fate rests solely in the hands of his narcissistic American rival
Sports.content:
Battle of boxing's most unlikeable stars: Conor Benn takes on troubled Ryan Garcia after burning Eddie Hearn with $10MILLION payday in his sights - but here's why Briton's fate rests solely in the hands of his narcissistic American rival

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

‘Who ya like buddy?’ It’s the most asked question in casino-ville as the hours tick down to this Saturday’s world title fight between two angry young men.

One, America’s extravagantly gifted but troubled world welterweight champion. The other, the ever-persistent English challenger who never stops throwing punches whether they connect or not. As if in manic obsession with defeating not only opponents but also his demons and a sceptical outside world.

So, Ryan Garcia or Conor Benn?

When the denizens of this neon gambling Strip in the Nevada desert ask that question they don’t’ want to know which of these two combatants you like personally more than the other. It is their way of trying to find out who you might be betting on to prevail in the atmospheric T-Mobile Arena.

Their inquiries are even more numerous than usual on such occasions as this. Because neither the Americans nor the Mexicans who are thronging here in support of their blood brother by heredity know very much about Benn. Other than the fact he is the son of a fabled icon of the British ring.

On his two previous US visits Benn Jr made hard work of beating men who looked more like nightclub bouncers than professional boxers. Of his exploits back home only the pair of fights against Chris Eubank Jr evoked any interest whatsoever on either side of this border.

What they are aware of is the two positive tests for performance enhancing drugs and the protracted legal battle to technically clear his name which kept him out of the ring for months. Just as they know about Garcia’s conviction and suspension for a similar finding.

Conor Benn is locked in the battle of boxing's most unlikeable stars in Las Vegas

Benn is lining up a $10m payday after burning his bridges with promoter Eddie Hearn

So, what’s to like?

There can be no doubting Benn’s work ethic. He trains like a dervish to manufacture the maximum possible out of however much natural-born ability he inherited from Nigel the Dark Destroyer. Nor does he ever give up. Eubank Jr had to go beyond the normal limits of even this battle-hardened business to inflict the only defeat of Conor’s career thus far. A loss he avenged, albeit in partly contrived and contentious circumstances.

Eubank the Younger was perilously drained in the rematch by a clause in the contract which prevented him rehydrating fully after struggling to cut poundage to meet the agreed catchweight.

What goes around comes around. If not in a full measure of the irony. Benn has had to sweat and strain down by almost a stone from middleweight to make the welterweight championship limit of 147 lbs. As he puts it: ‘Five weeks in hell.’

To say his body looks shredded is putting it mildly. But he has not been subjected to rehydration limitations following his Friday morning visit to the scales.

Eubank was handsomely rewarded to put his health on the line, and now Benn has been lured into similar jeopardy by the fortune – some reports say ten million dollars – he is receiving from UFC boss Dana White to be one of the first poster boys for his venture into boxing.

Benn tells it otherwise: ‘I’m doing this because I relish challenges. Have always wanted to strap on the same green WBC belt my dad was so proud to wear. To start getting the world titles that will leave a legacy for my kids. And to prove wrong everyone who doesn’t give me a chance of winning. That puts all the pressure on him, not me.’

Hearn backed the British fighter during his controversial doping ban saga

Ryan Garcia stands in his way of the WBC title, who is the more talented of the fighters

WEIGH-IN VERDICT: After all the brouhaha Conor Benn made the weight with a full pound to spare After what he described as 'five weeks of hell' dieting down by two divisions he scaled 146 lbs in readiness to challenge world welterweight champion Ryan Garcia here this Saturday night. He did so with a told-you so smile. Throughout the speculation as to whether he could shed the best part of a stone in his training camp journey from middleweight Benn had assured one and all that he would be comfortable at his long-ago weight. Good as his word he came in only half a pound heavier than Garcia. Although he is leaner of hip the muscle is still there on arms and torso. Complete with a six pack as a reminder of his constant work ethic. The slightly taller part/Mexican great white hope of American boxing does look more natural at the weight. But Benn does not appear stressed from all his exertions. Even so Garcia is still a solid odds on favourite in the Vegas betting

Whether or not Benn can take in sufficient liquids and pasta before entering the ring, the dangers to him are greater than those with which Eubank struggled. Garcia, one year the younger at 28 but the riper in championships experience, has authentic one-hit-knockout power.

Benn goes into his first world championship fight reliant on the cumulative effect of his non-stop output. The problem with this is that King Ry is probably the best counterpuncher in the world right now and Benn’s headlong style will likely suit him nicely, thank you.

To complicate the evaluation, both have blotted their copybooks as people. Garcia, the handsome heartthrob, burnished his bad-boy rock-star image by trashing a five-star hotel room. He also needed his family’s help with overcoming mental problems aggravated by a passing fancy for social drugs and booze.

Benn invited mockery for claiming initially that he failed his drugs tests because of eating enough eggs to fill the shelves of all the Tescos in London. Then, in order to collect his bonanza from Mister UFC, he unceremoniously dumped his long-time promoter Eddie Hearn who had bankrolled his hefty legal costs and loaned him half a million quid to help sustain his flamboyant lifestyle through that crisis.

Not much to like there.

So, when it comes to the fight, who ya like? The answer is not Conor Benn’s to give. Because the real question is which Ryan Garcia turns up.

If it is the narcissist whose arrogant complacency has cost him a couple of big fights, it may not be totally beyond the bounds of possibility that Conor could pull off one of the major upsets by a British boxer abroad.

If it is King Ry fully prepared and ready to unfurl all the majesty then we can only hope the son of Nigel is not seriously hurt.

Sports.title: Ricky Hatton's mother recalls last hug with boxing champion three days before he took his own life a year ago as parents speak out for first time
Sports.content:
Ricky Hatton's mother has recalled her last hug with him three days before he took his own life one year ago as his parents speak out for the first time.

Carol and Ray Hatton have urged people to tell their friends and family they love them before it's too late after the boxing champion hanged himself on September 14 last year.

One year on from Ricky's death, aged 46, his mother has revealed the last time she embraced her son.

Just days before he took his own life, the boxing champion had been in an argument with his parents but the family were 'building bridges'.

Carol decided to make an unplanned visit to his gym in Hyde and gave him a 'real proper hug'.

She told ITV News: 'I pulled up on the car park because I saw his car. He asked if everything was okay.

'I said "yeah, everything's fine". I said I'd like to see a bit more of him.'

Ricky's mother said he told her he wanted to see his father Ray the next week. However Ricky died three days later.

Former world boxing champion Ricky Hatton died by suicide in September last year aged 46

Ray and Carol Hatton (pictured at their son's funeral) have urged people to tell their friends and family they love them before it's too late

Ricky had previously opened up about his struggle with drug and alcohol addiction and had become estranged from his parents before the reconciled

She added: 'I'm so glad (I got to see him) because nobody knows when it's the last time you're going to see somebody.'

Ray, the boxer's father, said: 'You tell your grandkids how much you love them, you tell your wife how much you love them but I think, especially with men, don't ever be afraid of getting hold of your son and telling him you love him.'

Ricky had become estranged from his parents for around a decade before he reached out to patch up their relationship several years before his death.

He had survived previous suicide attempts and struggled with drug and alcohol addiction.

Ricky fell out with his parents over money and despite the dispute he still allowed Carol and Ray to see his newborn daughter Millie.

However the boxer became upset when his girlfriend Jennifer was not invited to a Christmas Day party.

Months later he received letters from his parents' lawyers saying they wanted to see their granddaughter.

But he told Manchester Evening News in 2013 that he responded by saying: 'I replied to my parents, through solicitors, and said we did not want them to have contact with Millie.'

Carol Hatton wipes a tear from her eye while reading a statement at her home after Ricky's death

Ricky had survived previous suicide attempts before he died in September last year

'We have never stopped them seeing her, as far as I was concerned they had just not been ******.

'I know that sounds harsh and I am sure they see it differently, but it is how I feel.'

He added that the situation 'was a mess', describing the family feud as 'bitter and horrible', referring to back-and-forth letters between his and his parents' lawyers.

This culminated in his father attacking him in a car park fist fight.

Angry about 'all that stuff you've written about your mum in that solicitor's letter', Ray then punched his boxing champion son in the face before Ricky hit back and his father then drove off.

But Ricky's parents are still struggling to come to terms with his death and Carol said the couple 'have to move forward' but will continue 'remembering him and loving him'.

Carol and Ray have now called for a statue of Ricky to be erected in Manchester, saying it would be a 'fitting tribute' to their son who 'brought a lot of pride' to the city.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury looks set for CARDIFF - at 2am: Welsh venue set to waive curfew to take boxing's biggest fight away from Wembley and New York
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury looks set for CARDIFF - at 2am: Welsh venue set to waive curfew to take boxing's biggest fight away from Wembley and New York

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Cardiff's Principality Stadium now looks set to be the unlikely winner of the venue war for boxing's biggest fight - by hosting Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury in the early hours of the morning.

The local authorities could today approve lifting the stadium's 10.30pm curfew to host the fight - stepping in after rows over holding it at Wembley Stadium or Madison Square Garden in New York.

Cardiff has history of hosting late-night boxing. Joe Calzaghe fought Mikkel Kessler at the Principality in 2007 at 2am. Fury and Joshua could fight at a similar time to satisfy broadcaster Netflix's huge audience in the United States.

Netflix had wanted the fight in New York to suit their prime timezones, while Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn pitched Wembley to host under the guise that Britain's biggest fight of the century should be hosted in the UK - and he has refused to budge unless contracts are rewritten with upgraded financial offerings.

Cardiff now appears to be the compromise. The Principality Stadium has an 80,000 capacity and a retractable roof - unlike Wembley - which could be useful in late November or December. A date of Saturday, November 28 has been mooted.

The Times report a press conference is tentatively scheduled for next week pending the approval.

Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua could now be set to fight in Cardiff, Wales in November

Joshua and his camp wanted the fight in the UK - while broadcasters Netflix wanted a US host

Wembley looked an ideal venue for the fight but the strict 11pm curfew has been a sticking point, despite London mayor Sadiq Khan saying he wanted to ensure allowances were made to host the fight.

Boxing dealmaker Turki Al-Sheikh has been insistent on a start time of 2am.

Netflix have been running s for Fury-Joshua as recently as Thursday night, clearly confident an agreement will be struck.

The streaming giant has yet to sign off on Cardiff but American sportswriter Dan Rafael last night reported he had asked Netflix if they would approve, with a source telling him: 'I think they're OK.'

A spokesperson for the Welsh Rugby Union said: 'We'd be delighted to host this fight.

'We are very keen to attract more boxing to the stadium, which has a rich history in the sport, enhanced by its closable roof, unrivalled sight lines and unique city-centre location.'

Joe Calzaghe trains at the Principality Stadium before his 2am fight there in 2007

Joshua has fought in Cardiff twice previously, beating Carlos Takam and Joseph Parker in the Welsh capital in 2017 and 2018.

While Joshua has left Hearn to do the talking on his side of the deal, Fury has been publicly speaking and threatening that the heavyweight contest will be called off.

This week he suggested he will no longer be fighting Joshua in another social media rant as rows over the location and contract surrounding the fight continued.

'So it looks like AJ has s*** his pants yet again,' Fury said on social media on Sunday. 'After 11 years, he's finally s*** his pants yet again.'

Last week, Fury, who regularly takes to social media to express his views on potential opponents, was keen to make clear he feels Joshua is not motivated by a love of his country. Earlier this year Daily Mail Sport revealed Joshua had in fact quit the UK to move to Dubai – even as thousands tried to flee amid rising panic in the Middle East warzone.

And Fury, a tax exile to the Isle of Man himself, brought up a 2020 speech at a Black Lives Matter march, where Joshua read out a letter from his friend Reece Campbell to urge attendees to stop spending money with white-owned shops and businesses.

'Show them where it hurts', Joshua had said. 'Abstain from spending your money in their shops and economies, and invest in black-owned businesses.'

Fury re-posted the video of the speech, writing: 'This is the man who loves England, absolute s*** bag! Total piece of s*** bully with zero guts! Don't let them deceive you! & Living in Dubai.'

Provided Cardiff hits no further stumbling blocks, the Welsh capital may now offer the solution to get the fight on at last.

Sports.title: Conor Benn hits out at 'spoiled brat' Ryan Garcia ahead of Las Vegas world title showdown - as Brit dismisses concerns over huge weight cut on eve of clash with 'insecure' rival
Sports.content:
Conor Benn knows there is a sizeable question hanging over him before he even gets into the ring with Ryan Garcia this weekend: can he still make 147lb?

Benn has not fought at welterweight for more than four years, having moved up through the divisions before competing at middleweight during his two-fight rivalry with Chris Eubank Jr.

Now, for the biggest fight of his career, taking on Garcia for the World Boxing Council (WBC) title under the bright lights in Las Vegas, he has to come all the way back down.

'I can't wait. It's going to be hard,' Benn told Daily Mail Sport during camp. 'I know it's going to be hard, but I believe I can do it.

'I think a lot of people are banking on the weight being an issue and me not having made 147 for four years. Ultimately, my discipline will prevail, and I'll continue to show why I can do what people say I can't do.'

Whether the weight cut affects Benn's strength and power on Saturday night will be one of the central questions of his WBC world title fight.

Conor Benn works out at the MGM Grand in Las Vegas ahead of his showdown with Garcia

Garcia has suggested Benn's move back down could leave him vulnerable, but Benn is dismissive of that concern.

'You think I've been up at middleweight, mixed it with someone who's competed at super middleweight? You think I'm worried about what a lightweight can do to me?' he said.

'You think I'm concerned in the slightest about this guy? I'm not concerned about one little thing he brings to the table… that silly left hook of his is useless. He can bring whatever he wants. It don't concern me.'

Benn's unusual route to this fight has been shaped by his rivalry with Eubank.

Their first meeting at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in April 2025 was the culmination of years of animosity between the two families, with Benn and Eubank Jr inheriting a rivalry that began with their fathers in 1990.

The fight itself was fought at a catchweight above 160lb, with Benn stepping up significantly from his previous division. Eubank won a close decision, leaving Benn to reflect on a performance in which he felt the occasion and the emotion had affected him.

Benn and father Nigel at the Mandalay Bay in Vegas - this is Benn's second fight since he renewed the family feud with the Eubanks

Seven months later, the pair met again at the same venue. This time Benn won the decision, dropping Eubank twice in the final round in a dramatic conclusion to their second fight. It left them level at one victory apiece and appeared to finally close the door on one of British boxing's most talked-about rivalries.

Benn insisted the atmosphere this week is nothing like those two nights when asked whether his hatred for Garcia compared.

'This is nothing like the Eubank fight,' he said. 'The Eubank fight, there was nothing pleasant or friendly or fake about the Eubank fight. There was a lot more raw emotion in that fight and I let that get the better of me the first time. That won't happen here.'

Garcia has been happy to trade insults with his British opponent, but Benn clearly has little time for his opponent's personality.

'He just carries on like a spoiled brat, like a big child who throws his toys out of the pram,' Benn said. 'I'm not worried about him in the slightest. If anything, I'm gonna have a bit of fun with him. He's a little bit sensitive, highly emotional, and a little bit insecure.'

There is also an uncomfortable shared history between the two men when it comes to drugs testing.

Benn's original 2022 fight with Eubank was cancelled after he returned two adverse findings for clomifene, something he has consistently denied intentionally taking. Garcia subsequently returned an adverse finding for ostarine following his 2024 victory over Devin Haney, which he also denied intentionally taking.

Both men were asked at the fight's press conference whether they had concerns that the other could use performance-enhancing drugs ahead of Saturday's contest.

Neither appeared keen to make it a central issue, with the focus instead returning to the fight itself.

Ryan Garcia, Benn's opponent, has also had controversy in his career over positive drug tests

Garcia has also questioned whether Benn's career has prepared him for this level of opposition, arguing that the Briton is taking a step too far by challenging for the world title.

JEFF POWELL IN LAS VEGAS An advance guard of a couple of hundred UK fight fans arrived here in time to see Conor Benn stage a public work-out three days before he challenges Ryan Garcia for the world welterweight title in the intimidating T-Mobile Arena. They kicked up a din as Benn went through a few minutes of snappy pad work in a temporary ring pitched between a bar waiting to serve them and the MGM Grand Casino’s sports book. While admitting he can’t wait to wolf down fish and chips after all the dieting to make the 147lbs welter limit he assured them: ‘I feel great and I’ll give my all to give you all a night to remember.’ But he refrained from removing his top to give them a glimpse of his body. Both he and Garcia looked sharp and calm in their brief appearances. The Benn faithful will be heavily outnumbered on Saturday night by the Americans and Mexicans rooting for King Ry but they are in good voice.

Benn's response was typically blunt. 'How is this too far? He quit against Tank Davis. He got outclassed by Rolly [Romero], and then got a world title shot with Barrios,' he said.

'Then there is me. Stepping up to fight the contenders up at middleweight, fight of the year up at middleweight, avenging my loss. Two big stadium shows. Just come off beating a two-time former world champion and having to make 147, which again I ain't made in four years in six weeks.

'What's he talking about? Ultimately, who cares what he thinks? I don't listen to quitters anyway.'

For all the talk, though, the immediate challenge is the scales. Benn has to get himself back down to a weight he has not made since 2022, before attempting to deal with one of boxing's fastest and most dangerous punchers.

He accepts it will not be straightforward, but he remains convinced the doubts surrounding him will only add to his motivation.

'If I'd listened to everyone that didn't believe in me, I'd be nowhere,' he said. 'But I continue to believe in me. And that's all that matters… you believing in yourself. I believe in me to get me to where I am right now, to revenge that loss against Eubank, to put on Fight of the Year against Eubank, to then fight for the WBC world title.

'I don't need nobody else to believe in me. Continue to doubt me because doubt fuels the fire.'

Sports.title: Tyson Fury claims Anthony Joshua fight is OFF in another social media rant: Gypsy King accuses AJ of 's***ing his pants' in talks over Battle of Britain deal
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury has suggested he will no longer be fighting Anthony Joshua in another social media rant as rows over the location and contract surrounding the fight continue.

The two British heavyweights had seemed set to finally face off later this year, but Fury had suggested his rival was stalling over the contractual agreements.

Joshua's promoter, Eddie Hearn, claimed last week that talks had 're-opened' – but things, if Fury is to be believed, seem to have again gone backwards.

'So it looks like AJ has s*** his pants yet again,' Fury said on social media on Sunday. 'After 11 years, he's finally s*** his pants yet again.'

The bitter tug-of-war over their heavyweight superfight has largely centered on a debate around hosting it at London's Wembley Stadium or broadcaster Netflix's choice of Madison Square Garden in New York City.

Last week, Fury, who regularly takes to social media to express his views on potential opponents, was keen to make clear he feels Joshua is not motivated by a love of his country. Earlier this year Daily Mail Sport revealed Joshua had in fact quit the UK to move to Dubai – even as thousands tried to flee amid rising panic in the Middle East warzone.

Tyson Fury (pictured) has claimed Anthony Joshua has bailed on their potential fight

Joshua (pictured) is still yet to sign the deal to fight Tyson Fury, Frank Warren has revealed, with a deadline for Sunday

And Fury, a tax exile to the Isle of Man himself, brought up a 2020 speech at a Black Lives Matter march, where Joshua read out a letter from his friend Reece Campbell to urge attendees to stop spending money with white-owned shops and businesses.

'Show them where it hurts', Joshua had said. 'Abstain from spending your money in their shops and economies, and invest in black-owned businesses.'

Fury re-posted the video of the speech, writing: 'This is the man who loves England, absolute s*** bag! Total piece of s*** bully with zero guts! Don't let them deceive you! & Living in Dubai.'

In an address to camera, Fury accused Joshua of trying to derail their fight to avoid being embarrassed: 'If I agreed to tie both hands behind my back and wear solid cement boots, Anthony Joshua would never get in the ring with me because I'll annihilate him.

'And he's a piece of s*** bully, and that's his game—bullying people like he tried to do to Daniel Dubois, and he got knocked spark dead out.

'The latest news from them is, 'Tyson don't want to fight in England'. Why the f*** wouldn't I want to fight in England, you sausage? 'Tyson only wants to fight in America'. Are you joking or what?

'Tyson is not in charge of this fight. Tyson didn't put the money up for this fight. Tyson is not the paymaster. Netflix are and Turki Al-Sheikh. Lovely. If it's in England, even better. I'll knock the motherf***er out even quicker. Prime time England, 10 o'clock, Wembley Stadium, 100,000 people. Why the f*** wouldn't I want it in England? Doesn't make any sense, does it?

'Like I said, who do you think you are? You and your little pathetic puppet Eddie Hearn trying to save you. There's no escaping, you know. I'll come to Watford (Joshua's hometown) and I'll set about you. I'll batter you in your own front garden, you piece of s***.'

Joshua's 2020 Black Lives Matter speech was brought back up by his great boxing rival Fury

'There is no getting out of this one. There is no getting out of this one. Get ready for this fight. I've had enough of your sauce to last me 11 years. I'm battering the f*** out of you, you useless dosser, piece of s***. That's what you are. And you know it as well, and everybody else knows what you are: a coward.'

Roaring out his title of the 'Gypsy King,' Fury added: 'You's are going down, and the cash cow is getting knocked out. Because after this, he won't be able to show his face in public ever again.

'You're a useless dosser, a big bodybuilding piece of s***. Too many weights, not enough speed. When I crack a big right hook off it, you'll go over like spaghetti legs Deontay Wilder. But he's 10 times the man you'll ever be, because he's got a pair of b*****ks like King Kong, and you've got a pair of b*****ks like two f***ing garden peas, you piece of s***.'

On Sunday, Fury revealed he has turned his attention to trying to fight Oleksandr Usyk for a third time – on the back of two defeats.

'So this would only lead me to a fight with Oleksandr Usyk,' he said. 'Let's do it again. Let's run it back in November. The ball is now in your court, Oleksandr.'

He added: 'Do you want to fight me this year, 2026, or are you calling it quits? Let me know, because I'm now looking for a new opponent.'

Fury's promoter Frank Warren, who suggested that in reality boxing's longest hatching deal had to be finalised by Sunday, told Daily Mail Sport last week: 'AJ hasn't signed yet.

'Tyson signed in January. He's training in Miami for the fight in early November and doesn't care where it takes place.'

There is debate around the contract and location of the fight, with Fury supposedly agreeing the match-up earlier this year

The original agreement stipulated England, putting Wembley Stadium on alert.

But Netflix, the mega-paymasters for the broadcast, have joined their Saudi partners in insisting on New York's fabled Madison Square Garden so as to maximise US revenue.

Joshua will need at least a two-month training camp for a fight of this magnitude and ideally nine to ten weeks.

It comes after Joshua was given ten days to agree a deal on August 26 with Warren previously warning: 'Unless AJ commits by the end of next week I'm afraid this will slip away like so many of those great fights which never happened.'

He added: 'At some point everyone has to say the most important thing is that it happens. Not this bulls*** about money.

'That everyone wants the fight. Does AJ really want it? I don't know. He's been through that tragedy of the car crash which killed two of his closest friends. Only he knows what he wants.'

Much of the discussions around Wembley centre on a willingness to allow a late start time – and late curfew – to suit the American TV market. Mayor Sadiq Khan this week stated that he is keen to host the fight and find a solution.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua's conqueror Andy Ruiz is PUMMELLED with punches and brutally beaten on his return to the ring after two years - but incredibly insists he WILL keep fighting
Sports.content:
Andy Ruiz, the man who condemned Anthony Joshua to his first ever professional defeat, suffered a horrific loss of his own on Friday night.

The 36-year-old Mexican was left bruised and bloodied as he lost to Poland's Damian Knyba on his return to the ring after two years out.

Knyba unleashed heavy punch after punch in the seventh round but Ruiz managed to ride it out, after being saved by the bell, to lose by a unanimous points decision.

Ruiz, who is now signed to British promoter Eddie Hearn, vowed to carry on despite losing his comeback fight to Knyba. The Pole now has a record of 18 wins and one defeat.

Rewind to June 2019, and Ruiz shocked the boxing world by upsetting the odds to knock Joshua out in the seventh round at Madison Square Garden.

Ruiz was a late stand-in for Jarrell Miller, who had failed a drugs test, and wasn't seen as a threat to Joshua's chances of remaining unbeaten and hanging on to his then IBF, WBO and WBA world heavyweight titles.

ANDY RUIZ IS SAVED BY THE BELL 🤯🤯🤯#TheFight | #RuizKnyba | Live NOW on DAZN and TNT ▪️ pic.twitter.com/JVQjG3KQM3 — DAZN Boxing (@DAZNBoxing) September 5, 2026

Andy Ruiz kneels down in front of the referee after being on the receiving end of heavy blows

Ruiz feels the full force of Poland's Damian Knyba during Friday's fight in New Jersey

Ruiz famously defeated the then undefeated Anthony Joshua back in June 2019

Joshua exacted revenge six months later and Ruiz has gone on to have just four more fights since due to injury problems, beating Chris Arreola and Luis Ortiz before drawing with Miller and now suffering his third loss.

Ruiz said after Friday's defeat in New Jersey: 'It was just a long layoff, and it was a great opponent.

'I didn't want to take an easy fight, so that's why I took Damian. He's a big guy. But we've got to take risks. I've still got it in me, man. I've just got to stay active and I want to fight again.

'Every time I tried to come in, he'd hold me really tight, and I just couldn't let my combinations go.

'He played a good game plan, but I'd love to run it back and do things a lot different.'

The judges scored the fight 117-110, 114-113 and 114-113 in Knyba's favour.

It wasn't the night Hearn was hoping for after signing Ruiz this summer but much of his current focus is on trying to finalise Joshua's highly anticipated fight against British rival Tyson Fury.

The bout has been proposed to take place in November after years of negotiations but the location of the fight appears to be a major sticking point.

Hearn and Joshua are said to want the fight to take place at Wembley Stadium in London while the Fury camp are reportedly leaning towards Madison Square Garden in New York City.

Sports.title: F1 drivers criticise Madrid circuit, Verstappen laughs: "I'll sort it out"
Sports.content:
While the Formula 2 and Formula 3 races around the IFEMA complex in Madrid have produced several crashes, the chaos in Formula 1 has so far remained limited.

Nevertheless, criticism from the drivers emerged after qualifying in the Spanish capital.

Over a single flying lap, the circuit is considered entertaining – although polesitter Lando Norris said the thrill certainly cannot be compared with Monaco – but the race promises to be considerably more problematic.

"I still need to figure out a corner where to pass," Max Verstappen said straight away at the start of the press conference.

"They did a good job with the tarmac, even though in some places it's already a bit too bumpy for a new track. But the corners, like I said before, you can't overtake.

"For the braking zones, they need to learn that it should never be that you have to steer and combine that under braking. It doesn't allow any kind of overtaking. So, in terms of track design, I think it can be better. I also think that input from the drivers on track designs can help a lot in the future."

After the press conference, it was time for Verstappen's session with the Dutch media in the paddock, which coincided with the start of the F3 sprint race. The four-time world champion and the reporters watch the start together, after which Verstappen turns his attention to the gathered media.

"Well, now we can stop watching, now everyone is just following each other," he said, again referring to the lack of overtaking opportunities. Not much later, a crash follows, but that is beside the point.

Verstappen believes that the braking zones have been wrongly designed, making it virtually impossible to bring the car to a stop alongside them Photo by: Steven Tee / LAT Images via Getty Images

The Red Bull driver stresses that it is not only the corners, but also the braking zones that have been designed incorrectly at the latest addition to the F1 calendar. If the braking was done in a straight line, there would be an opportunity to put a car alongside. But because many of the braking zones at the Madring require drivers to brake while turning in, that option disappears.

"Then there is only one line and that makes it very easy to defend as well," Verstappen clarified when asked by Autosport about the braking zones.

Asked what exactly needs to be changed to improve the racing, the Dutchman laughs: "Almost all the braking zones! If you give me the track map, I'll sort it out."

On a more serious note, Verstappen adds that he would indeed be willing to do that: provide his input and work together with the FIA and the track designers to see what could be improved.

"They can always ask me, ‘What do you think of this layout?’ I don't want to go into details now, because you have different track designers, but sometimes I do talk to someone about certain opinions and circuits. Ultimately, a driver knows very well what is needed or what a good corner should look like."

"There are also some good examples, like Austin. You can race well there. Certain corners are nice and wide. At least you can make a move there, and even if it doesn't work straight away, you can still fight on the corner exit. There are enough examples of how to do it properly."

Like Norris, Verstappen also believes that the pitlane in Madrid is way too long Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

According to Verstappen, the drivers were not asked for input on the new Madring beforehand, adding that this rarely happens anyway.

"In Jeddah, we were able to change a few things, but you should really do that beforehand, before the track is built."

Aside from the layout, there is another sticking point in Madrid: the particularly long pitlane. It is effectively split into two sections, as the pit boxes are interrupted by an IFEMA exhibition hall. Norris had already criticised this during the press conference, and Verstappen agreed with him.

"Yeah, we've already talked about that with the FIA and they understood our point as well. It's not convenient, it hasn't been thought through logically," Verstappen said.

It seems a missed opportunity, especially because tyre degradation has been very high so far. This would normally lead to additional pitstops, but because of the long pitlane and the importance of track position, teams are likely to try to minimise the number of pitstops on Sunday.

Verstappen wanted to take the banked corner flat out, but says that energy management prevents him from doing so Photo by: Alex Bierens de Haan / LAT Images via Getty Images

Charging the battery causes frustration for Verstappen in Madrid

Taken together, all these factors do not exactly promise an exciting race – aside from any potential chaos and crashes. The drivers enjoyed qualifying more, although Verstappen stresses that the shortcomings of the 2026 power units have once again come to the surface in Madrid.

"Considering the circumstances and what these cars are like, this qualifying was reasonably OK. It's just that I want to take that banked corner flat-out, but if I do that, then I lose more time on the straight afterwards.

"That means you have to come off the throttle, wait a little bit to charge the battery and then you have more top speed later. All those kinds of things. The same in Turns 18 and 19. You have to lift there as well, because if you stay flat-out, then you don't have any battery left afterwards."

All of these things combined mean Verstappen has not exactly enjoyed the Madring to the fullest so far, although he does see potential for the coming years.

"If they can maybe change the circuit in a few places, then definitely. Look, I'm never really a fan of street circuits, but there are worse ones on the calendar."

Sports.title: F1 Spanish GP: Norris snatches last-gasp pole from Antonelli
Sports.content:
Formula 1’s reigning world champion Lando Norris has claimed his third pole position of the 2026 season at the Spanish Grand Prix, beating series leader Kimi Antonelli at the debutant Madring circuit.

With a last-ditch effort Norris took a mere 0.011s out of Antonelli's benchmark to hand Mercedes its fourth consecutive qualifying defeat.

It was F1's first-ever qualifying session on the brand-new Madring circuit on the outskirts of Spanish capital Madrid, a challenging 5.4km circuit featuring a mixture of street sections and a high-speed purpose-built loop with little runoff areas.

But despite worries qualifying would be derailed by accidents and traffic woes, the session took place without noteworthy hiccups.

In the deciding Q3 shootout, Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton led the way after the first barrage of runs with a 1m32.079s lap, ahead of Mercedes duo Antonelli and George Russell, and his team-mate Charles Leclerc.

Red Bull had also shown flashes of competitiveness throughout qualifying, with Max Verstappen another contender for pole, but the Dutchman slipped up at the end of his first flyer and settled for fifth ahead of the two McLarens.

Heading out first of the contenders for the final runs, Antonelli took over top spot from Hamilton with a 1m31.835s effort, which most of his rivals didn't have an answer for.

But Norris did, drifting out of the final corner to set a 1m31.824s pole lap. Verstappen was third on a surprisingly competitive outing for Red Bull after the team had struggled earlier in the weekend, with Ferrari duo Hamilton and Charles Leclerc in fourth and fifth.

In the second Mercedes, Russell could only manage sixth followed by Oscar Piastri. Liam Lawson, Franco Colapinto and Arvid Lindblad completed the top 10,

Q2

Pierre Gasly, Alpine Photo by: Steven Tee / LAT Images via Getty Images

The first set of Q2 runs saw Nico Hulkenberg and Arvid Lindblad take a provisional Q3 spot in F1's midfield, leaving their respective team-mates Gabriel Bortoleto and Yuki Tsunoda on the bubble.

Both Alpines of Pierre Gasly and Franco Colapinto also came under pressure after not being able to complete their first flyer, with the latter surviving a huge scare as the back-end of his Alpine stepped out through the spectacularly fast La Monumental banking.

Colapinto gathered himself to execute a solid final lap that netted the Argentinian a Q3 berth in eighth, ahead of McLaren's Piastri.

Verstappen topped the session from Antonelli, Lindblad was the other midfield car to make it through at the expense of the two Audis - Hulkenberg 11th and Bortoleto in 12th.

Esteban Ocon qualified 13th for Haas, while a frustrated Gasly could only manage 14th after lamenting a radically different car balance compared to FP3.

Tsunoda and Albon followed in 15th and 16th.

Q1

Carlos Sainz, Williams Photo by: Alex Bierens de Haan / LAT Images via Getty Images

Russell led the way in Q1, pipping team-mate Antonelli at the end of the session by 0.056s as he survived a tap with the wall unscathed.

Red Bull looked particularly competitive, with Lawson a close third on softs and Verstappen fourth on the medium tyres, allowing the Dutchman to save a set of softs for later on. Ferrari drivers Hamilton and Leclerc followed the same strategy as they claimed a top seven spot.

It was business as usual at the bottom of the timesheets, with Williams once again on the cusp of a Q2 spot. Albon beat team-mate and crowd favourite Carlos Sainz by a mere 0.005s to grab the final Q2 ticket in 16th, the Anglo-Thai driver bouncing back from a tap with the wall in FP3 which forced him to sit out the majority of the session.

Sainz was still the highest-placed Spaniard, though, as there was little improvement for Aston Martin with Fernando Alonso qualifying in 18th. Cadillac's Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas finished at the bottom of the 20 cars setting a lap time, with Bottas unable to complete a clean lap after being impeded by Sainz.

Qualifying got underway without Haas driver Oliver Bearman. A "gutted" Bearman suffered a heavy crash at the end of Saturday's delayed third practice session, as Haas faced an impossible battle to restore the Briton's car in time for qualifying.

Lance Stroll was the other driver not to set a lap time on the Madring circuit due to what Aston Martin called a suspected water pressure issue. The Canadian is set for a back-of-the-grid penalty anyway for exceeding his Honda power unit allowance for the season.

Sports.title: F1 Spanish GP: Antonelli tops FP3 after Hamilton and Bearman cause red flags
Sports.content:
Formula 1 championship leader Kimi Antonelli will head into qualifying at the Spanish Grand Prix’s challenging Madring circuit with the fastest time - following a final practice session marred by two crashes.

The Mercedes driver fended off advances by Ferrari's Charles Leclerc to reclaim top spot after a lengthy stoppage during the middle of the practice session in Madrid.

FP3 was halted after 23 minutes when Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton locked up his front tyres into Turn 22, the final corner, bumping straight into the wall and dislocating his front wing.

Hamilton's tap with the TecPro wall would have been relatively innocuous if he hadn't just passed pit entry, and thus had to try and complete a full lap of the circuit on three wheels as his wing dragged on the ground and started piercing the front-right tyre.

Contrary to his team's instructions, the seven-time world champion attempted to make it round under the red flag until he had to abandon his effort midway through at the exit of Turn 14.

The barrier repairs that followed took so long that race control decided to stop the clock at 15m38s, ensuring that there would still be a reasonable amount of time left for drivers to resume practice.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

At that stage, Hamilton's team-mate Leclerc had the fastest time to his name, a 1m33.332s that beat Antonelli's earlier benchmark of 1m33.664s, while Hamilton was fourth behind McLaren’s Lando Norris.

After an extended delay of nearly 40 minutes as track workers realigned the barriers, action got under way for a last chance to fine tune cars set-ups ahead of qualifying.

Leclerc was the first frontrunner to embark on a hot lap, lowering his own benchmark to a 1m32.963s. That was initially faster than what Mercedes had in the tank, with Antonelli conceding three tenths, narrowly ahead of Lando Norris’ team-mate Oscar Piastri.

But on his second attempt Antonelli found a chunk of lap time to take over the lead with a 1m32.797s effort. Antonelli's time didn't come under threat, due to a late second red flag period for a crash by Haas driver Oliver Bearman.

In the final minute, Bearman lost the rear of his car into the Turn 10 right-hander, smacking into the concrete wall and sustaining significant damage to his car's left-hand side. Bearman's crash into the concrete effectively cemented Antonelli's lead ahead of Leclerc.

After having been farther adrift on Friday, McLaren appeared to have taken a tentative step forward as Piastri and Norris sealed third and fourth, just two tenths behind Antonelli.

Oliver Bearman, Haas Photo by: Steven Tee / LAT Images via Getty Images

Max Verstappen made a delayed start after only joining the action right before Hamilton's red flag. The Dutchman was fifth, 0.375s behind, as Red Bull continued to struggle over the Madring circuit's kerbs and generally lacked performance compared to its rivals.

Russell, who had to abort his pre-red flag flyer that yielded the fastest first sector time, didn't piece together a representative lap after the stoppage either and only managed sixth, followed by the second Red Bull of Liam Lawson who made a mistake on his final flyer.

Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg was eighth after surprisingly setting the fastest first sector, only to be blocked by traffic later on in the lap.

Hamilton dropped down to ninth by the end, with Hulkenberg's team-mate Gabriel Bortoleto rounding out the top 10.

The session ended early for Williams man Alex Albon, who tapped the wall at the start and disappeared into the garage for suspension repairs.

Sports.title: From "very high risk" to the "best race in Europe" - F1 drivers share first Madring impressions
Sports.content:
The Spanish Grand Prix's Madring circuit has received a thumbs-up from several leading Formula 1 drivers as they praised its high-commitment layout, although not everyone is as impressed.

Having sampled the 5.4km circuit on the simulator, drivers were bracing for one of the most challenging weekends of the year on a track that combines the unforgiving nature of a street circuit with plenty of medium to high-speed corners. But nothing beats the real thing, and following two one-hour practice sessions, in which drivers clearly took extra caution not to be caught out by the lack of runoff areas, the first verdicts are in on F1's newest venue.

"Honestly, it's more difficult than some tracks," said Oscar Piastri, who ended the day in fifth as McLaren struggled for performance compared to its rivals. "There's a lot of sections here where you're not really brushing up against the walls, you're kind of turning or heading at them and then you need to avoid them. So, it makes things quite challenging. Everyone is still getting up to speed, but when you get into a decent rhythm over one lap, it's pretty enjoyable."



Other than an FP2 crash for rapid Arvid Lindblad in the Racing Bulls, the day's F1 running was completed without major issues. The circuit's combined braking zones caused plenty of headaches as driver were careful to avoid lock-ups, while tyre wear, the rapidly changing grip levels and traffic proved to be some of the biggest headaches.

Ferrari's Charles Leclerc said: "It was exciting to drive on the Madrid circuit today. It’s a challenging street track, which is the type I usually enjoy and this one is no exception. I was quite impressed with the amount of grip there already was, considering that this is a completely new track with not much rubber on it so far."

Sergio Perez, Cadillac Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

As team-mate Kimi Antonelli topped the timesheets, George Russell's practice day reaffirmed his thoughts that the Madring was a "very high risk circuit", though he worried overtaking would be "very tough", a sentiment shared throughout the paddock.

The biggest positive noises came from Madrid resident Sergio Perez, who didn't have much to write home about regarding the performance of his Cadillac machine, but was effusive about the Madring both on and off the track. "Yeah, really cool track, really nice venue," the Mexican said. "Really happy to be here in Madrid. I think definitely this is going to become the best race in Europe.



"It's going to be a chaotic qualifying tomorrow and obviously a very chaotic race on Sunday, so a lot can happen. I'm really looking forward to it and as a team we just have to make sure we are able to execute a perfect weekend."

Not everyone is as enthused as Perez, though. Max Verstappen has never been the biggest admirer of street circuits, and what Madring has to offer hasn't swayed his opinion.

"Yeah, I don't know. I'm not a fan of street circuits so that will never never change," the four-time world champion said. "I will always prefer to drive on a track like Spa. I mean, what they have done in the way they have built everything up, I think they've done a really good job. But I'm not a fan of street circuits."

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin Racing Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

While the Madring isn't particularly tough on F1 2026's energy-starved power units, what is throwing things off kilter for both drivers and teams is the impact of the rapidly evolving track evolution on how their energy deployment works. That was especially difficult fro Fernando Alonso in the Honda-powered Aston Martin, who recovered from a clutch problem to complete the second half of FP2.

"It's going to be always tricky to get it right with the tyre temperature, battery state of charge at the end of the lap," the Spaniard said. "Sometimes if you do different a driving style in the last few corners, it seems that we are very sensitive to that with the Honda power unit."

Sports.title: F1 Spanish GP: Antonelli leads tricky second practice as Lindblad crashes
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli has topped second practice at Formula 1's Spanish Grand Prix, pipping Ferrari's Charles Leclerc on Friday afternoon at the new Madring circuit, while Arvid Lindblad crashed.

Antonelli set the fastest lap around the halfway mark in the second one-hour session as drivers and teams kept chipping away at their set-ups on the extremely difficult circuit in Madrid.

The 5.4km track, a hybrid of street portions and a purpose-built loop featuring several high-speed corners, proved tricky to tame from the outset. And with runoff virtually non-existent, teams made a conservative start to the weekend in first practice, sacrificing optimal lap time as drivers settled into a rhythm and built-up muscle memory.

Some of those training wheels started to come off in FP2, although lap times didn't take as much as a tumble as first thought, despite the improving grip levels.

Championship leader Antonelli led the early running on medium tyres with a 1m34.428s effort, which was soon beaten by Red Bull's Max Verstappen as drivers visibly had their hands full both keeping their cars out of the walls and finding clear air through the narrow, concrete-lined roads.

Turn 17's right-hander proved particularly tricky as several drivers went wide on exit, triggering track limit offences.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari Photo by: Alex Bierens de Haan / LAT Images via Getty Images

Antonelli soon reclaimed the lead with a 1m33.926s lap, with FP1 leading team-mate George Russell within a tenth.

The session went into overdrive at the halfway mark as the majority of drivers switched to the fastest soft-tyre compound, which is proving a handful to keep within optimal temperature ranges as the constant lateral loads are working Pirelli's rubber extremely hard.

Antonelli set the tone once more, stopping the clock after 1m33.662s to go top. Russell didn't immediately find an answer, with Ferrari duo Lewis Hamilton and Leclerc slotting into second and third, and Racing Bull's Lindblad an eye-catching fourth.

But shortly after, Lindblad's day came to a screeching halt as he slid into the barriers in Turn 13, a medium-speed left-hander. Lindblad escaped unharmed as the session was red-flagged with 25 minutes to go, with track marshals rushing to undo the British rookie's TecPro barrier realignment.

Partly due to the interruption, there were no further moves at the top, confirming Antonelli's lead ahead of Ferrari duo Leclerc and Hamilton. Behind fourth-placed Lindblad, Russell and Verstappen were fifth and sixth respectively, with Oscar Piastri first of the McLarens in seventh after a difficult day for the reigning world champions.

Piastri's team-mate, world champion Lando Norris, disappeared into the garage after just two laps with a transmission issue, forcing McLaren to change his gearbox.

Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

Yuki Tsunoda, who makes his third appearance of the season as Isack Hadjar continues to recover from his wrist injury, was eighth in the Racing Bulls car, with Haas driver Esteban Ocon and Red Bull's Liam Lawson completing the top 10.

As expected, it was a quiet start for crowd favourites Carlos Sainz and Fernando Alonso, finishing 16th and 17th respectively. Alonso faced a delayed start to the session as Aston Martin repaired a clutch issue.

Sports.title: Why Leclerc isn't using latest Ferrari ADUO2 engine in the Spanish GP
Sports.content:
Charles Leclerc is still feeling the pain of smiting the wall at the exit of the Parabolica in last weekend's Italian Grand Prix, and the result of the crash is that he will not be able to use Ferrari's latest Formula 1 engine spec during the Spanish GP.

It's understood Ferrari engineers deemed the 067/6 unit, fitted with the second package of modifications permitted by the FIA, to be sound, but they did not want to take the risk of running it at the Madring.

The reason is very simple: F1 regulations prohibit running an engine that cannot be worked on in all of its many homologated components. No cracks or breakages were found during the external structural checks, but the intention is to carry out more thorough X-ray examinations to determine whether there are any small areas of damage that may have gone undetected.

The decision not to risk the ADUO2 engine in the Spanish capital is therefore a logical one: the Madring circuit is new and the drivers need to run for as long as possible, while the engineers need to gather data in order to finalise a set-up that will have to be a significant compromise to combine the demands of very slow sections with those of the fast ones.

The Iberian capital, incidentally, is located 667 metres above sea level, an altitude similar to that of the Red Bull Ring in Austria. So the more substantial turbo compressor fitted as part of the ADUO2 package could have provided a performance gain in the slightly thinner air.

Any small issues with the power unit during Friday practice could have risked compromising the preparation for the GP, hence the decision to postpone the return of the engine under observation until FP1 in Baku.

Leclerc's car was badly damaged by Monza crash and the engine's structure is still being thoroughly checked

Leclerc, therefore, will have an ADUO1 engine at his disposal, while the trackside staff will be able to assess the actual performance difference between this unit and ADUO2, which Lewis Hamilton will be able to use as normal.

After the disappointment at Monza, Ferrari is quietly hopeful of performing well in Madrid. The track could suit the characteristics of the SF-26: a medium-to-high level of aerodynamic downforce is required, and the asphalt is not expected to provide a particularly high level of grip, which could favour those with excellent traction on corner exit.

Downforce should matter more than efficiency (we may see the additional flaps on the actuators of the movable wings reappear), and the Ferrari should be less affected by the power deficit to the Mercedes V6 because there are 22 corners and the opportunities to recharge the battery are considerably greater than at Monza.

Hamilton and Leclerc will need to focus heavily on single-lap pace, because a strong qualifying performance on a circuit where overtaking will be almost impossible could prove decisive.

If things do not go according to plan, however, it would not be out of the question for the Monegasque to put a second engine into service with ADUO2 (available in the pool), taking his first penalty for introducing a fifth power unit of the season, but ensuring that he has enough of a reserve to finish the championship without any further surprises.

Sports.title: F1 Spanish GP: Mercedes tops FP1 with Russell fastest at Madring
Sports.content:
Mercedes’ George Russell was fastest in the first-ever Formula 1 session at the brand-new Madring track – first practice for the Spanish Grand Prix.

Twenty out of 22 cars took to the brand-new track within the first 100 seconds of the session, with Nico Hulkenberg and Franco Colapinto emerging some time later.

The very first flying laps were somewhat tentative with most drivers in the 1m42s-1m45s bracket, but Lewis Hamilton, Max Verstappen and Lando Norris lapped in 1m39s straight away.

Lap times kept tumbling down in the opening part of the session, with Hamilton down to a 1m36.066s within just eight minutes. Consistently faster than anyone, the Ferrari driver successively improved the benchmark to 1m35.563s and 1m34.803s. Team-mate Charles Leclerc did go 0.120s quicker, but Hamilton narrowly snatched the top spot back in 1m34.620s.

After all drivers but Gabriel Bortoleto (on hards) spent the first half of the session on medium tyres, softs were brought into action.

However, Kimi Antonelli’s and Russell’s opening efforts – two each – on that compound fell 0.063s and 0.109s short of Hamilton’s medium-tyre reference.

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Clive Rose / Formula 1 via Getty Images

Russell’s third attempt, a 1m34.145s was good enough to go fastest, and he subsequently upgraded it to a 1m34.077s. Antonelli, in 1m34.363s, made it a Mercedes 1-2.

Meanwhile, both Leclerc and Hamilton went wide at Turn 17. The Monegasque only narrowly improved on his personal best, while his team-mate ended up as the only driver not to set his quickest lap on soft rubber – alongside Yuki Tsunoda, who was ruled out of the session with 25 minutes remaining by a power steering issue on his Racing Bulls.

Max Verstappen was fifth ahead of Lando Norris, Arvid Lindblad – who cleared the remainder of the midfield group – and Oscar Piastri.

Nico Hulkenberg, Liam Lawson, Gabriel Bortoleto, Pierre Gasly, Esteban Ocon and Franco Colapinto followed in a 1m35.5s-1m35.9s bracket.

Home hero Fernando Alonso was an encouraging 15th – by Aston Martin’s current standards – ahead of one Haas, both Williams, both Cadillacs and team-mate Lance Stroll.

The main incident of the session occurred when Lindblad, on a flying lap, came across the slow Mercedes and Ferrari of Antonelli and Hamilton in La Monumental.

Oliver Bearman, Haas F1 Team, Arvid Lindblad, Racing Bulls Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

“These same two guys, man!” the rookie ranted over team radio. “Like, I don’t know what they’re doing, they’re just stupid, right in the fast corner! It’s actually very dangerous, it’s been twice now.”

Hamilton was then involved in further impeding incidents at team-mate Leclerc’s and Hulkenberg’s expense. Carlos Sainz also complained about the way the seven-time world champion let him by in La Monumental.

Sports.title: What's behind Alonso's cryptic comments about his F1 future?
Sports.content:
Every Thursday, the media day in the paddock begins with a roundtable session with Mike Krack and Honda's chief engineer Shintaro Orihara. Besides the usual questions about power unit driveability and potential upgrades, one topic returns every race weekend: when can we expect an announcement about Fernando Alonso’s future?

Krack already said in Monza that the team is in no rush, and Alonso reinforced that message in Madrid. Asked when news about his future could be expected, he simply replied: "Not soon." The follow-up question about what exactly is causing the delay was brushed off by Alonso with a laugh: "Because I think it’s nice, no?"

On a more serious note, Alonso stresses that it mainly depends on one question: will Formula 1 be more enjoyable to drive next year?

The two-time F1 world champion has made no secret of the fact that the current regulations leave a lot to be desired. Alonso described the high-speed corners at Silverstone and Spa as "charging stations" and added that the current rules will always reward going slower through a corner so that drivers have more energy available to deploy on the straights.

The extent to which that changes for 2027 is crucial to Alonso’s decision about his future, even more so than Aston Martin’s competitive picture.

"I think it’s a matter of understanding what impact the rules for next year will have, or not, on the racing and on the driving side of things," he said.

"I think the current cars, as I said many times, are not the best cars to drive and to enjoy. But next year there is a step in the right direction, I think.

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin Racing Photo by: Alex Bierens de Haan / LAT Images via Getty Images

"But at the same time, I need to think what is the best programme for next year and sit with the team: behind the wheel or in another role, where I will be helping the most. That will be the most important thing to decide together."

After a lengthy political discussion, the FIA, F1, manufacturers and teams have agreed to adjust the ratio between the internal combustion engine and electrical power in two steps towards a 60-40 split in 2028. For 2027, the ratio will be 58-42, partly achieved by looking at fuel flow.

Given that Alonso is largely linking his future to the regulations, the obvious follow-up question is how the man from Oviedo currently views the plans for 2027: can the adjustments really put the driver back at the centre of things, or does Alonso – in line with Max Verstappen – believe that the current generation of cars is simply "numb" to driver input?

"I think it’s a step in the right direction. If it’s enough… These cars will always reward to charge the batteries in the highest-speed corners and at the end of the straights, because that’s the optimal lap time," Alonso said when asked about the 2027 regulations by Autosport.

"Because of these power units, at one point in the lap you need to charge the batteries, and you will charge the batteries in the most problematic places for fun. It will be in the high-speed corners and at the end of the straights. That is against any driver input or pushing the limits of the car.

"But, in a way, I still have some hope that next year’s rules will still have to be tweaked again, that this is not the final version."

Even more important to Alonso than how competitive Aston Martin will be, is whether the rules will improve by 2027 Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

That final quote is the most cryptic, but also by far the most interesting. It immediately raises another question: is Alonso hinting at further changes before the start of the 2027 season, or during 2027 if the new product still proves not to be good enough?

When Autosport approached Alonso after the press conference in Madrid to ask him that question, he clarified that he meant the former option – in other words, that he still hopes for further changes before the start of next season.

However, when asked by Autosport, the FIA says it is currently not aware of any such plans. As things stand, no further changes are planned for the start of next season.

It cannot be ruled out, however, that all of this is part of the political game, and that by not yet committing himself for next year, Alonso can exert some pressure to try and improve the series as a whole.

For Alonso to announce relatively late in the year that he will not continue would not seem logical, as it could put Aston Martin in a difficult position – all the more so because there are not many drivers still available on the market. All the seats at the top teams are locked in, while potentially interesting options such as Carlos Sainz are now off the market as well.

It therefore seems more than logical that Alonso will add another year to his long F1 career, although there is no need to say so publicly just yet, especially if Aston Martin is already aware of his plans behind the scenes – with Krack having indicated that he is "comfortable" waiting for the public announcement.

Nevertheless, it currently does not seem particularly likely either that Alonso’s wish for further changes before the start of 2027 will be granted, however unfortunate that may be. In order to still find that enjoyment, Alonso does not rule out new ventures into other racing series – such as Dakar and WEC – most likely in combination with F1. Asked in Madrid whether that is a realistic option, the straightforward answer was: "Yes."

Sports.title: Formula 1 drivers expect passing will be difficult in first race at Madring | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Formula 1 drivers predict overtaking will be difficult in the first grand prix on the new Madring.

Fernando Alonso , who was eliminated in the first round of qualifying, said his best chance of making up places will be if other drivers retire.

“I think to see the chequered flag will be the first target tomorrow,” said the Aston Martin driver. “After that, it’s going to be tricky to overtake.

“Looking at F3, F2, it was not an easy track to overtake. But anything can happen, especially if there is chaos in front of us, we need to benefit from that.”

Yuki Tsunoda, who failed to make the cut for the top 10, predicted it will be hard to move into the points places. “It is frustrating because it’s pretty important qualifying here, seeing as the overtake chances here are pretty difficult,” he said.

Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc is also concerned the race could be processional and expects tyre degradation will dictate the outcome.

“It’s going to be a tricky one to overtake on, I think,” said the Ferrari driver. “So I think the start will play an important role and I think tyre degradation will play a very important role as well because we’ve definitely felt a lot of front damage during free practise.

“So we’ll have to see how it goes some more, if it’s much better or not. But if not, it’s going be all about tyre management. Then I don’t know how likely it is for us to overtakes, but tyre management will be a thing.”

Sports.title: Sainz penalised, Antonelli, Russell, Leclerc and Bortoleto avoid grid drops for qualifying incidents | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Carlos Sainz Jnr has been given a three-place grid drop for impeding a rival in qualifying for the Spanish Grand Prix.

However four other drivers avoided grid drop penalties for incidents in today’s qualifying session at the Madring.

The stewards issued Sainz a three-place grid drop for impeding Valtteri Bottas during Q1. Both drivers were eliminated in the first round of qualifying.

“The team failed to inform the driver of car 55 [Sainz] about car 77 [Bottas] closing in on a flying lap and the driver did not take any action to make way for the incoming car,” the stewards noted. “The stewards determine that car 55 unnecessarily impeded car 77.”

Andrea Kimi Antonelli and Gabriel Bortoleto were given official warnings for failing to comply with the maximum time limit between the two Safety Car lines. In both cases the stewards accepted “that it was difficult for him to maintain the delta due to energy management requirements.”

Charles Leclerc was also cleared of the same infringement, but his Ferrari team was given a reprimand for giving him the wrong delta time.

“The driver of car 16 [Leclerc] returned to the pits after setting his final lap time in Q3 without any other cars interfering and did not comply with the delta time requirements,” the stewards noted. “During the hearing the team representative admitted that they provided the driver with a wrong delta time profile due to a miscalculation. Therefore the driver complied with the delta displayed on his dash, but as this delta time was not correct he inadvertently breached the delta time requirements.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“The stewards determine that in this case the team is exclusively at fault and the driver did not make any mistake. Therefore a penalty to the team is imposed. The Stewards also take into account that in this scenario the deviating delta time provided to the driver did not have any performance implication for car 16 or any other car.”

George Russell was also given an official warning for failing to rejoin the track correctly after he went off at turn five.

“The driver of car 63 [Russell] left the track at turn five to make way for an incoming car,” the stewards noted, “but rejoined the track without staying to the right of the bollard in the runoff area.

“The driver stated during the hearing that he stayed to the left of the bollard to rejoin earlier because he was worrying about impeding the car behind. However, the driver admitted that he could have gone around the bollard.

“The stewards acknowledge that the driver acted in good faith, but determine that it would have been possible for him to take the prescribed route.”

Sports.title: Norris snatches first Madring pole position off Antonelli | 2026 Spanish Grand Prix qualifying report
Sports.content:
Lando Norris claimed pole position for Formula 1’s first race at the Madring in a closely-fought session.

The reigning world champion took pole off current championship leader Andrea Kimi Antonelli by just a hundredth of a second.

Lewis Hamilton held provisional pole position after the first runs in Q3. However he only gained a few hundredths of a second on his final run and fell to fourth place behind Max Verstappen’s Red Bull.

George Russell was quickest in the first round of qualifying but had to settle for sixth place behind Charles Leclerc after making a mistake in the final corner on his last run.

Oscar Piastri was almost half a second slower than his team mate in seventh place. Liam Lawson took eighth for Red Bull.

Italian Grand Prix pole-winner Pierre Gasly was bemused by the change in his car’s handling after failing to reach Q3. “I don’t get it,” he told his team after qualifying 14th, “compared to P3 it’s a completely different car.”

However his team mate Franco Colapinto did reach Q3 despite flirting with disaster at the Madring’s signature high-speed corner, Monumental. Colapinto reacted quickly to control a sudden snap of oversteer. He went on to take ninth on the grid ahead of Arvid Lindblad.

The Audi pair dropped out in 11th and 12th, Nico Hulkenberg just two-hundredths of a second off Piastri and Lindblad’s identical times. Esteban Ocon took 13th while Yuki Tsunoda failed to join Lindblad in Q3

The two home drivers, Carlos Sainz Jnr and Fernando Alonso, failed to make the cut for Q2 by less than a tenth of a second. The Racing Bulls drivers eliminated the pair of them.

Alexander Albon was the only Williams driver to reach Q2, pipping Sainz by five thousandths of a second. The two Cadillacs also dropped out in the first round.

Oliver Bearman did not take part in qualifying as Haas were unable to complete repairs to his car in time following his heavy crash at the end of final practice. Lance Stroll, who will take a grid drop penalty for a power unit parts change, did not set a time due to what his team called a “suspected water pressure issue”.

Sports.title: Ben Sulayem wants rules changes to make Alonso’s Aston Martin more competitive | Formula 1
Sports.content:
FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem says he has spoken to Fernando Alonso about improving the team’s results.

Ben Sulayem said he does not want Alonso to leave Formula 1 because his car is not competitive. The team began the season with severe reliability and performance problems relating to its Honda power unit.

“There is no way we can allow Fernando Alonso, a great champion, to leave just because of the circumstances,” said Ben Sulayem. “That’s not the way to leave the stage.”

“He has to be successful and then he leaves whenever he wants. Not because he was forced to leave because of his performance.”

The FIA president said he has held discussions with Aston Martin owner Lawrence Stroll.

“I share the issues. The car is not performing. I met with the owner, with Lawrence yesterday, and I am going to do the changes and I will talk to him to make him, try to make them change his mind. It’s not acceptable.”

The FIA has already changed its Additional Development Upgrade Opportunity regulations earlier this year to give more assistance to the least competitive power unit manufacturers. Ben Sulayem indicated he discussed further changes with Alonso.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“I said to him, I saw [he was] very sad. I said, Fernando, I understand that it’s not acceptable that you are coming to your own country and then now after two times the world champion and you are [in] the last [place].

“We did something earlier, in May, legally, for the team towards the engine to go and improve. And then I said to him, I’m not going to tell you what we are going to do, please tell me what you want, because you are the driver, come and tell me what do you want us to do to improve these results?

“Suddenly, you see everything change. And then I get a call, and then I had a meeting yesterday. We are here also to support.”

Ben Sulayem has been accused of intervening to help Alonso and Aston Martin before. In 2023 the team successfully overturned a penalty call which went against them at the Saudi Arabian Grand Prix. The FIA’s Ethics Committee cleared Ben Sulayem after an investigation the following year.

Honda introduced a significant engine upgrade at the Dutch Grand Prix last month. Alonso used it to score the team’s best result of the season so far, taking ninth place.

However Alonso remains unhappy with the competitiveness of his power unit. During the first day of practice at the Madring he told his team on the radio: “with this engine we cannot do the same programme as the car in front” and he thought it would “be better to stop and try again next weekend.”

Alonso, whose Aston Martin contract expires at the end of the season, said on Thursday any decision on his future will be “not soon”.

“I think it’s a matter of understanding what the rules from next year will have an impact or not on the racing and on the driving side of things,” he explained. “I think the current cars, as I said many times, are not the best cars to drive and to enjoy.

“But next year there is a step, I think, in the right direction, hopefully. At the same time, I need to think what is the best programme for next year and sit with the team. Behind the wheel or in another role, where I will be helping the most, that will be the most important thing to decide together.”

Aston Martin team principal Mike Krack rebuffed questions about whether Alonso would continue at the team during yesterday’s official FIA press conference, telling one reporter: “Coming here, I knew that you were going to go on about this. So, I will not give you any names, and I will also not speak about any Plan B. All the next ones that will ask, I will give you the same answer.

“We very much hope that Fernando will continue. He’s very important for our team. He’s very important for Formula 1. He’s very important for the whole sport and motor sport in general. So, it would be a pity to not have him anymore. And because that would be so dramatic, I do not even want to talk about it or think about it.”
