Even when timely diagnoses are made, convincing people to keep taking their medication is another challenge, even if that treatment is keeping them alive. Government figures show that 82% of HIV-positive individuals in Brazil are taking HIV-suppressing antiretroviral drugs — a seemingly impressive number yet well short of the U.N.'s target of 95%.

Sponsor Message

Gustavo Passos, equality and rights officer at UNAIDS Brazil, says this gap undermines the country's push to eliminate AIDS as a public-health threat. "On the treatment part, we're losing ground each year," he says. "The data we have implies that it's related to how people connect with health services."

Passos says that many people living with HIV feel stigmatized even by healthcare professionals, fearing that their status will be illegally disclosed without their consent, which causes them to lose trust in the system meant to support them.

Gabriel sees this dynamic play out in daily life. "It's about being judged if you're seen taking your treatment each day, and the pressure that puts on people," he says. "If someone feels judged, a lot of times they will stop the treatment."

"A lot of homophobia and transphobia"

While Brazil is commonly depicted to outsiders as a place of uninhibited sexuality — on social media, it's popularly described as one of the most promiscuous countries in the world — the reality is quite different.

Since 2014, lawmakers at federal, state and municipal levels in Brazil have proposed more than 200 pieces of legislation to ban all discussions of sex and gender education in schools. The legislative trend has continued to surface elsewhere: Two years ago, protests broke out in major cities over a proposal to equate abortion with homicide.

As Grinsztejn points out, Brazil has very high rates of violence against sexual minorities, citing Rio as a notable example. "The best gay destination in the country has a lot of homophobia and transphobia," she says. "The number of murders of trans people is one of the worst on the planet." Most victims are young: While general life expectancy in Brazil is 76, the transgender population's life expectancy is 30-35, which Grinsztejn says has been attributed to high rates of violence.

Sponsor Message

She says that this feeds into wider perceptions of HIV as a disease of immorality and deviance, driving discrimination.

Her fiancé never spoke to her again

Fabiana de Oliveira, a 57-year-old activist with the National Network of Women Living with HIV, an organization formed by women living with HIV and AIDS, says HIV discrimination in Brazil is also heavily gender-skewed.

toggle caption Ian Cheibub for NPR

She recalled her own experience of being diagnosed with HIV at 26. Her fiancé and partner of eight years, whom she suspected of giving her the virus, never spoke to her again. "I never saw him after that day," she says. "His family came to the hospital to check if I had HIV, and told me that I was no longer welcome in their house."

Living in Catanduva, a municipality in the state of Sao Paulo with just 100,000 people, she grew accustomed to feeling the judgment of others and even herself. "Women in Brazil are never the ones who are being cared for," says de Oliveira. "We are expected to take care of everything, the husband, the children, so it's hard to equate HIV as being part of your identity. You end up asking yourself, 'Was this my responsibility?' and it places a lot of burden on your mental and emotional health. Many women living with HIV in Brazil end up isolating themselves."

When it comes to the persistently damaging effects of stigma, the irony is that Brazil has also played a major role in innovations which have the potential to ultimately end the HIV epidemic. Lenacapavir, a twice-yearly injectable drug which can block HIV with virtually 100% effectiveness, was recently approved by regulators after reviewing global clinical trial data, including research carried out in Brazil. The country is now leading a large real-world study of lenacapavir across multiple cities to understand how the drug can be effectively implemented in public-health settings.

Sponsor Message

But de Oliveira is skeptical about whether such innovations can have the necessary impact without wider education campaigns and more openness in discussing HIV.

"People are more afraid of how society is going to perceive them than they are of the virus," she says.

Yet Gabriel has also seen firsthand how mindsets can change when people learn more about HIV. In the months and years after he disclosed his status, he was able to explain to his family and friends that he wasn't going to die, and correct misconceptions about how the virus could be transmitted.

"When I was able to explain more, some of my friends did eventually come back," he says. "Even if I originally felt discriminated against, it later allowed everyone to be more present and more aware."

David Cox is a freelance health journalist who has written for publications around the world including NPR, The New York Times, Wired and The Guardian. He has a Ph.D. in neuroscience.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

World.title: OPINION: 25 years on, a nation still mourns
World.content:
OPINION: 25 years on, a nation still mourns

toggle caption Spencer Platt/Getty Images/Getty Images North America

Yesterday marked a quarter century since the 9-11 terrorist attacks. I still remember — I will always remember —walking the streets of Lower Manhattan through rows of faces in photographs pasted on lampposts and walls with urgent, wrenching words:

"Have you seen my wife?" "Last seen, 8:20 AM, Tuesday." "Have you seen our daughter?" "…our father?" "…my best friend?"

The question marks pierced into you like hooks.

The attacks of September 11, 2001, were attacks on America. But America is made up of the world.

The 2,977 people who were killed that day included people from more than 90 nations -- Canada, India, Great Britain, South Korea, the Dominican Republic and more. That's America.

Sponsor Message

This week, I remembered a poem dedicated to the 43 members of the Hotel Employees and Restaurant Employees International Union who came to work that morning at Windows on the World restaurant, atop the World Trade Center's North Tower. None of them survived the tower's collapse.

The poem is called 'Alabanza: In Praise of Local 100', by Martín Espada. It reads, in part:

Praise Manhattan from a hundred and seven flights up, like Atlantis glimpsed through the windows of an ancient aquarium.

Praise the great windows where immigrants from the kitchen could squint and almost see their world, hear the chant of nations: Ecuador, México, Republica Dominicana, Haiti, Yemen, Ghana, Bangladesh.

Alabanza. Praise the kitchen in the morning, where the gas burned blue on every stove and exhaust fans fired their diminutive propellers, hands cracked eggs with quick thumbs or sliced open cartons to build an altar of cans.

Alabanza. Praise the busboy's music, the chime-chime of his dishes and silverware in the tub.

Alabanza. Praise the dish-dog, the dishwasher who worked that morning because another dishwasher could not stop coughing, or because he needed overtime to pile the sacks of rice and beans for a family floating away on some Caribbean island plagued by frogs.

Alabanza. Praise the waitress who heard the radio in the kitchen and sang to herself about a man gone. Alabanza.

After the thunder wilder than thunder, after the shudder deep in the glass of the great windows-

Sponsor Message

Twenty-five years later, we still shudder to think of that day, and pause to praise those we lost in that thunder.

Excerpted from Alabanza: New and Selected Poems 1982-2002. Copyright (c) 2003 by Martín Espada. Used with permission of the publisher, W. W. Norton & Company, Inc. All rights reserved.

World.title: A cancer survivor hoped to work — then she lost her Medicaid disability coverage
World.content:
A cancer survivor hoped to work — then she lost her Medicaid disability coverage

toggle caption Kyla Hailstone

Taya Hailstone has been in remission from childhood Hodgkin lymphoma for five years. But the cancer's lasting damage to her organs and nerves can make basic tasks, like loading a dishwasher, hard.

For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

Still, Montana's health department decided last year that Hailstone is no longer eligible for low-cost disability health coverage through Medicaid. The department switched her coverage to the state's Children's Health Insurance Program, another Medicaid program — three months before she aged out.

Before making the decision, the state didn't seek records from the medical team treating Hailstone, according to letters from those doctors reviewed by KFF Health News. Rather, the administrative ruling came after state officials learned the now-19-year-old had stopped receiving Social Security disability payments. She said she did that because she hoped to get healthy enough to work and save some money — beyond what's allowed under the strict income caps tethered to those payments. But her health changes day to day, and she said for now she's still too sick to consistently work.

Sponsor Message

Hailstone, who lives with her mom, has been able to keep Medicaid coverage while they appeal the case. She said that without Medicaid she can't afford the treatment to manage the aftermath of her cancer.

"It feels like this process was made to make you give up," Hailstone said.

Patients with disabilities have long struggled with administrative hoops, blunders and confusion when trying to qualify for federally subsidized health coverage because of their illness. Now, new federal Medicaid work requirements mean states face the additional task of deciding who qualifies for a medical exemption. That means reviewing medical cases for an even larger swath of Medicaid enrollees.

Attorneys, researchers and advocates who specialize in public aid said disability cases like Hailstone's — though separate from the incoming work requirements — are an indication that states aren't ready to decide who should be exempt from those requirements. As a result, they said, more people will be denied coverage in an opaque process.

"This will be the story of millions of people," said Anthony Wright, who heads Families USA, a national nonprofit that advocates for ways to make healthcare more accessible.

Jon Ebelt, a spokesperson with the Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services, said the state doesn't comment on individual Medicaid cases.

Sponsor Message

An estimated 18.5 million people will have to meet the new federal requirements, by proving they're working, going to school, or volunteering to keep their Medicaid coverage, according to the Congressional Budget Office. More than 40% of those enrollees live with a chronic health condition, according to KFF.

Some will be excused from those rules if they can prove they're too sick to work.

More than 5 million people are expected to lose Medicaid coverage by 2034 because of the work requirements, according to the CBO.

Work requirements become law

Many Republican policymakers and the Trump administration have touted Medicaid work requirements to preserve coverage for the neediest. Congress made that national policy through last year's One Big Beautiful Bill Act and gave states until January 2027 to implement work-for-coverage rules.

Some states are starting those checks early. Montana began in July. Nebraska initiated work requirements in May.

In the federal law creating the work requirements, Congress allowed states to exempt people who have an illness that qualifies them as "medically frail." Many states created plans for those judgment calls, only to be surprised when federal officials released rules for the requirements that went beyond what Congress outlined, by also requiring enrollees to prove their illness makes it too hard to work.

Families USA and other organizations have argued the new rules force states to set up a patchwork of systems that, together, would be larger and more complicated than the Social Security Administration's own disability review system. Last year, that federal program cost more than $5 billion to administer to roughly 7 million people nationally. For comparison, Wright said, the federal law provided $200 million for states to share as they implement the work requirements. States are paying contractors millions of dollars to prepare often already flawed public aid systems to meet the new standards.

In June, 25 states sued the Trump administration over the medical frailty rules, arguing they're too hard for patients to meet and for states to assess. That case is ongoing.

Sponsor Message

Hailstone was diagnosed with blood cancer at age 10. Her intestines tore, which led to their partial removal. As a result, her body struggles to process food and she can face severe dehydration. She said lingering side effects from her cancer treatment can leave her mind foggy and cause her hands and feet to swell enough that it's hard to grip a fork or walk across a room.

toggle caption Kyla Hailstone

Cancer dominated nearly half her life. It left mental scars, too.

"Some days you feel fine and then you suddenly crash," Hailstone said.

Hailstone and her mom live in Roundup, a central Montana town of roughly 2,000 people. They regularly make the nearly two-hour round-trip drive to Billings for specialized care. She typically has three medical appointments a week to see her physical and occupational therapists and a mental health counselor.

Hailstone said she's lucky she has her mother's help navigating Medicaid. Her mom, Kyla Hailstone, said that the state hasn't clearly defined how it determined her daughter's disability status and that its appeal process has been slow and dysfunctional.

Taya Hailstone would qualify for Medicaid based on her income if she can't prove her eligibility for disability coverage. But that would mean proving she's too sick to meet the work requirement — putting her in the same position of having to rely on a state review of her illness.

"If I lose this, this is life-changing," Hailstone said.

"Things fall through the cracks"

Hailstone qualified as disabled through the federal government as recently as 2024, about a year before the state said it was dropping her coverage. State officials can do their own medical review to determine whether someone meets the federal definition of a disability to access Medicaid.

"Whether that happens is always a bit of a crapshoot just based on state capacity," said Megan Dishong, deputy director of the Montana Legal Services Association, which helps low-income people navigate public programs. "Things fall through the cracks."

Sponsor Message

Ebelt said the state health department accepts disability decisions from the Social Security Administration. The state agency can conduct an internal disability determination if a person doesn't have one from the SSA, but Ebelt said it doesn't have to if a person qualifies for coverage another way.

"We are committed to treating every client with respect and helping those who are eligible receive appropriate Medicaid coverage," Ebelt said.

Montana instituted a three-month grace period for the work requirements. State officials won't begin disenrolling people for noncompliance until October.

Pamela Herd, a University of Michigan social policy professor who has studied bureaucratic obstacles to public benefits, said convoluted disability cases are common enough for attorneys to specialize in accessing aid.

"When we've designed public programs in ways that people can't figure out whether they're eligible without consulting lawyers, we've done something wrong," Herd said. "That has huge, huge implications for what's to come."

Montana officials have said they'll automatically review medical records that could help patients qualify for an exemption. Even so, the federal guidelines released in June mean patients will probably still face additional steps to guarantee an exemption.

Meanwhile, already overstretched doctors worry they'll face the burden of judging whether someone's illness qualifies them for a work exemption.

Dishong said that between now and October, Montana officials could offer more clarity on how the process will work. She said she's worried the state will end up "with a slow-roll mess" instead.

"This is a problem that's just starting," Dishong said.

As for Hailstone, she's now reapplying for Social Security disability payments. That aid would limit how much she can work. But it would also guarantee access to Medicaid.

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

World.title: Trump meets Ireland's leaders before heading to his golf club in Doonbeg
World.content:
Trump meets Ireland's leaders before heading to his golf club in Doonbeg

toggle caption Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

President Trump held talks Saturday in Dublin with his Irish counterpart, Catherine Connolly, during a weekend visit that's more about a major golf tournament hosted on a course he owns on the country's Atlantic coast. He also met with Ireland's Prime Minister Micheál Martin.

Trump will address the U.S. and Irish business leaders at the U.S. ambassador's official residence in Dublin before traveling to his oceanfront golf club in Doonbeg, on the other side of the country, to watch the Irish Open.

Connolly is a left-wing politician who was among those who protested when Trump visited Ireland in 2019 during his first term in office. She is now Ireland's elected, largely ceremonial head of state. A supporter of the Palestinian cause, she in the past has criticized U.S. policy in the Middle East and called Trump a "bully."

Sponsor Message

The Irish president met Trump at the end of a red carpet at her official residence. They shook hands and chatted before going inside. He emerged alone a few minutes later and saluted as an Irish Defence Forces band played the U.S. national anthem and inspected an Irish Army honor guard.

Connolly then joined Trump outdoors to introduce the U.S. and Irish delegations before the leaders went back inside for their closed-door talks.

Trump's visit is the latest example of blending his official duties and personal interests.

Trump visit irks some Dubliners

Police put up a cordon around Dublin's 1,750-acre (700-hectare) Phoenix Park, where he met Connolly at her residence, Áras an Uachtaráin. He will meet Martin, the taoiseach, at the government's Farmleigh state guesthouse and stop by Deerfield, the U.S. ambassador's residence.

Some residents expressed annoyance over the disruption.

"He's causing mayhem in this city because he wants to go down to Doonbeg and play golf," said taxi driver Christopher Fox, emphatically not a fan of Trump. "The world's in turmoil and this fella's down playing golf."

University student Mina Petrovski said Trump's "attitudes towards women, towards immigrants, towards minority communities in general are abhorrent." She said it's "shameful that the Irish government is welcoming him with open arms."

Sponsor Message

Separately, a collection of left-leaning opposition parties, anti-military groups, pro-Palestinian organizations, environmentalists and others plan to demonstrate against Trump in Dublin on Saturday.

Eric Trump defends family's presence in Ireland

Trump's son, Eric, says the family is loved in Ireland, despite the protests planned over his father's visit.

Speaking to Irish national broadcaster RTE on Friday in Doonbeg, home to the Trump International golf resort, Eric Trump said the course is the largest employer in the area.

"Go down to Morrissey's tavern in Doonbeg and hear from a real Irish person as to whether or not they like President Trump and the Trump family, go have them attest to what we've done for the country and what we've invested in the country and the love and respect that our family has always shown them," he said.

Trump flew overnight to Ireland after observing the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks that killed nearly 3,000 people in New York, Washington and Pennsylvania. The Republican president spent the two nights before Friday's solemn observance giving lengthy speeches at a political pep rally in Dallas.

Trade on agenda for Trump's talks with Martin

Martin invited Trump to visit Ireland when they met at the White House on St. Patrick's Day this year, and Ireland's political leaders will likely see the visit as a chance to maintain warm trans-Atlantic relations despite differences over trade and foreign policy, issues the White House said Trump wants to discuss.

Martin said before Trump arrived that he looked forward to discussing issues of "mutual interest" and "reaffirming the strong economic, cultural and people-to-people ties between Ireland and the United States."

Martin also said he hopes to see an Irish winner lifting the trophy on Sunday. Ireland's Shane Lowry topped the leaderboard at the tournament's halfway point.

Trump enjoys golf

Trump plays golf just about every weekend at clubs he owns in Florida, New Jersey and Virginia. His attendance at the Irish Open continues his trend of appearing at high-profile sporting events — and having a hand in organizing some of them in ways that benefit his family business. His clubs in Doral, Florida, and Bedminster, New Jersey, have each hosted professional golf tournaments this year.

Sponsor Message

The Irish Open is the second European Tour event to be held at a Trump property this year. The Nexo Championship was held last month at Trump's golf course in Aberdeen, Scotland.

Last year, Trump went to Scotland for five days to play golf at his club in Turnberry and later inaugurated a new Trump golf course in Balmedie, Aberdeenshire. During that visit, he held talks with the British prime minister and the president of the European Commission.

World.title: The secret quest to preserve Palestinian writer Raja Shehadeh's diaries
World.content:
The secret quest to preserve Palestinian writer Raja Shehadeh's diaries

toggle caption Yazeed Abu Khdeir

The world's leading Palestinian writer, Raja Shehadeh, has been on a mission to save his most personal work: his diaries.

The award-winning author of more than 20 books has been documenting decades of Palestinian life, starting in 1967 at the very beginning of Israel's occupation of the West Bank when he was a teenager.

toggle caption Raja Shehadeh

His diaries capture a unique voice and front row view of history: his meetings with world leaders, his work as a human rights lawyer, and his role as legal advisor to the Palestinians during peace talks with Israel.

Shehadeh, now 75, feared his diaries and archives — kept in his garage in the West Bank city of Ramallah — were at risk of destruction from Israeli military operations. (The Israeli foreign ministry did not respond to requests for comment about Shehadeh's fears.)

toggle caption Hannah Harper



So he took part in a two-year, discreet effort to spirit them to Scotland, where he has spent many summers. The archives are now at the University of Edinburgh, and the University of Exeter in England has published thousands of pages online .

Sponsor Message

Shehadeh spoke with NPR's Daniel Estrin about his decades of diary writing, and the secret effort to preserve his archives.

The interview text below has been edited for length and clarity.

How keeping a diary consistently for so long impacted who he is as a writer

It's been a daily effort...in order to understand better what is happening around me, in order to record and document what is happening. I started when I was...fifteen years old, just before the occupation. It has been a very good discipline because it helped me understand myself and what's happening around me...I was feeling that we are entering into a historic period that needs to be documented. So I went about writing everything down that was happening and preserving whatever I could preserve.

Excerpts from Shehadeh's diary during Israel's invasion of Ramallah at the height of the Palestinian Intifada in 2002

April 2, 2002

Last night was very noisy. I was awakened many times from the sound of the bombing and shooting ...

My mood was not good today. I just got too many telephones. The problem then became that the news spread that my spirits (so it was interpreted are down) so I got more calls from those who thought it is their duty to call me to help raise my morale ...

I am beginning to feel like a prisoner in the house, in solitary confinement ... I am thinking of exercising by pacing around the house ...

Then Samer called to say: now they have lifted the curfew ... I was glad to lift the garage door and to turn my car on ... There was absolutely no one on the street. There was dirt and stones and wind and fog but no cars ...

I continued driving up to the center and then saw two big tanks- how big they look, like elephants in a zoo where they don't belong, parked by our office blocking the street entirely ...

The satellite stations show the suffering of the Palestinians like a soap opera ... [Palestinian leader Yaser] Arafat is a rebel rouser. He is now very popular and he dramatizes everything. The Palestinians rather than be a force of change are a source of drama and emotionalism throughout the arab world ...

On Shehadeh's anger at Palestinian leaders for signing a peace accord in the 1990s that didn't stop Israeli settlement expansion

toggle caption Raja Shehadeh

My diaries after that point showed a great anger which I was glad I didn't publish. I mean, it was good that I put all my frustration and anger in the diaries because otherwise I would not have been able to live in Palestine because I was so angry and so frustrated by the leadership and so critical of it. And so the diary played an important role in helping me vent that frustration without getting myself into trouble.

Sponsor Message

The leadership...didn't realize that the settlements were the disastrous thing and that they had to be stopped, and no agreement should happen without all settlement activities stopped, and they didn't do that.

On his diary entries documenting Israel's expanding control of the West Bank

I started recording the changes in the geography and in the roads and in the landscape and in the effect of the settlements. I used to walk a lot in the West Bank hills, and after the walks, I would record what I saw and how I felt and how the land looked.

I was so confused by what was happening and so wanting to understand it, and so writing it helped me understand it. I had my own way and my own nonconformity. And so describing my world in words helped me grasp it better.

Shehadeh's fear for the safety of his archives due to Israeli military operations

toggle caption Mariana Cook

I n the Nakba (the Arabic word for "catastrophe," commonly used to refer to the displacement and dispossession of Palestinians when Israel was established) in 1948, they destroyed so many of the journals and private papers of Palestinians, and they were never found again. And then in 1982 in Lebanon, in Beirut, they went to the Palestine Research Center and took all the papers and all the journals and everything there and destroyed it. And in 2002, in the re-invasion of Ramallah, they went into so many homes and destroyed the private papers and everything. And so I was worried that they would do the same for me.

In 2023, with the Gaza war and the destruction of so much of the archives in Gaza, I became really worried and thought that I must do something to preserve these diaries. I kept the diaries in the garage. If the soldiers, as they did once, (would) enter my house, go to the garage and see them, they would just throw them all over the place and maybe set fire to them.

Sponsor Message

The two-year effort to move the archives from the West Bank to Scotland

I was very worried that the Israelis would stop it. So the first step was to digitize...page by page by page by page according to the highest standard with the cooperation of the University of Edinburgh University and Exeter University. And so three people worked day and night to digitize the diary … and all the documents that I had collected as well.

And the second step was to slowly start sending the documents out by ordinary mail without raising any attention to it.

Shehadeh's 40-year quest to investigate the 1985 killing of his father , a prominent lawyer — and the Israeli police investigation files of the killing, which Shehadeh obtained in 2025

toggle caption Raja Shehadeh



In the archive is the process by which I went about trying to get the police to investigate and the feelings that I had about it, which extended from '85 to 2025.

It was clear that they had not investigated the main culprit, the man who had sent the letter to my father from prison threatening to kill him if he did not withdraw from a case of land that the family thought belonged to them or they were squatting on it. My suspicion, strong suspicion, is because this man was a collaborator, and he wanted to be protected, and Israel wanted to protect him as a collaborator.

This is where it ended. We could not go beyond that.

toggle caption Raja Shehadeh



The Israeli police revealed all the investigation, but all the investigation was extraneous. It was distracting because the main suspect was not investigated, and that we have found out.

I had always suspected that it was this man who did it, and when I realized through this case that they have actually not investigated him, I felt that my suspicions were correct, and it gave me closure.

Sponsor Message

About Shehadeh's diary entries documenting Israel's transformation of the West Bank over the years

I understood from early on that it was a matter of...staying put and persevering. Because I realized that what the Israelis wanted was to make life so difficult for the Palestinians in the occupied territories, to make them leave.

The only antidote to that is sumud [Arabic for "steadfastness"]. Staying put and entrenching our existence by building institutions, by making work for people, by making it clear that we are here to stay. And I never changed my mind about this. I always realized that sumud was the most important resistance to what Israel was trying to do.

What Shehadeh hopes his legacy will be

toggle caption Raja Shehadeh

I'm not so worried about legacy, but I'm concerned that, through the diaries, people will understand how things happened and the developments that things went through. That's very important for me, and this would be perhaps a greater way that I would have served human rights and truth than any other way, whether through my writing of books or articles or speeches. The diaries might bring about the results that I haven't been able to achieve in any other way. I think that is the important thing.

World.title: Miami crash raises concerns about the jet's operator, and why it's flying for Amazon
World.content:
Miami crash raises concerns about the jet's operator, and why it's flying for Amazon

toggle caption Chandan Khanna/AFP via Getty Images

In the moments before an Amazon cargo plane crashed at Miami International Airport on Sunday, automatic warning signals were blaring in the cockpit. One pilot warned the other that the plane was coming in too fast, according to details of the cockpit voice recordings released this week by the National Transportation Safety Board.

But the flight crew pushed ahead with the landing anyway.

"In my 60 years of flying, I've never seen such a terrible performance from a crew," said Ross Aimer, the CEO of Aero Consulting Experts, and a retired airline captain who worked in the industry for more than 40 years.

Sponsor Message

The plane was traveling roughly 180 miles per hour when it touched down awkwardly on the runway, flight data recordings showed. The pilots tried briefly to take off again before the plane hurtled roughly 1300 feet past the end of the runway and smashed into two vehicles on the ground.

Five people were killed, all of them workers for a company that cleans planes. Five more were injured.

"It was a very, very unstable approach from the beginning, from the get go," Aimer told NPR. In that situation, he says, pilots are trained to go around and attempt the landing again. "These fellows should have gone around long before even getting close to that airport."

The cargo plane crash in Miami is raising concerns about the safety culture at 21 Air, the little-known carrier that operated the flight for Amazon. Former pilots were sounding alarms about the company's safety practices long before Sunday's accident, though the company disputes their claims.

It's also prompting questions about the retail giant's practice of contracting with multiple smaller carriers instead of operating its own fleet of planes.

"The main question would be," Aimer said, "why is it that a major company, a very rich company like Amazon Prime, is contracting their flying to several of what I would call fly by night operations like 21 Air?"

toggle caption Chandan Khanna/AFP via Getty Images

Amazon vigorously disputed that characterization. An Amazon spokesperson says its carrier model is standard practice across the aviation industry, and that it contracts with carriers that are certified by air safety regulators at the Federal Aviation Administration.

Sponsor Message

"Nothing is more important to us than safety — this includes the safety of the people who operate flights in our network, the safety of the communities around the airports we use, and the safety of the people who handle our cargo," Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement to NPR.

The Miami crash is the third major accident involving a 767 flying for Amazon. In 2019, a flight operated by Atlas Air crashed into Trinity Bay during its approach to Houston, killing the two crew members and one passenger on board. The NTSB found the probable cause was pilot error. (Atlas Air is still a major cargo airline, but no longer operates flights for Amazon.)

In 2024, another Boeing 767 flying for Amazon overran the runway at Vancouver International Airport in Canada. In that case, the Cargojet crew reported mechanical problems with the wing flaps on the plane. No one was injured during the high-speed landing. The plane was damaged, but later repaired and returned to service, Amazon said.

Amazon is not the only shipper to suffer a deadly crash. In November, a UPS cargo jet exploded shortly after takeoff in Louisville, Kentucky, killing all three crew members on board and 12 people on the ground. The NTSB investigation has focused on a faulty part in an engine bracket on the McDonnell Douglas MD-11.

Pilot experience

Amazon currently contracts with nine different air carriers, with more than 100 planes total in service, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company. They include major names like Alaska Airlines, Allegiant Air and Cargojet, as well as lesser-known carriers like 21 Air that specialize in cargo.

21 Air operates a total of eight planes for Amazon, according to Cirium, including the Boeing 767 involved in the Miami crash. The company, which is headquartered in North Carolina, also flies for DHL.

For pilots, smaller cargo airlines such as 21 Air often serve as "a stepping stone into a bigger and better job," said Aimer, who spent much of his career flying for United Airlines.

Sponsor Message

"They attract guys that are not that experienced," Aimer said. "And even if they are, they're only looking to get on to a better job, like with UPS, with FedEx."

The crew of the 21 Air flight that crashed in Miami had relatively little experience with the type of plane they were flying. The captain had been certified on the Boeing 767 for less than five months, while the first officer had been certified on the 767 for less than 18 months, according to the NTSB.

21 Air did not reply to NPR's requests for comment. But in a statement to The Wall Street Journal the company said, "Our entire organization has focused on deploying the right training, protocols and procedures in all aspects of operational safety."

The company said it would evaluate the NTSB's findings.

Past safety concerns

Former 21 Air employees raised concerns about the safety culture at the airline long before the Miami crash. Karl Seuring, a veteran pilot and the former president of 21 Air's pilot union, said he was not surprised by that accident.

"We anticipated and we feared it. And we knew the day would come, and there wasn't anything we could do," he said.

toggle caption Joe Raedle/Getty Images

Seuring says he was fired in 2022 for raising concerns about the 21 Air's safety standards after being told repeatedly that "it's not going to change," according to the federal whistleblower lawsuit he filed. His lawyer, Mike Anello, shared documents from the case with NPR.

"Everywhere I looked there are issues," wrote Don Helmig, the departing safety director, in an email to the company's owner in 2021, in which he accused the company's leaders of paying "lip service" to safety. "In my opinion, what they wished me to do is say nothing, but that is not how Safety is supposed to operate."

The company's CEO at the time pushed back on those allegations in his testimony for the lawsuit. He denied that 21 Air discouraged employees from reporting their safety concerns, and said the company follows "all the rules."

Sponsor Message

The company also had trouble attracting experienced pilots, Seuring said, because it paid them less than other carriers. Seuring says he presented management with a plan to change that.

"If we want to get experienced pilots here, we have to be willing to compensate them," he said. "And then, unfortunately, when that was lower than standard, guys would simply go elsewhere with opportunities that looked more promising."

Amazon says it's aware of reports of the former 21 Air employees' safety concerns.

"We believe the allegations pre-date our relationship with the company and the current leadership team at 21 Air. Nonetheless, we take any allegation related to safety with the utmost seriousness," Nantel said in a statement.

Investigation ongoing

Both 21 Air and Amazon say they are cooperating with the NTSB investigation into the Miami crash.

NTSB chair Jennifer Homendy says investigators are seeking to understand how the two companies work together.

toggle caption Joe Raedle/Getty Images

"We're going to want to see what that relationship is. Who does what? What safety provisions might be in any sort of contracts or any sort of policies? And then we'll see from there we might even have additional information that we seek," Homendy said during a press briefing on Monday.

At a briefing on Tuesday, Homendy said she was not familiar with complaints about the safety culture at 21 Air. But she did encourage the public to share anything that might be "relevant to this investigation."

Amazon is a financial supporter of NPR and pays to distribute some of our content.

World.title: Céline Dion ends 6-year concert hiatus with emotional Paris performance
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Eleven minutes before 9 p.m. local time, the lights went down and screams erupted as Céline Dion took the stage in a Parisian suburb for her first concert in six years.

Dion, 58, opened the show at Europe's largest indoor concert venue with a rendition of 1998's On Ne Change Pas, stopping partway through as she was moved to tears.

"I promised not to cry," she told the crowd in Nanterre, wearing a pleated black gown and enormous glittering necklace.

"Tonight I want to sing for you, for me, for life."

Dion wiping her tears on stage. (Thomas Samson/AFP/Getty Images)

Thousands of devoted fans packed Plenitude Arena on Saturday to watch Dion's return to the stage, opening a sellout Paris residency after a battle with a rare neurological disorder sidelined the singer's career.

"I've already cried three times," said Melanie McGill, a fan from Los Angeles sitting on the upper level.

Dion performed 26 songs across her discography over more than two hours, including anthems of the 1990s like My Heart Will Go On, All By Myself and It's All Coming Back to Me Now. After starting The Chase with a mistake, she paused and asked the crowd if she could start the track again.

"Finally. It's amazing we’re all together. I made a promise. I made a promise to come back and be back on stage," the singer said early in the show.

"Thank you so much for your support, your patience and, if I may say so, I am everything I am because you loved me," she continued, quoting her own 1996 power ballad.

Dion closed with S'il Suffisait d'Aimer, the critically acclaimed hit single to Dion's bestselling French language album of the same name.

Dion opened the show with 1998's On Ne Change Pas, written by Parisian singer-songwriter Jean-Jacques Goldman. (Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters)

Concertgoers, who made their way through many barricades to get inside the venue, wore anything from jeans and graphic T-shirts to sparkly mini skirts and floor-length gowns for the occasion.

One woman wore her wedding dress.

"I cancelled the party with all my family and friends to come see Céline," said Fanny Sucheyre, who celebrated her one-year wedding anniversary at the concert.

"I said to myself, if one day I had the chance to see her, I would wear my best dress. So it's my most beautiful dress."

Fanny Sucheyre wears her wedding dress on the way into Dion's show. (Sarah Leavitt/CBC)

"It's a dream. I haven't slept for three days. I'm 50 years old and right now I feel like I'm 15," said Guylene Richardson, who saw the show with her daughter, both in Dion concert tees.

"With [Dion's] disease, I didn't think she would come back, so it's great. I'm really happy for her. I'm happy for us."

One of the bestselling artists of all time, Dion announced a diagnosis of stiff person’s syndrome — which causes stiffness and muscle spasms — and disappeared from the spotlight in 2022. She broke her hiatus to perform Edith Piaf's Hymne à l'amour from the Eiffel Tower during the opening ceremony of the 2024 Paris Olympic Games.

Dion is scheduled to perform a series of 26 concerts over the next eight months. The City of Light buzzed with anticipation for the singer's comeback, with signs dotting the length of the Champs-Élysées and the famed river Seine.

World.title: Alberta separatists expect a win, regardless of numbers that say otherwise, poll suggests
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Alberta separatists think they’re going to win a referendum that surveys suggest they are poised to lose by a wide margin, according to exclusive new polling.

And that mismatch of expectations has consequences for what comes next — including the likelihood that Albertans shouldn’t expect this issue to be put to rest with this one vote, say the pollster and a political scientist.

Abacus Data CEO David Coletto presented the results of the new poll, done during the first week of September, to CBC’s West of Centre on Friday.

On Oct. 19, Albertans will vote on a question with two choices: Option 1 is to stay in Canada, while Option 2 supports commencing the legal process to hold a binding referendum on Alberta separation.

That ballot question will be in addition to nine others that focus on constitutional and immigration issues.

Coletto’s poll found 64 per cent of respondents would vote to remain a province in Canada and 24 per cent would vote to start the separation process. Nine per cent were undecided and three per cent said they would skip the question.

But the poll also found that Option 2 supporters have surprisingly high expectations, believing that the separatist option will garner a winning 57 per cent of votes.

Coletto chalks it up to the political bubbles people live in and the natural hopefulness that comes with their strong support of the separatist camp.

Lisa Young, a political science professor at the University of Calgary, says that inflated expectation is worth noting — especially in the context of post-referendum ramifications.

"What he found, I think, should be setting off alarm bells in all of our heads," Young told West of Centre.

"If you do walk into this with the expectation that Option [2] is going to get 57 per cent and the actual outcome is 28 per cent ... the first question is going to be, 'Was this a proper result? Can we trust the outcome?'"

Premier Danielle Smith has said the upcoming referendum will be a gut-check of where Albertans stand, and that the province can hold a vote and move on .

But Young and Coletto don't see it that way.

In the event that the winning side supports remaining in Canada, the poll found many Option 2 voters expect the separatist movement to keep growing. Only six per cent of them said they expect the issue will be settled.

"There seems to be this assumption in the UCP premier's office ... that if you let this group let off steam, it will make the issue go away," Young said.

"This does not simply go away afterward. We're going to live with it one way or another for the next months, if not years."

A ballot for the Oct. 19 Alberta referendum shows the question about separating from Canada and the two options voters will choose between. (Kory Siegers/CBC)

Who is the typical Option 2 voter?

According to the polling, the typical Option 2 voter is a conservative partisan, somewhat more likely to be a man and tends to be slightly older than the provincial average.

They are more likely to live in small cities or in bedroom communities around Calgary and Edmonton. While rural Alberta contributes more than its share, the communities ringing Alberta's main metropolitan centres provide the most voters.

But the group is more distinguishable by its grievances than its demographics, the poll suggests.

It says Option 2 supporters are far more likely to put being an Albertan ahead of being a Canadian, and have a more favourable view of the United States and Donald Trump. That said, the group is split on whether Alberta should become a U.S. state.

The group also shares near-unanimous agreement that Alberta contributes more to Canada than it gets back, the province’s interests are ignored in Ottawa, and the rest of the country does not respect Alberta, the poll suggests.

Young said she wonders if the separatist camp is adequately reflected among people who were polled.

"I did start thinking back to 2016 in the United States," Young said. "People wouldn't tell a pollster that they were going to vote for Trump because it was seen as sort of socially unacceptable."

Coletto said he's confident his poll factored in as many Option 2 voters as possible, but he also acknowledged this is not a typical election.

"Partisan politics can get divisive. But this is being felt much more deeply and much more emotionally on both sides."

"Whatever side you're on, you've still got to live together no matter what happens going forward."

Do they actually want to leave?

What Option 2 voters hope to get out of a favourable result varies significantly. When asked to identify their main motivation for choosing to commence the process for a binding referendum, only 26 per cent said independence.

The rest are voting for leverage, to send a message or on principle, Coletto said.

"For many Albertans who are inclined to look at Option 2, it's not just a black or white, in and out."

That result aligns with recent messaging from the separatist camp.

“Independence isn't actually on the ballot,” Keith Wilson, with independence group Let Alberta Decide, told West of Centre last month.

“Voting Option 2 sends a message that no, we can do better. We want a more respectful and balanced and fair relationship with Ottawa.”

“Others are prepared to vote for Option 2 when they don't even support independence. And that's why I have some optimism we're going to win on Oct. 19.”

University of Calgary political scientist Lisa Young, left, and David Coletto, CEO of Abacus Data, speak to CBC's West of Centre on Friday. (Diane Yanko/CBC)

Methodology

Abacus Data surveyed 1,000 Alberta adults online from Sept. 4 to 7, 2026, six weeks before the Oct. 19 referendum. Results are weighted by region, age and gender to census data. A probability sample of this size would carry a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 points, 19 times out of 20. For subsets, the margin of error is larger.

World.title: New statues added to controversial Prime Minister's Path in Wilmot, Ont.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Four statues of former Canadian leaders were added to the Prime Minister's Path project in Wilmot, Ont., on Saturday. Not everyone was pleased.

The contested project, now run by Createscape Waterloo Region, held an afternoon unveiling with the leadership of Wilmot Township at a municipal park by Castle Kilbride in Baden, a small community west of Kitchener.

"Obviously we're very happy that [the project] has found its footing once again," Don Bourgeois, chair of the board and president of Createscape Waterloo Region, told CBC News.

"Our purpose is to help create public art that has that emotional attachment, but also gets people... to have discussion about the future of Canada, the history of Canada, of art and what art is about."

The four new statues depict Sir John Abbott, Sir John Thompson, Sir Mackenzie Bowell and Sir Charles Tupper. They join statues of Sir John A. Macdonald, Kim Campbell, Sir Robert Borden, William Lyon Mackenzie King and Lester B. Pearson.

Around a dozen protesters attended, decrying the project as insensitive and poorly conceived.

Don Bourgeois, chair of the board and president of Createscape Waterloo Region, stands beside a statue of Lester B. Pearson. Bourgeois said the project is returning with an educational component to provide context behind each prime minister. (John Dalusong/CBC)

Project's rocky path

The Prime Ministers Path project was first proposed in 2013 . The project aimed to honour former Canadian leaders with 22 bronze statues placed in a park to celebrate Canada's 150th birthday.

The project faced controversy from the beginning, however, with Kitchener councillors rejecting the idea of having the statues at Victoria Park in 2014 and Waterloo's Wilfrid Laurier University backing out of the agreement to put the statues at the school in 2016.

The statues would later find a home at Castle Kilbride in the village of Baden that same year.

By 2020, the statue of Sir John A. Macdonald was put in storage after a public call for it to be removed for his role in the residential school system. The project was then cancelled by the township's council in 2021, leading to the removal of the statues.

A protester holds up a sign that says, 'take away John. A' in Baden, Ont., on Sep. 12, 2026. Behind the protester is Sir John A. Macdonald's statue. (John Dalusong/CBC)

Last April, Wilmot council voted to proceed with the project. The vote involved giving Createscape Waterloo Region custody of the nine statues it owns, as well as entering into an agreement with the group to display the statues in municipal parkland for the next 20 years.

The project now includes an added educational component, with the Six Nations of the Grand River playing an important role, Bourgeois said.

"The Six Nations [of the Grand River] will be involved in making sure that our website, which will include historical educational materials, reflects the issues that resulted from decisions of the prime ministers over the last century and a half," he said.

But the addition of an educational component is not enough, said Benny Skinner, who uses they/them pronouns, and led Saturday's protest.

"If you actually take the time to learn about the prime ministers, the history of who they are and what they've done, and you learn proper authentic history that includes Indigenous peoples history, what you'll realize is that this is an extremely insensitive and poorly thought-out project," they said.

Indigenous people included 'from the beginning'

The project has been criticized as insensitive to Indigenous people since its inception.

When Wilfrid Laurier University declined to host the statues in 2016, opponents of the project said there had been insufficient consultation and celebrating the country's past prime ministers would be culturally insensitive given the university is built on land that traditionally belonged to Indigenous people.

Bourgeois insists that Indigenous perspectives have been taken into account.

"They were included in a sense right from the beginning, that issue with respect to how Canada, through the prime ministers' leadership, have dealt with First Nations was part of the discussion," Bourgeois explained.

"But clearly, we failed to communicate that properly. We failed to do it in a fashion that was sufficiently collaborative."

That has changed, he said: "Today, thankfully, we're down on a different path."

Benny Skinner (pictured) said Indigenous perspectives were not sufficiently reflected in the renewed Prime Ministers Path project. Don Bourgeois of Createscape said the involvement of Six Nations of the Grand River will help address concerns. (John Dalusong/CBC)

But Skinner, who was co-lead for the consultancy the last time there was a community engagement for the project, said concerns raised during consultations were not heeded.

"They're looking for an Indigenous person to check off that it's fine so that they can continue to do this project the way that it is," Skinner said.

"None of the Indigenous people I have spoken to, in the hundreds, about this project, want this project on these lands."

Sculptor Nathan Scott believes it is important to highlight all aspects of Canadian history. He sculpted the four newest statues in 2019, referring to them as "the unfortunate four" for what he sees as their limited achievements in office.

"I'm a proud Canadian. I love our history," he said. "It wasn't always done perfectly. It's the good, bad and sometimes there's ugliness to it, but it's who we are."

"And if we don't have history, if we try to erase it, who are we? Who are we at all?"

Nathan Scott rests his hand on his sculpture of Sir Robert Borden. Scott finished the newest statues in 2019, calling them 'the unfortunate four,' but was forced to hide them following backlash. (John Dalusong/CBC)

13 statues to go

Future changes to the project could yet win over opponents, Skinner said. They proposed changing its name, moving it to a hidden area so people don't have to see it and better collaboration with Indigenous people.

For his part, Bourgeois said the educational aspect of the project will remain important. This includes hosting educational symposia where the history and work of each prime minister will be discussed.

For now, the long-term goal remains completing the remaining 13 statues, he said.

Though Canada has had 24 prime ministers, Justin Trudeau and Mark Carney won't be included in the current project — to avoid it becoming "a little bit too political," Bourgeois said.

World.title: Time for a digital divorce? Trade war puts spotlight on Canada's relationship with U.S. big tech
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | Canada's data in foreign hands: why digital sovereignty matters: Just Asking 1:05:27 Canada’s data in foreign hands: why digital sovereignty matters

Trade and political tensions between Canada and the United States have raised concerns about Canada's digital sovereignty, but what does that term mean, and how can Canada promote it?

While it may sound like jargon, experts say digital sovereignty can be defined simply.

It's about regulation, Vass Bednar, managing director of independent public policy think-tank the Canadian Shield Institute, told CBC Radio's Just Asking.

"Fundamentally, our digital sovereignty is our ability to regulate digital environments using the tools that we have," she said, including regulation of algorithms that influence what information we see online.

It's also about choice and the law, according to Michael Geist, Canada Research Chair in internet and e-commerce law at the University of Ottawa.

"It's fundamentally about both the ability to make Canadian choices … so we have alternatives to some of the larger — predominately U.S. — players, and also ensuring that Canadian law applies," he told CBC Manitoba's Information Radio last week.

The federal government also has a definition.

"Digital sovereignty means Canada stays in control of its own digital future — including its data, technology and essential online services — instead of relying on foreign companies, foreign systems or foreign laws," a government webpage reads.

"Think of it like this: Just as we want our homes, money and identities protected in Canada, we want the same protection for our digital information and services."

A mid-August X post from the U.S. Trade Representative account said a potential trade deal between Canada and the U.S. would include "digital trade alignment," which prompted expert concerns and speculation about digital sovereignty. Only days later, talks between the two countries fell apart at the last minute, reportedly over American insistence that U.S. streaming companies be exempt from Canadian content rules.

After talks broke down, President Donald Trump signed an executive order that Lake Ontario be renamed Lake America. Google and Apple Maps quickly implemented the change for American users, but some Canadians reported seeing it on their maps.

So, how American is our tech?

Right now, Canada doesn't have many alternatives to American technology companies and digital platforms.

"We are heavily dependent on the American big tech companies when it comes to our Canadian businesses and the public sector," said Shion Guha, assistant professor in information and computer science at the University of Toronto, on Just Asking.

The federal government also uses the Microsoft Office and Microsoft 365 platforms. In January, Shared Services Canada, which is responsible for providing IT services to the government, renewed its agreement with Microsoft in a deal worth $940 million over seven years.

University of Toronto assistant professor Shion Guha says Canada's public and private sectors both lean heavily on U.S. tech. (Submitted by Shion Guha)

Guha was part of a study on the federal government's AI Register which found that Microsoft was the single biggest supplier of systems, accounting for 42 of 409.

"An American big tech company is very heavily intertwined, not just with things like email or OneDrive … or Microsoft Office, but also in the types of predictive analytics and other types of AI products that the federal government has currently acquired," Guha said.

"This type of dependence on one big tech company is generally not a good thing for any kind of sovereignty."

There is precedent for switching, Bednar said, noting, "France has been a little bit ahead of the curve here."

France's Interministerial Directorate for Digital Affairs announced in April that it will remove Microsoft's Windows operating system from government computers. Open-source software Linux will replace it.

The French government also developed Tchap, an instant messaging application, and mandated its use for public sector employees, citing security and privacy concerns. The French government says over 600,000 public sector employees use the app.

The French government developed Tchap, a messaging app for public sector employees, as a way to promote security. (https://tchap.numerique.gouv.fr/)

What can Canadians do?

But if getting the Canadian government to switch platforms could be difficult, getting Canadians to change everything from their credit cards to their cloud storage to their social media and instant messaging platforms and more could be even harder.

Gander Social launched in July, marketing itself as a nicer, Canadian alternative to U.S. social media platforms. The company posted on Facebook last week, saying it's approaching 50,000 users, though Bednar pointed out that Prime Minister Mark Carney isn't among them.

WATCH | Gander wants to make social media more Canadian: Homegrown app Gander wants to make social media more Canadian | Duration 2:03 Gander, a new social media app similar to X or Bluesky, was designed for Canadians — but many are skeptical that being homegrown alone will be enough to get users to try it.

But having Canadian options doesn't mean Canadians will want them, Guha said.

"There is a certain amount of inertia in getting Canadians to switch to things, because convenience usually rules over most things," he said.

"Just because we can, or do, have Canadian alternatives — and they may provide better features, they may be good for us — doesn't mean that we can overcome the social inertia to get people to switch."

But it is one way ordinary Canadians can promote digital sovereignty, Bednar said. Though she also acknowledged it's going to require more "institutional imagination in Canada" to move forward.

Staying sovereign in the AI age

The Canadian government released its National AI Strategy in June. In it, the government pledges to develop a home-grown supercomputer, as well as "sovereign cloud, AI, cyber and quantum initiatives."

Geist said the government should take an approach that balances building Canadian AI programs with access to foreign ones.

"If a single government gets to determine whether or not you have access to those frontier models, they're really determining whether or not you've got the very best tools to counter things like cybersecurity threats," he said.

Guha said the federal government has also started referring to the data centres that help power AI and other services as "critical infrastructure."

The federal government's five principles for data centre construction, released earlier this month, require projects to "strengthen Canada's long-term digital resilience, security and compute capacity." They also say that the facilities must follow Canadian laws on cybersecurity and data protection.

"If we don't make the rules here, we will have to follow someone else's,” AI Minister Evan Solomon said at a news conference announcing the principles, which arrive amid concerns about the U.S. government using its laws to access Canadian data.

A data centre under construction at Steeles Technology Campus in Toronto. Building more data centres in Canada is one way of promoting digital sovereignty, says Michael Geist, but many Canadians have voiced opposition to having them in their communities. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

Bednar said Canada's current effort to assert its sovereignty against the U.S. is different from those of the past because of how much more of our lives exist digitally.

"Digital ... is the infrastructure of our economy," she said.

"It is just as, if not arguably more, important than manufacturing, automobiles, aluminum, steel — take your pick."

World.title: 'Canadian renaissance': Stars share their love for homegrown films on the red carpet at TIFF
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

This is the opening weekend of the Toronto International Film Festival. And a several big ticket films are making world premiers to kick off the celebration of all things cinema. And that includes a new Canadian film about an underdog 'Evil Knievel' wannabe. CBC's Eli Glasner has more from the red carpet premier of 'The Stunt Driver'.

As tensions between Canada and the U.S. creep into the film industry, Jay Baruchel is more than confident his country can stand toe to toe with its southern neighbour.

"We will be fine," the Ottawa-born actor said on the red carpet Friday ahead of the world premiere of The Stunt Driver at the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF).

"We have never done anything but punch above our weight, and our record is pretty bloody strong when it comes to that.… We always find a way through."

He's one of a number of Canadian actors sharing their love of the country's film industry and Canada in general on the TIFF red carpet after the festival kicked off Thursday night.

Baruchel, known for films such as BlackBerry and She's Out of My League, is in the driver's seat of the new underdog film, which is based on the true story of stuntman Ken Carter.

Baruchel portrays Carter, known as The Mad Canadian, who attempted to jump over the St. Lawrence River in a rocket-powered car in the 1970s — partially driven by a desire to outdo his American rival Evel Knievel.

The timing of the film's debut during the ongoing trade war between Canada and the U.S. "added an extra sense of urgency … and a vitality" to the film, Baruchel said.

The cast and director of The Stunt Driver on the red carpet for the film at the Toronto International Film Festival in on Friday. (Laura Proctor/The Canadian Press)

"If you've ever been talked down to, if you've ever been dismissed ... you understand where this comes from," he added, calling the story "an indignant middle finger."

The trade war gained took on a cultural dimension ahead of TIFF when, earlier this month, U.S. President Donald Trump singled out Canada during the announcement of a proposed federal incentive to keep U.S. film productions in the U.S. rather than travelling abroad, stirring up concerns in the Canadian film industry.

The two film industries have long been close.

"It's been over a hundred years that there's been a very solid bridge built between the entertainers and artists and business people of Canada and the U.S. when it comes to making movies," TIFF CEO Cameron Bailey told CBC News on Thursday, noting that the opening film at TIFF, Being Heumann, is a U.S. production that was shot in Toronto.

Members of the production and cast of Below on the red carpet at the Toronto International Film Festival on Thursday. (Laura Proctor/The Canadian Press)

At TIFF, Canadian actors and artists say they aren't feeling cowed — but instead feel inspired to champion Canadian art.

"Art can reflect who we are as a country and … who we are as people," Canadian actress Laurence Leboeuf, who plays Carter's wife Gloria in The Stunt Driver, said on the red carpet Friday.

'Canadian renaissance'

Devon Bostick, a Toronto-born actor who co-wrote Closing Night — which also premiered at TIFF — added that he feels "we're part of a Canadian renaissance right now." The film tracks a movie star (Sarah Paulson) as she attempts to connect with her estranged family.

"I live in the States now and from afar I just think Canada's got it going on, and I feel like it's a beacon of light, that what is happening here is thriving and resisting," the Mile End Kicks actor said.

WATCH | Sarah Paulson, Devon Bostick on Canada: Stars at 'Closing Night' red carpet show Canada some love | Duration 0:21 Actor Sarah Paulson and writer Devon Bostick, who's from Toronto, talked about their love for Canada during the world premiere of their new film, Closing Night, at TIFF on Saturday.

When asked if he had any concerns about the Canadian film industry amid trade tensions, he quipped, "I think I'm not afraid for Canada, I’m afraid for the States."

Mary Walsh, a comedian and actress known for her work with This Hour Has 22 Minutes, echoed those sentiments when she arrived on the red carpet for the upcoming Netflix miniseries Below on Thursday.

"The Canadian film industry is bigger than it's ever been, and it's growing. And the more Mr. Trump threatens to attack us, the more we pull together and become stronger," she said.

WATCH | Mary Walsh champions Canada's film industry: Trump's threats only make Canada's film industry stronger: Mary Walsh | Duration 0:24 Comedian Mary Walsh talked about the strength of the Canadian film industry during a TIFF red carpet on Thursday. She's in Toronto promoting Below, a new miniseries filmed in her home province of Newfoundland and Labrador.

Walsh, who hails from St. John's, plays the mayor of a small, shrinking town in Newfoundland in the new horror series.

She said the U.S. upping its aggression against Canada could be the "kick in the arse that the Canadian film industry needed," to back its own artistic works more fully.

"As a country we must support our own … culture, and we do a somewhat good job of that. But at times, you know, Canadians aren't always behind Canadian culture. They've sort of looked to the larger thing to the south, and so I think our eyes are sort of turning back to ourselves.

"If Mr. Trump did only one good thing, only one good thing, it would be that it made us realize that we are a country, and a country worth working together to save and to be."

World.title: AI industry needs to slow down for safety measures to catch up, Anthropic CEO says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The CEO of Anthropic said on Saturday that the artificial intelligence industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up.

Without it, Dario Amodei warned, AI could be capable within six to 12 months of leading a swarm that could take over the entire internet, among other risks.

Amodei also offered a plan in a post on his website to increase checks on the industry, one part of which he said Anthropic is undertaking by itself already. The others would require co-ordination among the broad industry and with governments around the world, including authoritarian ones.

"I believe that if slowing down bought us even an extra year or two before models reach critical levels of capability, and we used that time to advance alignment, we could greatly reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong," Amodei said.

Both Elon Musk, who runs xAI, and Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, said in posts on X that they agree with Amodei.

"This has been a primary topic of discussions we've had at OpenAI in recent weeks," Altman said.

The stakes are high, even as some critics dismissed earlier warnings as hype to gin up excitement. Anthropic, an AI research and safety company, said two days earlier that it blocked efforts by bad actors to use its AI models for malicious activity such as cyberattacks, surveillance and research that could have led to biological weapons.

In July, rival OpenAI shook the industry after saying its AI system hacked into another AI company on its own in an "unprecedented cyber incident."

Amodei's post comes only a few days after one of Anthropic's researchers announced he's resigning over concerns that Anthropic and its competitors are not acting responsibly in AI development.

WATCH | Anthropic insider warns AI could kill all humans within a decade: Chance AI kills all humans within a decade, Anthropic insider warns | Duration 2:08 Two AI experts are warning that AI is getting too smart, too quickly. One former employee accuses Anthropic and OpenAI of 'gambling with our lives.' A current Anthropic safety executive said he thinks there's a ten per cent chance AI kills all humans within a decade.

Another former Anthropic employee, Joe Benton, wrote in a Substack post published on Friday that he left his job as part of a safety team "to hold AI companies accountable" and that humanity "may not survive this transition."

"Many of the people I know who work on safety research at AI companies want to do what is right for the world," Benton said in his posting. "But they feel their companies are trapped in a race to build superintelligence: either they stop and other, less conscientious people take their place; or, they continue, and risk participating in enormous harm themselves."

To help rein in such risks, Amodei suggested that all companies at the frontier of AI commit to giving "ongoing, employee-like access" to a team of outside evaluators, who can monitor safety practices. He said Anthropic already plans to do so itself, including offering desks in its offices, access badges and company laptops.

The other parts of Amodei's suggested plan may be more difficult to implement. One asks the U.S. government to potentially issue waivers that would allow American AI companies to co-ordinate and set safety standards without running afoul of antitrust laws.

Another asks the U.S. and other democratic governments to try to co-ordinate with authoritarian governments, so that companies from China and other countries don't accelerate their efforts when U.S. rivals are intentionally pacing theirs.

"The measures I propose to advance the frontier at a safe pace will not be easy," Amodei said. "But I believe we owe it to humanity to try."

Altman said in his post that third-party evaluators with employee level access is a "great idea," and pledge to introduce such a measure in the near future.

World.title: Your guide to the U.S. midterms, and why they're crucial for Donald Trump
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The upcoming U.S. midterm elections will determine whether Republican President Donald Trump will be free to pursue his agenda during his final two years in office or whether he'll face constraints from a Congress where the Democrats hold new power.

Here's what you need to know about the midterms.

Why do U.S. midterms matter?

The midterms are a contest for control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, which together make up the U.S. Congress.

The party that controls the Senate holds sway over presidential appointments to cabinet, the courts and senior posts in federal agencies. The party that controls the House can launch impeachment proceedings and has the power to initiate budget bills .

If one party controls both, it has broad influence over legislation as well as the potential to thwart some presidential actions.

How is the race shaping up?

The Democrats are generally excited about their prospects in the midterms and the Republicans a little worried.

History gives the Republicans plenty of reason to fret. The incumbent president's party has suffered a net loss of seats in Congress in all but two midterms since the 1930s. The only exceptions were Bill Clinton (1998) and George W. Bush (2002), when each had sky-high approval ratings.

Trump's approval rating is anything but sky-high .

What's at stake?

With slim majorities in each chamber, the Republicans have little wiggle room to lose seats and still maintain their hold on Congress.

The Democrats need to flip just four districts to take control of the House (if they hold on to all their current seats). The Democrats also need to take just four Republican-held states to win control of the Senate. But that's a tougher task than flipping the House because there are far fewer Senate seats up for election and winning each requires a statewide victory.

A person votes in a primary election in Oak Park, Mich., on Aug. 4. (Nic Antaya/The Associated Press)

All 435 seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are up for grabs, as members of the House are elected to two-year terms.

Only 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate are up for election this fall. U.S. senators are elected to six-year terms.

When does voting happen?

Midterms, like the word implies, come at the two-year mark of a president's four-year term. This year, midterm election day is Nov. 3.

Many U.S. voters will choose to vote before then, either in advance polls or by mail-in ballots, a method the Trump administration is trying to restrict.

You may also have heard that people across the U.S. have been voting at various times since the spring in primaries, which are the contests to select each party's candidates. In most states, only people who are registered Republicans or Democrats can vote in the party's primaries.

How does Trump factor in?

Trump is not on the ballot in the midterms, but his influence on the campaign will be unavoidable.

Only one president si nce 1950 has headed into a midterm with an approval rating below 40 per cent: George W. Bush in 2006 (at 37 per cent), when his Republicans lost 30 seats in the House and six in the Senate.

Despite his low polling numbers, Trump is vowing to give "a lot of speeches" in states and districts where the races are tight to help Republican candidates. Some of those candidates are quietly asking the White House to keep him away, according to reporting by Politico.

What are the key issues in the midterms?

While U.S. polls differ slightly on the precise numbers, there's a strong thread of consistency suggesting the top issue of concern among voters right now is the cost of living.

Whether it's gas prices pushed up as a result of the war against Iran or the prices of consumer goods rising because of Trump's tariffs, pocketbook issues predominate the midterm polling.

Only one U.S. president since 1950 has held a polling approval rating below 40 per cent on the day of a midterm election. Trump is on track to be the second. (Mark Schiefelbein/The Associated Press)

Trump, as the dominant figure in U.S. politics for the past decade, will undoubtedly be an issue, particularly for moderate Republican or swing voters who backed him in the 2024 presidential election but have soured on him since then, according to polling.

Turnout in midterms is always lower than during presidential election years, so each party will be striving for ways to motivate their base. For the Democrats, weakening Trump's power could be that driving force. For the Republicans, stoking fear about what a Democratic-controlled Congress would do to the economy is a key advertising message.

Where are the key Senate races?

Of the 35 Senate seats up for election this time, fewer than 10 are considered by campaign analysts to be at risk of changing hands.

The Republicans are considered most vulnerable in North Carolina and Maine, but polling suggests they also are in tough to hang on to their Senate seats in Ohio, Alaska, Iowa and even Texas, where no Democrat has won a statewide election since 1988.

The Democrats' biggest challenges to hold appear to be in the Senate races in Michigan and New Hampshire.

Where are the key House races?

More than 80 per cent of House seats are considered safe for either the Republicans or the Democrats, according to the University of Virginia Center for Politics newsletter Crystal Ball, which has forecast and analyzed every election for U.S. president, House, Senate and state governors since 2002.
