World.title: EU Moves to Curb Airbnb-Style Rentals to Boost Long-Term Housing
World.content:
The EU has introduced a framework to support long-term rentals in tourist-heavy cities. Airbnb warns it creates regulatory uncertainty without improving long-term housing outcomes.

The EU has announced an affordable housing plan aimed at encouraging long-term rentals and making housing more accessible for Europeans.

Unveiled on Wednesday, the plan aims to create clarity and predictability in how rules are applied by local authorities, particularly in neighbourhoods popular with tourists where short-term rentals have displaced residents.



“Lack of affordable housing is a matter of concern for so many of our European citizens,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a press statement. “Essential workers and students cannot afford to live where they serve and study. But most importantly, it is about fairness. Today, we are delivering for all Europeans.”

“The new rules are designed to help competent authorities identify ‘areas under housing stress’ using a common methodology,” a Commission press release explains.

Housing in Europe is getting worse

The latest data on access to accommodation across Europe are worrying, and have pushed the Commission to intervene.

Recent Eurobarometer data shows that 50 per cent of European city dwellers think that housing is an urgent problem they experience. House prices have skyrocketed faster than local incomes across most European capitals, rising 64.9% between 2015 and 2025 and rents 21.8%, according to EU data.

Even people who cannot afford to buy are facing rising rents, which consume 40% of household income, and middle-class families are also increasingly facing a reality where they can’t afford to buy or rent, but also aren’t eligible for social housing.

Many residents in cities like Lisbon, Barcelona and Prague complain that short-term rental platforms like Airbnb have removed homes from the market and pushed prices up, often forcing them to move.

Short-term rentals represent only 1.2% of the EU’s total housing stock, but they can account for up to 20% in some tourism hotspots. With too few homes being built where demand is strongest, Brussels estimates it needs more than 2 million new homes every year to fix the problem.

Airbnb, the largest worldwide platform for short-term rentals, has criticised the plan as not sufficiently clear.

“Airbnb shares the Commission’s ambition to make housing more affordable. But as drafted, the Affordable Housing Act will not add a single home to the long term rental market, while adding regulatory uncertainty for hosts across European cities,” the company wrote in a press statement after the Commission’s announcement.

The plan must now be negotiated by the EU co-legislators before being approved.

World.title: Prague’s Industrial Palace to Reopen to the Public for Guided Tours
World.content:
After a major renovation costing more than CZK 3 billion, Prague’s Industrial Palace at the Výstaviště exhibition grounds will open its doors to the public in two weeks.

From September 25 to October 11, visitors will be able to explore the history and architecture of the landmark and see how it has been transformed during the renovation on guided tours organised by Výstaviště Praha and Prague City Tourism.



According to Výstaviště Praha, the palace will not remain open to the public on a regular basis after the tours. Instead, it will serve as a venue for exhibitions, trade fairs and other scheduled events.

The renovation of the Industrial Palace, including the reconstruction of its fire-damaged left wing, began in February 2022, more than 13 years after the wing was destroyed by a fire in October 2008.

The approximately one-hour guided tour costs CZK 91. Organisers say the symbolic price refers to 1891, the year the Industrial Palace first opened. Tickets are available through the Prague City Tourism website. Places are limited, and some tour dates have already sold out.

The first major event scheduled at the renovated palace will be the Designblok festival in early October.

Built in Just Ten Months

The Industrial Palace was built for the 1891 Jubilee Provincial Exhibition based on designs by architect Bedřich Münzberger. It is considered an important example of both artistic and technical heritage. The building was the first in the Czech lands to feature an architectural design based on a prefabricated iron structure.

Contemporary records show that 450 workers completed the building in just ten months, despite flooding and severe frosts affecting the exhibition grounds during construction.

From the beginning, the palace served as a venue for exhibitions and cultural events, although it was originally intended as a temporary structure.

Between 1952 and 1954, the communist government decided to repurpose the building, ordering its main hall to be converted into a social and dance hall. The building was also renamed the Congress Palace and became part of the Julius Fučík Cultural and Recreation Park, which operated at the site at the time.

One Wing of the Palace Was Destroyed by Fire

On October 16, 2008, a fire destroyed the left wing of the Industrial Palace after items left on an electric hot plate caught fire. The person responsible was never identified.

The renovation did not begin until early 2022. Under the original plans, the work was supposed to be completed last year.

However, once the foundations, floors and suspended ceilings of the right wing were uncovered, it became clear that the condition of the historic building was worse than expected, leading to additional work and delays.

World.title: New York Inspired New Residential Project in Prague’s Smíchov
World.content:
A new seven-story residential building planned for Prague’s Smíchov district has moved closer to construction after securing a zoning decision.

The project, known as Smíchovská Žehlička, is being developed by BPD Partners and Top Estates and is expected to be completed in 2029.

The building will contain 66 apartments as well as eight commercial units for shops, services and restaurants. It will also include shared coworking and community spaces. The total gross floor area is expected to be close to 8,000 square meters.

The project is planned for a wedge-shaped site between Kováků and Na Zatlance streets, directly below Mrázovka Park. The unusual shape of the plot and the significant difference in elevation between the two streets have made the site particularly difficult to develop.

The project has been in preparation for more than a decade. BPD Partners, the investment group owned by Czech businessmen Vasil Bobel, Petr Pudil and Jan Dobrovský, began working with architect Patrik Hoffman on the scheme in 2010.

Inspired by New York’s Flatiron Building

The shape of Smíchovská Žehlička is largely determined by the site’s narrow, wedge-shaped plot and surrounding streets. The design also takes inspiration from New York’s Flatiron Building, whose distinctive triangular form became a response to an equally unusual urban site.

The Prague project aims to use the constraints of its location in a similar way. Rather than attempting to conceal the site’s difficult geometry, the design makes it a defining feature of the building.

The residential units and commercial premises will all be offered for sale. The development will also provide shared areas intended for coworking and community activities.

If permitting and construction follow the current schedule, Smíchovská Žehlička could be completed by the end of 2029.

World.title: Award-Winning Holocaust Documentary to Premiere in Prague
World.content:
Award-winning Holocaust documentary UnBroken will have its Czech premiere at Prague’s Edison Filmhub on Friday, September 25.

The screening will take place alongside the opening of the new “Rescuers of Children” exhibition at the National Pedagogical Museum.

Director, producer and writer Beth Lane will attend the Prague screening.



The documentary tells the story of Lane’s mother, Ginger Lane, and her six siblings, who survived the Holocaust after being hidden for two years by German farmers Paula and Arthur Schmidt.

The seven Jewish children were sheltered on the couple’s farm in Brandenburg, about 60 kilometers east of Berlin. They survived the war and emigrated together to the United States in 1946.

They are believed to be the only known family of seven Jewish siblings to have survived the Holocaust and later emigrated together as a family. Ginger Lane, now 86, is one of two surviving members of the family.

Paula and Arthur Schmidt were later recognized by Yad Vashem as Righteous Among the Nations, an honor given to non-Jews who risked their lives to save Jews during the Holocaust.

Their story is also featured in “Rescuers of Children,” the new exhibition at the National Pedagogical Museum. The exhibition examines the experiences of children and other vulnerable people during the Holocaust and presents stories of individuals who risked their lives to help those facing persecution.

The Prague screening follows the documentary’s German premiere in Dachau on July 17, where UnBroken received the inaugural Lichtbrücke Prize for Human Rights in Film.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by UnBroken (@unbrokenthefilm)

The film premiered in 2023 at the Heartland International Film Festival, where it won Best Documentary Feature Premiere. It has since been screened in more than 50 cities, including at the United Nations in New York and Vienna, the Museum of Jewish Heritage in New York and the Pilecki Institute in Warsaw.

UnBroken was released on Netflix in the United States in April 2025 and has since surpassed 1.5 million streams there.

The Czech premiere will take place at Edison Filmhub in Prague on September 25, 2026.

World.title: GALLERY: One of Europe’s Largest Aquariums Set to Open in Czechia in 2028
World.content:
A new public aquarium costing around CZK 700 million is planned for the Brno Exhibition Centre, with construction expected to begin in 2027 and the first visitors arriving in the second half of 2028.

The project, called Green Planet: National Aquarium, will occupy Pavilion C at the Brno Exhibition Centre. It is expected to contain around 100 aquariums and water tanks holding more than four million liters of water.



The facility will be home to about 400,000 animals representing roughly 500 species, including rare species. Developers say the project will rank among the largest aquarium complexes in Europe.

Brno Mayor Markéta Vaňková said the aquarium could attract around 500,000 visitors during its first year of operation, including people from across the South Moravian Region and neighboring countries.

The main attraction will be a 2.5 million-liter ocean tank featuring a 55-meter underwater tunnel.

Visitors will be able to walk through the tunnel while observing marine life around and above them. The aquarium will also feature hundreds of other aquatic species across its various tanks.

The developers say the number of animals will put the complex among Europe’s largest aquariums. They estimate that it will contain around 36 times as many animals as the Barcelona Aquarium.

The project is also designed around reducing water consumption.

According to the plans, recirculation systems will clean and treat water before returning it to the tanks. The developers say efficient water management will be one of the project’s priorities.

Czech and international specialists are involved in preparing the aquarium, which is expected to include both educational and visitor-focused elements.

World.title: Prague to Host Central Europe’s First Climate Week
World.content:
Prague will host the first international climate week in Central Europe from September 14 to 20, with more than 50 conferences, seminars, workshops and other events planned across the city.

Climate Week Prague will bring together representatives from climate research, finance, government, business and other sectors to discuss how cities and economies can respond to climate change.

The official opening will take place at the Prague Planetarium on Monday, September 14, at 2:30 p.m.



Speakers will include former European Commissioner for Climate Action Connie Hedegaard, Deputy Director-General for Climate Policy at the European Commission and a former Czech environment minister Jan Dusík, and Prague Mayor Bohuslav Svoboda of the ODS party, who is supporting the event.

The program will cover a broad range of issues, including how cities can adapt to rising temperatures, water management, energy, construction, agriculture and transport.

Finance will be a major part of the agenda. The CEE Sustainable Finance Summit, running from September 14 to 16, will examine the impact of geopolitics and artificial intelligence on Europe’s economic competitiveness.

Climate Week Prague has been organized by a coalition of independent organizations led by the International Sustainable Finance Centre. The group also includes research institutions, the Climate Facts think tank, banks, investors and trade unions representing workers in the construction and energy sectors.

The organizers say the increasing effects of climate change, including more frequent heat waves, were among the main reasons for launching the event.

Data cited by Fakta o klimatu illustrates the change in Prague’s summer temperatures.

Between 1961 and 1990, the city recorded seven tropical nights, when temperatures remained at or above 20 degrees Celsius throughout the night. Over the following 35 years, that number increased to 165, according to data from the Czech Academy of Sciences’ Institute for Global Change Research.

Average summer minimum temperatures in Prague also increased during the period, rising from 13 to 15 degrees Celsius, according to Fakta o klimatu.

The local figures come as international assessments warn of further warming. Reuters reported earlier in September, citing the United Nations Environment Programme, that global temperatures are expected to exceed the key 1.5-degree-Celsius threshold above pre-industrial levels within the next few years.

Further warming is expected to contribute to more extreme weather and increase pressure on ecosystems, glaciers and low-lying coastal cities.

World.title: Prague’s Petřín Funicular to Return to Service on September 22
World.content:
Prague’s Petřín funicular will resume passenger service on Tuesday, September 22, 2026, following a two-year reconstruction of the railway and its infrastructure, the Prague Public Transit Company (DPP) has announced.

Service will begin at 7 a.m., with the new fourth-generation cars departing from both Újezd and Petřín stations.

Trains will then run according to the regular timetable, with departures every 10 minutes until 10:15 p.m.



The reopening comes almost exactly two years after the previous funicular was taken out of service. The third-generation cars made their final journey on September 13, 2024, after prolonged heavy rainfall destabilized and eroded sections of the hillside.

New cars increase capacity

The two new cars were designed by Czech designer Anna Marešová and built by Swiss manufacturer CWA Constructions SA. The vehicles cost a combined CZK 137.7 million and were delivered to Prague in April.

Each car can carry up to 120 passengers, compared with a capacity of 100 on the previous vehicles. The design also introduces glass roofs, giving passengers a clearer view of Petřín Hill during the journey.

Air conditioning, however, will not be installed. Because of technical limitations, the cars will instead use forced-air ventilation. The decision has already drawn criticism from some Prague residents, who have questioned how comfortable the cars will be during hot summer days, particularly given their large glass roofs.

The two-year reconstruction involved more than replacing the vehicles. Workers strengthened the foundations beneath the track, installed new rails and upgraded the funicular’s traction system.

How much will the new funicular cost?

A single journey will cost CZK 100 when purchased on site. Passengers using the PID Lítačka mobile application will pay CZK 90.

Passengers with valid long-term Prague public transport passes covering one month to one year will continue to ride without paying an additional fare.

The same applies to holders of 24-hour and 72-hour passes, children under 15 and passengers aged over 65.

World.title: Prague Botanical Garden to Host Grape Harvest Festival
World.content:
The Prague Botanical Garden will host its traditional grape harvest festival at St. Clare’s Vineyard on September 12 and 13, bringing two days of wine, fresh burčák, live music and activities for visitors.

The festival, known as Vinobraní na Vinici sv. Kláry, will feature wines from producers across the Czech Republic, Moravia and other countries.

Visitors will also have the chance to taste white and red burčák made from grapes harvested this year at St. Clare’s Vineyard.



The first grapes for the festival have already been picked by hand. Workers harvested 2,700 kilograms of table grapes and the Modrý Portugal variety. The grapes are now being used to produce this year’s burčák, a young wine that is still undergoing fermentation and is traditionally associated with the Czech grape harvest season.

Alongside wines from the St. Clare’s winery, the festival will present a selection of wines from other producers from the Czech Republic, Moravia and abroad.

Two days of live music

Music will be a major part of the weekend program. Saturday’s main stage lineup includes Jordan Haj and Emma Smetana, YES BROTHERS and 20 MINUTES.

On Sunday, visitors can see the Děda Mládek Illegal Band, BRASS AVENUE, MOVEBREAKERS and OFF BEAT ORCHESTRA. A second music stage will also operate near the St. Clare’s wine shop.

The festival program includes more than music and wine. Visitors can join guided tours of the vineyard, take part in workshops and creative activities, or attend the Vínohrátky educational program. The guided tours are included in the admission price.

The event will run from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. on both September 12 and 13. Activities will take place at St. Clare’s Vineyard and in the Ornamental Garden of the Prague Botanical Garden.

Tickets bought at the venue cost CZK 280 for adults and CZK 180 for children and young people aged 3 to 17.

Online tickets purchased by September 11 are CZK 250 for adults and CZK 150 for children and young people. Children under three can enter free of charge.

World.title: A new must-see in Budapest: rediscover the Citadella – photos
World.content:
If you live in Budapest, you already know the silhouette. High above the city on Gellért Hill, the Citadella and the Liberty Statue have been part of Budapest’s skyline for generations. Locals have even given the statue an affectionate nickname: the “bottle opener”, inspired by its unmistakable shape.

The Hungarian Bastille

Following a comprehensive renewal, the Citadella has reopened as a modern cultural and community destination, bringing together history, architecture, green spaces and some of the most spectacular views in Budapest. But behind the panorama lies one of the most fascinating historical locations in the city.

Source: Várkapitányság

Gellért Hill itself takes its name from Bishop Gellért, who, according to tradition, was martyred here nearly a thousand years ago. Centuries later, following the defeat of the 1848–49 Hungarian Revolution and War of Independence, the Habsburg authorities built the Citadella above the city, a fortress that came to be seen as a kind of “Hungarian Bastille” and a powerful symbol of oppression.

Its walls still bear traces of the Second World War, while the Liberty Statue above the fortress has witnessed another dramatic chapter of Hungarian history. The monument became associated with Soviet rule, and during the 1956 Revolution the symbols of communist power surrounding it were torn down. Yet the central figure survived, was later reinterpreted, and today remains one of the defining symbols of Budapest.

Source: Várkapitányság

Few places tell the complex story of the city quite so vividly.

To understand Hungary, start at the Citadella in Budapest

At the heart of the renewed Citadella, the Bastion of Liberty offers an immersive introduction to thirteen centuries of Hungarian history in more than 1,700 square metres. In around half an hour, visitors can gain an insight into the events that shaped Hungary, making it an ideal starting point for anyone who lives, studies, works or does business here.

Source: Várkapitányság

Interactive installations, cinematic storytelling and audiovisual experiences bring the past closer, while an audio guide available in 10 languages makes the exhibition easily accessible to Budapest’s international community.

The experience is also an ideal addition to a business programme in Budapest. International colleagues, clients and partners can discover the country behind the destination and gain valuable cultural and historical context in a compact, engaging format.

Tailor-made programmes are available for corporate and professional groups, contact us to request an individual offer. For an entirely different experience, discover the Citadella during one of our sunset walks. Watch Budapest change as the sun sets over the city and experience the renewed fortress and its panoramic terraces in a unique atmosphere.

Source: Várkapitányság

From fortress to public space

For much of its history, the Citadella was designed to keep people out. Today, the opposite is true. The renewal has opened the former military fortress to the city. New passages connect the two sides of Gellért Hill, while a distinctive V-shaped opening breaks through the once-enclosed fortress walls.

At its centre, a new public park of more than 6,000 square metres is surrounded by renewed green spaces, walkways and panoramic terraces, transforming the Citadella into a place to meet, walk, relax and experience Budapest from above.

Source: Várkapitányság

If you missed – Gellért Hill: Budapest’s iconic landmark of history, liberty and breathtaking views

See Budapest differently

Walk through Citadella Park, explore the renewed fortress walls and take in the city from the Round Bastion Terrace and Roof Garden 360.

Bring friends who have just moved to Budapest. Visit with family, introduce international colleagues and business partners to Hungary, or simply rediscover one of the city’s most familiar landmarks for yourself.

Because living like a local is about more than knowing the city. It is about understanding the stories behind it. The Citadella has watched over Budapest for generations. Now it is Budapest’s turn to rediscover it.

Live like a local. Discover the history. See Budapest differently.

Citadella reopening: Budapest landmark with one of the city’s best panoramas welcomes visitors again

World.title: Inside the Karpacz Economic Forum 2026: Poland’s rise, political divides and the future of the V4
World.content:
Three days, more than 6,500 participants, hundreds of panel discussions, politicians, businesspeople, local government leaders and experts – the Karpacz Economic Forum 2026 was an impressive event by its sheer scale alone. Yet what was even more interesting on the ground was seeing how the economic and political figures of one of Europe’s most dynamically developing countries view their own situation. And also how differently the very same economic figures can be interpreted.

All this took place not in Warsaw, Kraków or another major Polish city, but in Karpacz, a mountain resort near the Czech border.

A small town that becomes one of Poland’s centres for three days

At first glance, the choice of venue may seem surprising. Karpacz is hardly a conventional conference city, yet the Hotel Gołębiewski and the surrounding infrastructure have enough capacity to host an event attended by several thousand people without major disruption.

According to the official summary by Forum Ekonomiczne, more than 6,500 participants attended the 35th Economic Forum, held between 8 and 10 September, with more than 500 debates, panels and other events taking place. The programme covered eight major thematic areas, ranging from the economy and international politics to digitalisation, artificial intelligence and healthcare.

The true scale of the event could best be appreciated on site. Conference rooms were spread across several floors of the hotel and in pavilions erected in front of the building, while gala events and banquets were held on a separate floor. According to the organisers’ official information, even the logistics centre itself was located 3.5 kilometres from the main conference venue.

According to an on-site report by wroclaw.pl, around 500 media representatives, 1,200 local government officials and 900 foreign delegates arrived in Karpacz. Although a significant part of the programme was held in Polish and focused primarily on Polish issues, interpretation was available for the more important panels, making much of the conference accessible to international participants as well.

Karpacz Economic Forum 2026. Photo by Daily News Hungary

Karpacz Economic Forum 2026: a strong economy facing serious dilemmas

One of the most interesting lessons of the three days for me was just how differently the same economic data can be interpreted.

Poland is recording particularly strong growth by European standards. The European Commission’s May forecast projected GDP growth of 3.5 percent for 2026, while unemployment remains exceptionally low. At the same time, the picture is far from problem-free: the Commission expected a budget deficit of 6.5 percent and a further increase in public debt.

The OECD’s June forecast was somewhat more cautious, projecting growth of 3 percent in 2026 and specifically highlighting risks related to energy prices, global demand and the geopolitical situation in the region.

In Karpacz, therefore, the same economic performance was presented in one discussion as proof of a successful convergence model, and in another as the starting point for examining the challenges facing a country entering a new stage of development.

Perhaps this was precisely what made the forum so interesting: within just a few conference rooms of one another, it was possible to hear entirely different conclusions drawn from the same economic reality.

Karpacz Economic Forum 2026. Photo by Daily News Hungary Karpacz Economic Forum 2026. Photo by Daily News Hungary

Both government and opposition figures turned out in Karpacz

Numerous prominent figures from Polish political life also attended the forum. The organisers highlighted the participation of, among others, Defence Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, Deputy Prime Minister and Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski, Development Minister Katarzyna Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, Science Minister Marcin Kulasek, Deputy Speaker of the Sejm Krzysztof Bosak and former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki, while numerous state secretaries were also present.

The presence of right-wing and opposition politicians was particularly conspicuous. Morawiecki received a standing ovation, while Krzysztof Bosak’s appearance also prompted a strong reaction from the audience. According to the report, former Prime Minister Beata Szydło and former Defence Minister Mariusz Błaszczak also spoke at the event. Andrzej Duda, Poland’s president between 2015 and 2025, likewise appeared at several events.

The gala dinners were among the forum’s most spectacular occasions. This was where awards recognising outstanding achievements in the economy, business and public life were presented. Perhaps the most important of these, the 2026 Person of the Year award, went to Infrastructure Minister Dariusz Klimczak.

In case you missed it – Looking beyond price per square metre: how the new-build housing markets of Budapest, Warsaw and Bucharest differ

Morawiecki: the V4 must continue even when countries are led by different political camps

Mateusz Morawiecki’s appearance was particularly interesting to me because I also had the opportunity to put a question directly to the former Polish prime minister at the forum.

Karpacz Economic Forum 2026. Photo by Daily News Hungary

I asked whether, if he were to return to government following Poland’s 2027 election, he would continue Visegrád Group cooperation even if Hungary’s prime minister were Péter Magyar rather than Viktor Orbán.

Morawiecki gave an unequivocal yes.

According to the former Polish prime minister, the V4 must be maintained at all costs, and it must not be allowed to fall apart or lose its significance again simply because the countries concerned are governed by political forces with differing views.

The essence of his answer was that regional cooperation must survive party-political differences. Poland, Hungary, Czechia and Slovakia share numerous economic, infrastructural and geopolitical interests that remain regardless of which political camp happens to be in power.

The message is particularly noteworthy because the V4 has been on hold in recent years precisely because of foreign-policy and political differences among its member states.

Polish–Hungarian rail links: Budapest to Warsaw took ten hours 20 years ago – and still does today

A much more critical assessment of the state of Polish–Hungarian relations was heard during another panel.

Balázs Szabó, president of the Polish Nationality Self-Government of Dunakeszi and the Association of Modern Polish Thought, said that in his view the previous Hungarian government had not done enough over its 16 years in office to develop Polish–Hungarian relations in practical terms, with transport providing one of the clearest examples.

Karpacz Economic Forum 2026. Photo by Daily News Hungary

Szabó pointed out that around 20 years ago it took roughly ten hours to travel by train from Budapest to Warsaw, and that journey times have not decreased substantially since then.

He considered this particularly problematic given that Hungary undertook a major international railway investment in another direction: the Budapest–Belgrade railway line was upgraded, while no project of comparable scale was launched towards Poland.

According to Szabó, a modern Budapest–Warsaw connection would go far beyond tourism.

A north–south railway connection could also be of strategic importance for logistics, freight transport and closer links between the countries of the region. While new north–south logistics corridors and high-speed rail connections are being developed across Europe, Hungary is not yet a major player in these networks.

Szabó said, however, that some change may already be perceptible. He noted that Dávid Vitézy, transport and investment minister in Hungary’s new government, has already spoken about developing rail connections towards Poland. This does not yet amount to a concrete investment project, but he believes it is an important indication that the issue could once again make its way onto Hungary’s transport policy agenda.

Vitézy is indeed preparing a large-scale railway development programme: according to a 11 September report by 24.hu, the minister spoke about a comprehensive HUF 3.5 trillion – approximately EUR 9.6 billion – rail and transport development framework.

More than fifty Hungarians attended the forum

The composition of the participants was also interesting from a Hungarian perspective. More than fifty people from Hungary registered for the event, several of whom also spoke in panel discussions.

In previous years, the Hungarian delegation regularly included ministers from the Orbán government as well as political and public figures close to the former governing party. This year, several Fidesz politicians or participants linked to the previous period of government could again be seen at the event, while high-level representation from the new government led by Péter Magyar was much less noticeable.

Among those present was former Speaker of the Hungarian National Assembly László Kövér, who had originally been scheduled for two events but ultimately took part in one panel discussion. Péter Márki-Zay, mayor of Hódmezővásárhely, also travelled to Karpacz and attended several events. Their encounter even made it into the Hungarian press: 24.hu reported that, according to Márki-Zay, László Kövér declined to shake his outstretched hand.

The composition of the Hungarian participants was also interesting in light of the fundamental change in Hungary’s political situation a few months earlier. The personal and institutional network built up over recent years was still clearly visible at the forum, while relations between Hungary’s new government and the Karpacz Economic Forum are evidently still at the beginning of a new era.

I was invited to one of Central Europe’s largest economic forums, as the owner of DNH MEDIA GROUP Ltd., by the Warsaw Enterprise Institute Foundation to attend both the event and the press trip that followed.

Karpacz Economic Forum: much more than just an economic conference

By the end of the Karpacz Economic Forum 2026, this was perhaps my strongest impression: although it is called an economic forum, for three days it effectively becomes a Central European meeting place where economics, politics, geopolitics, infrastructure, technology and business are almost inseparable.

Karpacz Economic Forum 2026. Photo by Daily News Hungary

Conversations in the corridors and over dinner were at least as important as those taking place on stage. And across the hundreds of panels, it was sometimes possible to hear completely different answers to the same question depending on whether one was listening to a minister, an opposition politician, a businessperson or an economist.

By many indicators, Poland has every reason to look to the coming years with optimism. At the same time, Karpacz also showed that rapid economic growth does not in itself eliminate dilemmas. On the contrary: the greater the country’s economic and political weight becomes, the more important the question of how it chooses to use that strength.

From a Hungarian perspective, one of the most important lessons may have been something that emerged in two very different discussions: Polish–Hungarian relations cannot be built solely on the political friendship of whichever parties happen to be in government. Whether the issue is the V4 or a modern railway connecting Budapest and Warsaw, long-term cooperation requires relationships and infrastructure capable of surviving changes of government.

As we wrote after the election, Polish–Hungarian friendship could gain new momentum. Magyar and Tusk discussed exactly this in Warsaw.

World.title: Former PM Orbán reveals why he nominated man for high state honour later convicted for sexual abuse of many children
World.content:
Former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán has revealed why he nominated the paedophile director of the children’s home in Bicske for a high state honour.

Péter Magyar, Hungary’s prime minister, today published a document proving that the director was nominated for the award in a submission bearing Orbán’s signature. Proceedings had already been brought against him in 2011, yet the nomination went ahead on the recommendation of Zoltán Balog, then minister for human resources.

Orbán brushes off question

Asked today in Kötcse why he had nominated the director of the Bicske children’s home in 2016 – he has since been convicted of paedophile offences – Orbán replied that someone had put his name forward and that the press should ask the person responsible.

Péter Magyar speaking in the Hungarian Parliament. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Anita

Magyar had earlier published the nomination document, which bears the name of Orbán, who was prime minister at the time, as the signatory. It said the director deserved the honour for his work educating disadvantaged children and preparing them for independent lives.

If you missed – Sexual abuse, starvation, squalor and accident hazards: Orbán’s government concealed the reality of Hungary’s children’s homes

The scandal surrounding János Vásárhelyi erupted in 2016, after a former resident of the Bicske children’s home took his own life, having grown tired of nobody believing him. Vásárhelyi was convicted in 2019, but the first official complaint and police investigation against him dated back to 2011, after two employees of the home reported that several children had accused him of sexually abusing them. Police closed the investigation in 2012, citing a lack of evidence.

Nomination came from Zoltán Balog

“It was the same Zoltán Balog who recommended the paedophile director of the Bicske children’s home for a state honour to Viktor Orbán, and who later secured a presidential pardon from Katalin Novák for Endre Kónya, an accomplice in the paedophile abuse,” Magyar wrote on Facebook on Saturday.

Paedophile Hungarian director to be released from prison: one abuse victim died by suicide

World.title: Péter Magyar’s remarks point to a radical U-turn on same-sex couples’ right to adopt
World.content:
Péter Magyar was asked at a press conference on Saturday, where he presented a report on the child protection system, whether the government planned to change the current rules requiring ministerial approval for adoptions by single people and same-sex couples.

Same-sex couples already faced an uphill battle

The prime minister repeated his earlier view that anyone who believes a child is better off with criminals or in inhumane conditions than with either a single parent or two good same-sex parents is a particularly evil person.

He said the system would be changed because such decisions should not be made by a minister, but by professionals capable of determining the conditions and support a particular child needs in order to grow up to become a happy and well-balanced member of society.

Péter Magyar answering press questions. Photo: MTI

Orbán governments had previously tightened rules

The legislation still in force was passed by Parliament at the end of 2020 through an amendment to the Civil Code. In practice, it took effect on 1 March 2021, when a government decree made the adoption of children by single people subject to the personal approval of the minister responsible for family policy. At the time, the post was held by Katalin Novák, the former president who later resigned over the child abuse scandal in Bicske.

The Orbán government justified the measure by arguing that children’s healthy development could be ensured only in families made up of a man and a woman – a father and a mother.

As same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt in Hungary, they had previously been able to apply as so-called sole adopters. In practice, the ministerial approval requirement restricted this avenue. Applications were later assessed by ministers responsible for family policy, including the heads of the Ministry of Culture and Innovation.

If you missed: Is it acceptable to take children to Budapest Pride? Row erupts over a photo shared on Facebook

Adoptions became considerably harder

During the first two years after the measure was introduced, the ministry approved almost every application submitted by a single applicant who had already been deemed professionally suitable. The decision was not made personally by the minister, but by one of the ministry’s administrative departments on the basis of the documents.

This was misleading, however, because the multiple layers of administration and the recommendation process slowed applications down, meaning that a significant proportion never reached the decision-makers. In 2024, for example, just 11 single parents managed to adopt a child in Hungary.

Meanwhile, 2,416 children were waiting to be adopted in 2025, while 1,478 approved prospective parents were registered, according to figures from the Hungarian Central Statistical Office.

Check out some more articles concerning the adoption of same-sex couples in our LGTBQ in Hungary archive.

World.title: How a brilliant Hungarian entrepreneur helped America after 9/11 – and asked for nothing in return
World.content:
A car escorted by eight police motorcyclists arrived outside the company’s headquarters carrying damaged, burned and mangled storage devices. The Americans could only hope that the world-leading Hungarian firm Kürt would be able to recover the data damaged in the 9/11 terrorist attacks. The company, founded by Sándor Kürti, went on to perform an astonishing feat.

Bush was stunned by the company’s expertise

“Tell me – what makes you so good at what you do?” President Bush asked Sándor Kürti, the founder and chairman of the world-leading Hungarian data-recovery firm Kürt, during an official visit to Budapest.

The company had achieved what seemed impossible: it recovered invaluable data from storage devices that had plunged to the ground with the Twin Towers, and had been badly damaged and burned in the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks.

Attack against the South Tower. Photo: Wikimedia Commons

Images of the 9/11 attack on New York’s symbolic World Trade Centre shocked the world. But in Budapest, someone immediately recognised that the aftermath might require specialist technical assistance. Dea Csuba, a Kürt employee, suggested that the United States might need the expertise of the Hungarian data-recovery company.

Sándor Kürti. Photo: Wikimedia Commons

The firm soon contacted the Hungarian embassy in Washington and offered to restore data from computer storage devices recovered from the ruins of the Twin Towers. What is more, it asked for no payment.

The United States accepted the offer within a few days, while the FBI imposed strict confidentiality requirements on the company.

Damaged drives were sent to Budapest

The Hungarian experts did not even need to travel to America. The hard drives recovered from the rubble were transported to Hungary, where the extraordinarily difficult recovery operation began.

The result surprised even the Americans. According to Sándor Kürti’s recollection, the company managed to recover around 96 per cent of the data believed to be lost in the 9/11 attacks. Only information stored on devices physically destroyed by the intense heat generated when the aircraft struck the towers was lost for good.

President Bush learning about the terrorist attack in a school. Photo: Wikimedia Commons

Although the company received not a single dollar directly for its assistance, the operation proved to be a turning point commercially. Kürt became known around the world and grew into one of the leading names in data recovery and information security.

If you missed: 9/11 terrorist attack commemorated in Budapest – photos

Thanks from the governor and the president

The story also had a diplomatic sequel. First, George Pataki, then governor of New York, personally thanked Sándor Kürti. Later, when George W. Bush visited Budapest, the American president also wanted to meet him.

The inauguration of the Budapest statue of George H. W. Bush, the father of the 43rd President. Photo: Facebook/Zoltán Kovács

Bush approached Kürti during a parliamentary dinner. Kürti recalled that the president was delighted to finally meet him in person.

He remembers Bush’s words verbatim: “Alex, I’m so glad to finally meet you.” The president then asked what made the Hungarian company so good at what it did.

As Kürti spoke about the firm’s work, Bush held his hand in a lengthy handshake, according to Index.

Cyberattack hits Hungary’s State Treasury as experts trace attack to Russian servers

World.title: Viktor Orbán on the past 16 years: everything was lawful and appropriate, all else is political propaganda
World.content:
Viktor Orbán, the Fidesz president and former prime minister, dismissed as political propaganda a series of complaints filed in connection with the previous government, speaking to reporters on Saturday before a meeting in Kötcse.

‘Everything was lawful and appropriate’, says Orbán

The party leader was asked about the investigation into the Volán case involving allegedly overpriced bus purchases, in which, among others, the former chief executive of the Hungarian National Asset Management Company has been summoned to give evidence.

Mr Orbán said that, in this particular case, the internal investigation had been launched by the previous government. He added that he was familiar with all the complaints recently filed in connection with the former administration.

“They are all political propaganda. Every one of these cases was lawful and appropriate,” he said. “I would be happy to explain them one by one,” he added.

‘The country can count on us’

“Our job is to be ready. If the country needs us, it can count on us,” Mr Orbán said in Kötcse, in Somogy County, on Saturday.

Speaking to reporters at the closed-door Civic Picnic, organised by the Foundation for a Civic Hungary, the Fidesz president and former prime minister said Hungary had enjoyed “16 fantastic years” as a result of civic and national-conservative government.

Hungary had been in a “colonial” position in 2010, but they had succeeded in creating an independent, sovereign and successful country, Mr Orbán said.

He added that the right had won four elections in a row, before losing one after 20 years. “I wish the right only had to lose an election once every 20 years,” he said.

Diesel support, migration, the future of his political group

Regarding a proposed monthly payment of HUF 5,000 for diesel-car owners, he said that an amendment to this year’s budget was before Parliament, including HUF 500 billion set aside in case of an energy crisis. “There is money available. Our proposal is to reinstate the protected price, which should never have been scrapped,” the former prime minister said. The budget contained the funds to do so, he added: “Give it to the people.”

Asked about migration policy, he said Hungary had “protected Europe and neighbouring countries” for more than a decade. “There is no migration at all in the Czech Republic and Slovakia, and there is no larger influx in Austria because Hungary protected Europe’s external borders,” he said.

If you missed – Former state secretary: Former PM Orbán ordered Hungary to pay more for a telecom company than the owners had asked

The former prime minister also said there were currently numerous initiatives within Fidesz, all of which he supported. The right had always been diverse, he said, but its members had agreed on three things.

Migrant crisis in the EU. Photo: depositphotos.com

“We agreed that Hungary’s sovereignty was paramount; that freedom was essential; and that the traditions and heritage handed down to us by our forebears must be preserved and built upon,” Viktor Orbán said.

As leader of the right and prime minister, he added, it had been his task “to turn this diversity into a measure of effective government action”.

Former state secretary: Former PM Orbán ordered Hungary to pay more for a telecom company than the owners had asked

World.title: PM Magyar: Orbán government knew about child abuse but did nothing – Tisza government pledges immediate action
World.content:
The government will submit a package of legislation to Parliament next week aimed at strengthening children’s rights and safety, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said in Budapest on Saturday. He was speaking at a press conference presenting a report on the country’s child-protection system.

Rules to be tightened

Magyar said the rules governing content accessible to minors would be tightened, including material that depicts sexual violence or sexuality explicitly, or promotes exploitation and manipulation.

Child-protection requirements covering outdoor advertising, political s and media content will also be strengthened, he added. The Prime Minister said the law would also set out stricter requirements for how the state must deal with children stranded in hospital, ensuring that no child is left there for months simply because the system has failed to find suitable care.

Photo: MTI

The state would “never again turn its head away”, Magyar said. It would no longer conceal reports or abandon children and professionals working in the field. “The era of denial is over,” he said. “From now on, there will be action, the provision of the necessary resources and strict accountability.”

Government launches emergency programme

The government will also launch an immediate child-protection crisis programme worth around 10 billion forints. “We cannot afford to wait for next year’s budget; immediate action is needed,” Magyar said at the press conference, where he outlined the report and the Government’s planned measures.

According to the Prime Minister, around 6 billion forints will be spent on direct professional programmes, while a further 3.4 billion will fund developments, preferably before the end of this year. The professional programmes will create 184 new places, or places with new functions. They will also strengthen the protection and care provided at 15 specialist children’s homes, while immediate crisis accommodation will be established for 80 children, he said.

Photo: MTI

Magyar added that targeted care would be introduced for children with autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disabilities and severe psychological or behavioural problems. A residential rehabilitation programme for children with addiction problems will also be launched, while around 440 million forints will be allocated immediately to support vulnerable adolescent girls and young mothers.

If you missed – PM Magyar unveils major changes: Huge pay rises, tougher environmental fines and radical concession changes

Child abuse was systematic and ongoing

Child abuse within the child-protection system was systematic and ongoing, while the Orbán government knew about it but did nothing, Magyar said at the press conference in Budapest. He said the Interior Ministry, led by Sándor Pintér, knew precisely what was happening, MTI wrote.

According to the ministry’s own internal data, 1,959 cases of child abuse were recorded in state-run child-protection institutions in 2024, followed by a further 1,684 cases in 2025. Police complaints were filed on 2,249 occasions over the two-year period – an average of more than three reports every day. The true figure could be considerably higher, as many cases of abuse remained hidden, the Prime Minister said.

As a private citizen and a father, Magyar said he found it incomprehensible that the Orbán government had known about the abuse and had even created the conditions in which it occurred, yet did nothing when it saw the consequences.

In Magyar’s assessment, the Orbán government had not merely failed politically; it had also failed a basic test of humanity.

Former school guard jailed in Hungary for sexually abusing two vulnerable minors

World.title: Anti-Austrian fury erupts after Hungarian Harley-Davidson rider is fined in Austria
World.content:
A Hungarian Harley-Davidson rider paid a EUR 2,400 fine — equivalent to roughly HUF 1 million — on the spot in Austria after police said her motorcycle was 10 decibels louder than the level recorded on its registration document.

The woman knew her bike was not entirely compliant with regulations, but had not expected the breach to have such serious consequences. The case has sparked outrage among Hungarian motorcyclists, while a Hungarian living in Austria said the real question should be why anyone would travel to a country known for particularly strict checks on noisy vehicles with a modified motorcycle — and then seek to stir up anti-Austrian sentiment on social media.

Motorcycle exceeded permitted noise level

The incident took place in the Faaker See area of Carinthia during European Bike Week, a Harley-Davidson gathering. According to the rider’s account, police inspected the motorcycle for more than half an hour before carrying out a noise-level test.

Hungarian Harley-Davidson rider received huge fine in Austria because of her modified motorcycle. Photo: depositphotos.com

According to the woman’s post, the measurement showed that the motorcycle was “only” 10 decibels louder than the figure recorded in its registration document.

At the end of the inspection, she was fined EUR 2,400, which she paid on the spot by bank card. The roadside technical inspection cost a further EUR 20, while the motorcycle’s number plate was removed and its registration document was withheld.

The rider was not, however, ordered to have the motorcycle taken away immediately. She was allowed to return to her accommodation under police escort, sparing her the additional cost of motorcycle recovery.

It was not “just” 10 decibels

A Hungarian living in Austria who responded to the incident pointed out in a Facebook post that the additional 10 decibels should not be dismissed as a minor discrepancy.

The decibel scale is logarithmic: according to the account, a 10-decibel increase represents ten times the sound intensity, while the human ear perceives the noise as roughly twice as loud. In other words, this was not a difference of just a few per cent.

The source said Austrian authorities, particularly in Carinthia and Tyrol, had for years been carrying out targeted checks on modified and excessively loud exhaust systems. During major motorcycling events, they apply a zero-tolerance approach.

She could have faced a far larger fine

Under Austria’s Road Traffic Act, fines for unauthorised technical modifications and excessive noise can reach as much as EUR 10,000. By comparison, the EUR 2,400 penalty was relatively moderate; it merely appears steep to a Hungarian pocket.

It is important to note, however, that the rider did not publish the official document relating to the fine. It is therefore impossible to establish with certainty which offences were involved, or on what legal grounds the final sum of EUR 2,400 was calculated.

The removal of the number plate and registration document was not an arbitrary act by the police either. In cases of substantial noise violations, Austrian regulations allow — and in certain circumstances require — authorities to prevent the vehicle from being used any further.

She knew the motorcycle was not fully compliant

One of the most significant details in the case is that, by her own account, the rider was aware that her Harley-Davidson did not fully comply with the regulations.

Despite this, she set off for the motorcycling event. That was why the Hungarian living in Austria raised the issue of self-reflection in her post. She argued that anyone planning to attend an event such as European Bike Week should take particular care to check local regulations in advance, since the authorities around Faaker See pay special attention to loud and modified motorcycles during the event.

Local residents also regularly complain about the motorcycle noise generated during the gathering, which can continue around the clock and places additional pressure on the police.

If you missed it: PHOTOS: Harley-Davidson festival in Budapest – two bikers died

Anti-Austrian sentiment spills over

The incident prompted furious reactions in Hungarian motorcycling groups. According to the account, the comments included anti-Austrian slurs, accusations of Nazism and a series of crude insults.

The author who responded to the incident said the original post had presented the case in an excessively one-sided manner and had mainly served to fuel hostility towards Austrian police. Meanwhile, the fact that the motorcycle had not been fully compliant in the first place — and that a 10-decibel excess constitutes a significant breach — had been pushed into the background.

She and several commenters stressed that, in their experience, Austrian authorities would have acted in exactly the same way against an excessively loud Austrian or German rider as they did against a Hungarian national.

Mystery solved: Here’s which unit the WWII German motorcycle found in the Danube was linked to – photos

World.title: Kosovo Ex-President Thaci’s Defence Seeks Acquittal in Obstruction of Justice Trial
World.content:
The defence teams of former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci and four others co-accused of obstruction of justice in Thaci’s war crimes trial at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague have called for their acquittal, accusing the prosecution of charging them based on conversations that did not result in any witness-tampering or intimidation.

The prosecution claims that that during visits at the Detention Centre in The Hague, where Thaci is being held, he told the other four defendants – Hajredin Kuci, Fadil Fazliu, Isni Kilaj and Bashkim Smakaj – to instruct certain witnesses in his war-crimes trial about what to say in court.

But Sophie Menegon, Thaci’s lawyer, told the court during closing statements on Thursday that Thaci was “on trial for having a conversation in the Detention Unit [where he is being held pending the verdict in his war crimes trial]. There is no allegation of a bribe, compulsion, or threat against witnesses.”

She added: “There is no allegation of actual interference with witnesses …There isn’t any victim in this case …The prosecution asks you to send Mr Thaci to prison for six years over conversations inside a detention unit that resulted in zero real-world impact.”

The claims are based on recordings of the visits as well as physical evidence found also at Kilaj’s home in November 2023 – less than a month after Kryeziu and Kilaj met Thaci – allegedly printed via the only printer at the detention centre that Thaci could use.

Thaci and his four-co-accused have denied wrongdoing.

Smakaj’s lawyer, Jonathan Elystan Rees, in his closing statements on Friday, called for the acquittal of all the defendants.

“You should find Mr Smakaj and all the other defendants not guilty, whether individually or collectively,” he said, because Smakaj’s actions did not obstruct or have an impact on the course of justice.

Smakaj “cannot be convicted on the allegation that he intentionally aided in disobeying court orders, because he was completely unaware of the court’s orders”, Rees said.

He added: “There is no evidence from the prosecution, nor any legal obligation, requiring my client to be aware of the operational guidelines and functioning procedures of the detention centres.”

The lawyer for Isni Kilaj, Ian Edwards, told the court on Friday that Kilaj did not take any action after visiting Thaci at the Detention Centre in The Hague, saying he “neither called nor met with any witnesses”, so showing a lack of intent to obstruct justice.

“Everything else is mud that the prosecution is throwing at Mr Kilaj, hoping that some of it will tarnish his reputation,” he added.

David Young, lawyer for Fadil Fazliu, highlighted that his client was not even questioned by the prosecution.

“We can infer that the prosecution adopted a strategic approach of not interviewing them, of not questioning these individuals regarding the allegations. Is this the right way to initiate investigations or bring charges? I believe not. I state clearly that it is not,” Young told the court.

Alexander Admiral, lawyer for Hajredin Kuci, told the court that his client had been charged based on a wrongful translation of a message he sent to one of the witnesses in Thaci’s war-crimes trial, former Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA fighter Rrustem Mustafa.

According to Admiral, the message had been misinterpreted as passing a note from a third individual when the rightful translation revealed that Kuci was passing his support to Mustafa and was basically “a man calming an old friend”.

During the prosecution’s closing statements on Thursday, it was claimed that Thaci tried to influence Mustafa and another former KLA, fighter, Bislim Zyrapi, both of whom were testifying in his war-crimes case.

The testimony of both men favoured Thaci’s defence.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was created specifically to try former members of the KLA; it is located in The Hague and staffed by international judges and prosecutors due to doubts about the Kosovo justice system’s own ability to try former KLA fighters, many of whom are considered heroes in Kosovo. Witness-tampering has been one of its key concerns from the outset.

World.title: Kosovo Parliament Hit by Fresh Dispute Over Deputy Speakers
World.content:
Kosovo parliament session on September 11, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

Kosovo’s parliament failed to find a way out of a fresh crisis on Friday when MPs reconvened in two attempts to elect new deputy speakers.

The legislature derived from the June 7 snap partliamentary elections has not yet been inaugurated because the ruling Vetevendosje party refuses to support proposed candidates from two opposition parties, Vlora Citaku, from the Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, and Kujtim Shala, from the Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK.

Under the constitutional rules, parliament cannot be considered inaugurated until the speaker and all five deputies are elected.

Albulena Haxhiu from Vetevendosje was elected speaker on Wednesday, Ardian Gola, from the same party, was installed as deputy on Friday.

When Citaku of the PDK received only 44 of a minimum of 61 votes on Friday, her party colleagues left the session and accused Albin Kurti’s Vetevendosje of blocking the inauguration of parliament.

“As of today, the PDK has no reason to participate in parliamentary sessions and we will take the case to the Constitutional Court,” Bedri Hamza, the PDK leader, said as soon as speaker Albulena Haxhiu interrupted the session.

In the June elections, Vetevendosje won 53 of the 120 seats in the chamber, well ahead of the next-placed PDK, which won 22 seats. The LDK came third with 18 seats.

Vetevendosje claims it can call on 62 MPs to form a new government, again relying on the support of MPs from ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk and Bosniak – plus one of the Serb MPs.

However, the wider crisis that led to the June 7 elections has not been solved, as parliament needs to elect a new president of Kosovo within two months of its inauguration. Failure to do so would trigger another election, the fourth within less than two years.

As the post-election blockage enters its second month, Kurti and LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku agreed on August 31 to nominate Bekim Sejdiu, a former Constitutional Court judge and former diplomat, as Kosovo’s president. But, days later, six LDK MPs refused to support his candidacy, making the necessary quorum impossible.

For a president to be elected, a candidate must win at least 80 votes in the first two rounds. In a potential third round, they need a simple majority of only 61 votes.

Arberie Nagavci, head of Vetevendosje’s parliamentary group, said its MPs would not support any candidate for deputy speaker who is against the deal on the new president. Both Citaku and Shala have announced their opposition to Sejdiu’s candidacy.

“Of course, the MPs who are in favour of the Vetevendosje-LDK agreement [on the president] have the support of our 53 MPs,” Nagavci said after the interruption of the session.

Parliament will resume work on Sunday.

World.title: Bosnia Charges Seven Over Deadly Fire at Tuzla Elderly People’s Care Home
World.content:
Investigators inspect the scene after the fire at the nursing home in Tuzla, November 5, 2025. Photo: EPA/NIDAL SALJIC.

Prosecutors in Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Tuzla Canton on Friday indicted seven people over the fire at a Tuzla nursing home in November 2025 that killed 15 elderly residents and injured more than 30 others.

The indictment charges former nursing home director Mirsad Bakalovic, service head Zinaida Razic Halilovic and Mustafa Azabagic, who was responsible for fire and occupational safety at the facility.

Three employees of the Tuzla-based company Inproz, which prepared the nursing home’s 2021 fire risk assessment, are also indicted: Nedim Dzambic, Mirsad Zukancic and Jasmin Softic. The seventh defendant is Ibrahim Sarajlic, a fire safety inspector in Tuzla Canton.

The defendants are charged with serious offences against public safety. Bakalovic is also charged with abuse of office and authority, the prosecutor’s office said.

Prosecutors allege that between April 2021 and November 4, 2025, the defendants failed to implement or order legally required fire safety and general safety measures, despite knowing the facility was classified as a high-risk building.

The nursing home run by the city of Tuzla housed 180 elderly residents, 110 of whom were seriously ill, immobile or living with disabilities.

According to the indictment, the failures included inadequate supervision of residents with limited mobility, inappropriate accommodation and allocation of residents according to their health and mobility, and an inadequate fire prevention and protection system.

Prosecutors said these failures prevented the timely detection and containment of the fire, the early detection and reporting of fire and carbon monoxide in residents’ rooms, the evacuation of residents, and the removal of smoke and heat from the building.

“As official and responsible persons, by failing to install prescribed fire protection equipment and by failing to act in accordance with regulations or technical safety rules, they caused a danger to people’s lives, resulting in the deaths of several people,” the prosecutor’s office said.

The fire broke out in a resident’s room on November 4 and quickly spread. Fifteen residents died, with autopsies establishing a direct causal link to carbon monoxide poisoning or other complications related to the fire, prosecutors said. More than 30 people were injured.

The indictment has been submitted to the Tuzla Cantonal Court for confirmation.

Prosecutors have also asked the court to ban all seven defendants from holding public or professional positions or performing certain activities for 10 years.

World.title: North Macedonia Govt Finally Reveals Independence Day Celebrations’ Cost
World.content:
North Macedonia’s government spokesperson, Marija Miteva (R) and State Lottery director Aleksandar Klimovski (L) at a press conference in Skopje. Photo: BIRN.

The series of celebrations marking the 35th anniversary of North Macedonia’s Independence Day, September 8, cost a total of 5.5 million euros, of which almost 4.9 million euros came from the State Lottery, government spokesperson Marija Miteva told a press conference on Thursday.

The rest of the money, some 650,000 euros, Miteva said, came from “socially responsible” companies.

The financial disclosure followed a BIRN Macedonia report published on Wednesday showing that the government had effectively tasked the State Lottery with taking care of the events, by choosing a production company that would organise them according to the government’s requirements.

Four months ago, the government announced its plan for a series of events marking the anniversary, culminating in a September 8 concert in Skopje by world-famous DJ David Guetta. Since then, officials had repeatedly declined to say how much the events would cost, or who was paying for them.

The government at the press conference focused on its argument that the almost 5 million euros coming from the State Lottery, which is fully owned by the government, was not taxpayers’ money.

State Lottery director Aleksandar Klimovski told the press conference that the government, as the company’s sole shareholder, had ordered it to allocate the money from its undistributed 2024 profits to the celebrations.

But he insisted it should not be considered budgetary funds because it remained on the company’s account and was therefore “corporate money” until formally transferred to the state budget.

This supported the Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski’s claim on Wednesday, who, confronted by reporters, maintained that the events “cost the budget and the citizens zero denars”.

The funding arrangements raised questions about transparency. In June, BIRN reported that the government was refusing to disclose the financial details of what it described as spectacular celebrations under the slogan “Silno svetnal den” [Brightly shining day], despite repeated requests for information.

On Thursday, Boban Miloseski, the owner of Avalon production, which the State Lottery hired to carry out the celebrations, apologised for an earlier incident on September 7, at a press conference organised by Avalon and the Interior Ministry ahead of Guetta’s September 8 concert in Skopje.

Asked why the cost of Guetta’s contract had not been made public, and whether a clause prevented disclosure, Miloseski had responded: “Do I look like an idiot to you?”, calling the question a provocation. In his apology, he said he uttered these words under a lot of “stress and fatigue”, before he had time to properly think it through.

Besides Guetta, the celebrations in Skopje and across the country featured other world-famous performers and DJs, including José Carreras, Steve Aoki, Paul van Dyk and Paul Oakenfold.

World.title: Week in Review: Tests and Pressures
World.content:
The lavish funeral of the convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic, complete with military honours and attended by senior Serbian and Bosnian Serb officials, drew condemnation from EU states and renewed questions about how deeply the glorification of wartime figures remains embedded in regional politics.

Experts told BIRN that the spectacle in Serbia reflected a state-sponsored politics of memory rather than Serbian society as a whole, while warning that Mladic’s funeral has become entangled with election campaigns and could further damage already strained regional relations.

Writing from Brussels, Gjeraqina Tuhina argued that this is also a test for the EU: after years of accommodating Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic, Brussels must decide whether its opposition to war-criminal glorification will have consequences beyond strongly worded statements.

World.title: Concentration Camp to Hotel Catwalk: Montenegrin Fortress’s Makeover Puts History at Risk
World.content:
So the thought of a fashion show being staged on Mamula last month seems grotesque. What is even more worrying is how a place of suffering became a playground for luxury, with the survivors and their families witnessing the quiet obscuring of history.

Eighty years after the concentration camp was dismantled and the Italians fled, an Egyptian investor opened the renovated Mamula fort as a luxury hotel. Under the name Mamula Island Hotel, it was unveiled in 2023 and functioned briefly under this name before the Banyan Group took over and rebranded it as Mamula Island by Banyan Tree, a makeover that went into effect for the 2026 summer season.

When the news about the Montenegrin government decision to lease out the former concentration camp to be turned into a luxury hotel was first announced a decade ago, it caused an outcry, with many former prisoners speaking out against it. Many in the Montenegrin public viewed the commercialisation of this historically significant site of suffering as the loss of an important part of Montenegrin’s history.

The decision triggered international outrage as well, prompting major media outlets to write about the controversy. The government even received a letter from the then UN Secretary general Boutros Boutros-Ghali who expressed concern over the endeavour.

However, the government stood by its decision, citing that they had only two options: either let the fort and the island be abandoned to decay or find an investor who would restore it and open it for visitors. The authorities were very vocal in reassuring the public that the island’s history would be preserved and would become a crucial part of the new development.

Which it was. Sort of.

Mamula Island by Banyan Tree has an accompanying memorial gallery named Historical-Memorial Gallery Mamula, where the details of the island’s dark past along with personal artefact, testimonials and the names of prisoners are laid out on display.

For the fashion show, the invited public came, some of them even visited the memorial gallery. They posted photos, they were or tried to be respectful and then they went on to see the show, ate and slept in the soft beds of their hotel rooms, former prisoners’ holding cells where inmates slept on the hard limestone floors or improvised bunk beds, squeezed in with several dozen other people.

Supporters of the hotel project claim the site needed a curator and that history will not be erased by the renovation or the change in the function of the fortress, and that letting the fortress decay was also a form of erasure.

This last argument is true. Leaving Mamula fortress exposed to the elements and cause it to decay into ruin. But preserving a building does not necessarily preserve memory authentically.

The walls of the fortress hold the truth – bodies crammed against one another, straw mattresses on wooden boards, a gasoline barrel used as a toilet. Luxury hotel rooms do not preserve that memory.

New lives for old buildings?

World.title: Student-Led Movement Launches Election Challenge to Serbian Government
World.content:
Hundreds gathered in Serbia’s second city Novi Sad on Thursday evening for the first pre-election rally held by the student opposition movement ahead of early parliamentary elections scheduled for October 25.

Their electoral slate – called Student List – Students are Winning – will include 250 candidates chosen by students involved in the long-running protest movement triggered by the November 2024 Novi Sad railway station disaster.

The student movement has become the strongest opposition force in Serbia, and the decision to participate in the elections represents its first direct entry into electoral politics. It hopes to defeat the Serbian Progressive Party led by Aleksandar Vucic, which has been in power since 2012.

World.title: French Judiciary Prepares Warrant for Suspected Jean-Michel Nicolier Murderer
World.content:
September the 13th, 2026 – The French judiciary is currently preparing an international arrest warrant for Spasoje Petković, known as “Štuka”, the suspected Jean-Michel Nicolier murderer.

The French judiciary is preparing an international arrest warrant for Spasoje Petković, known as Štuka, suspected of the murder of French volunteer Jean-Michel Nicolier at Ovčara back in 1991. Index reports that news of progress in the investigation being conducted in Paris has brought new hope to the Nicolier family that justice will finally be served after 35 years. The family’s lawyer confirmed that the investigating judge at the War Crimes Department of the court in Paris is currently working on the warrant. Paul Nicolier, brother of the murdered Vukovar defender, told RTL that they received the news with “great satisfaction and deep emotion.”

the nicolier family will never give up on justice

“We’re extremely grateful to the French judicial authorities for all their efforts. We hope that, 35 years after the murder, all the circumstances of his death will finally be clarified and that those responsible for it will answer before the court,” said Paul Nicolier. He emphasised that this is an extremely important step that the family has been waiting for years and that sends a clear message: “Thirty-five years after the crime, the judiciary has not given up, and neither have we.” He stressed that the family has always wanted only the truth and justice for Jean-Michel. “Our lawyers Ghislain Dubois and Arnaud Bilen have our full and unconditional trust. We sincerely thank them for their commitment, determination and tireless work. For Jean-Michel, for our family and for his memory, we will go all the way,” concluded the brother of the murdered volunteer.

previous demands to serbia to extradite the suspected murderer fell on deaf ears

The Nicolier family had previously threatened Serbia with a private lawsuit and, through the embassy in Paris, demanded the urgent extradition of Štuka. According to information published by RTL, France has already questioned Petković, and the investigation is nearing its end. He told the French judge that he is not guilty, but investigators have reportedly gathered sufficient evidence against him. During the investigation, several people were questioned in Croatia and Serbia. One of the last persons questioned was someone hiding in Norway, who is suspected of having participated in the relocation of mass graves at Ovčara.

The exact location of Spasoje Petković Štuka is not known. It is only known that he lives under a changed identity at a secret location. Jean-Michel Nicolier joined the defence of Croatia in the summer of 1991 as a member of HOS. After being wounded in Vukovar, he was transferred to the hospital, where he awaited the fall of the city. From there, members of the JNA and Serbian paramilitary units took him to Ovčara. According to the testimonies of survivors, he was tortured and killed at Ovčara. His remains were only exhumed after 34 years from a mass grave. In the court proceedings for the crimes at Ovčara conducted in Belgrade, Štuka had the status of a repentant witness. He allegedly admitted guilt in exchange for freedom, and several witnesses accused him of the murder. One of them stated that Štuka, after killing Nicolier, even went as low as to steal 20 francs from his pocket.
