World.title: Despite population decline, Rishiri Island’s kombu harvest goes on
World.content:
It’s 2 a.m. in late July on Rishiri Island, and steady rain beats at my window. A text comes from my contact: “The weather is too uncertain. We’ll wait until 4 a.m. to make the call.”

Finally, at 5:30 a.m. — an unusually late start for the island’s kombu harvest — the day begins.

The crew unloads ropes of kelp from the boat and heads for the drying grounds. They mutter with concern; they may not get the sunshine needed for a successful drying day. But the island has been plagued by rain and clouds for two weeks and they need to get on with it: Harvest season is nearly over.

World.title: Japan’s homegrown peppers can pack an unsuspecting punch
World.content:
Spiciness isn’t a flavor that usually comes to mind when you think of the average Japanese dish, but even so, peppers have a long history in the country.

Capsicum peppers were introduced to Japan in the 16th century, and by the Edo Period (1603-1867), two distinctly Japanese varieties had become established. The first is the small, fiery-hot takanotsume chili pepper. About 2 to 5 centimeters long, the name of this spicy hot pepper means “hawk’s talons” because the sharp, curved fruit is said to resemble the claw of a bird of prey.

The second locally cultivated heirloom pepper is the shishitō (literally, “lion’s head“) — so named because the fruit’s bumpy exterior mirrors the noggin of a shishi (a mythical lionlike guardian beast). Although most shishitō are quite mild, you may occasionally run across one that is quite spicy. This random trait was never bred out of the variety — on the contrary, fans of the peppers rather look forward to being taken unawares by a particularly piquant shishitō.

World.title: Trump envoys arrive in Kyiv in new push to end Russia’s war
World.content:
U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Kyiv for the first time amid skepticism that Washington’s renewed peace outreach would end Russia’s four-and-half year old full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

President Donald Trump’s hand-picked negotiators were greeted by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the historic St. Sophia’s Cathedral in central Kyiv after arriving in the capital by train.

“There will be an opportunity for extensive discussion,” Zelenskyy said. “I thank Trump for allowing them to come.” Sunday’s talks will also include officials from the U.K., Germany and France, according to the Ukrainian leader, Zelenskyy said.

World.title: Chubu Electric chairman Satoru Katsuno may step down over data fraud
World.content:
Chubu Electric Power Chairman Satoru Katsuno is considering how to take responsibility for an earthquake risk data fraud scandal involving its Hamaoka nuclear power plant, including the possibility of resigning, informed sources have said.

Chubu Electric is suspected of cherry-picking earthquake vibration data during regulatory screening for restarting the No. 3 and No. 4 reactors at the Hamaoka plant in Shizuoka Prefecture.

The misconduct is believed to have occurred since at least 2012, prompting some to argue that Katsuno, who became chairman in 2015, should be held accountable.

The company has been involved in a series of scandals, including improperly billing costs for decommissioning the No. 1 and No. 2 reactors at the Hamaoka plant and overcharging customers for electricity.

Industry officials have criticized Katsuno, with some saying that “there is no way he can remain in the position” and that “it is only a matter of time before he resigns.”

Chubu Electric is scheduled to hold a news conference on Monday to disclose the details of a report by an investigation committee on the data manipulation.

World.title: Justice Ministry to test GPS tracking of sex offenders on parole
World.content:
The Justice Ministry plans to launch a pilot program to track sex offenders on parole with GPS devices from as early as fiscal 2027, which begins next April.

Justice Minister Hiroshi Hiraguchi told a news conference Friday that expenses related to the pilot program were included in the ministry’s fiscal 2027 budget request.

Only parolees who consent to participate in the program will be monitored with GPS devices, which are not slated to be attached to parolees’ bodies.

“We are thinking of trying a method that can be handled under the current law,” Hiraguchi said.

The offenders rehabilitation law requires parolees to receive guidance and supervision from probation officers and volunteer probation officers. The system is intended to help prevent recidivism and promote rehabilitation by allowing probation officers to provide guidance if signs of possible reoffending are detected.

Under the program, the ministry is considering providing guidance through interviews and other methods if parolees’ location data indicates behavior potentially linked to crime.

The program will be conducted in a way that places as little burden as possible on parolees. The type of GPS device to be used has yet to be decided.

If the program proves effective, it will be implemented on a full scale.

The second Recidivism Prevention Plan, adopted at a cabinet meeting in 2023, states that the government will “consider measures to enhance the treatment of sex offenders,” citing examples of systems introduced in foreign countries.

World.title: Japan adopts measures to stamp out invasive longhorn beetle
World.content:
Japan is moving to stamp out the red-necked longhorn beetle, an invasive species that threatens trees including cherry and plum.

The government adopted a series of control measures on Friday, such as halting the expansion of areas damaged by the pest, scientifically known as Aromia bungii, by 2030, as well as providing financial support to affected local governments.

The central government will hold a briefing session for municipalities as early as this month.

“We will engage in systematic and wide-area pest control to enable its eradication in Japan,” Environment Minister Hirotaka Ishihara told a news conference after a task force meeting.

The government will encourage 22 of the country’s 47 prefectures, where damage has been confirmed, to develop regional pest control strategies, while urging other regions to implement preventive measures and remain vigilant for early detection.

World.title: How a billion-dollar sanctions dodge kept Chinese goods flowing to Iran
World.content:
Iran has used a barter-like arrangement to bypass sanctions on its oil sales and buy billions of dollars’ worth of goods from China, including military gear, two senior Iranian sources and three other people familiar with the matter said.

The secretive trade mechanism, in which Iranian oil is exchanged for credits for Chinese imports, has provided a financial lifeline for Tehran in recent years as the United States stepped up economic and military pressure over its nuclear program, according to the sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

It has also helped China, the world’s biggest crude importer, retain access to discounted Iranian oil while shielding banks and companies that export to the Islamic Republic from international scrutiny or penalties, they said.

World.title: Actor and narrator Reo Morimoto dies at 83
World.content:
Reo Morimoto, a Japanese actor and narrator known for his gentle voice, died on Sept. 4. He was 83.

Morimoto, whose real first name was Haruyuki, was from Nagoya.

His agency said Friday that he died suddenly of an unknown cause.

Morimoto made his acting debut in the 1967 drama series “Koukousei Jidai” on public broadcaster NHK.

Reo Morimoto gained popularity as a narrator thanks to his distinctive and calm delivery. | JIJI

He gained popularity as a narrator thanks to his distinctive and calm delivery.

His notable roles include those in the television drama series “Kiiroi Namida” (Yellow Tears) and “Ai to Iu Na no Moto ni” (In the Name of Love) as well as the film “Kids Return.”

He narrated a number of variety shows and commercials and was well known for his narration in the children’s series “Thomas & Friends.”

World.title: How to solve Hong Kong’s triple whammy: ageing population, baby dearth and job losses?
World.content:
In the fourth of our series of previews on the five-year plan and policy address, to be announced on September 16, Fiona Sun and Edith Lin analyse how to improve livelihoods in the city by tackling the impact of demographic changes and technological advancement. Read part one here , part two here and part three here

Twenty-eight-year-old Hong Kong resident Fong and his wife want to have a child but he knows they cannot afford one for now.

He earns about HK$10,000 (US$1,275) a month as a construction worker and lives in a subdivided flat in Prince Edward, paying roughly HK$3,000 a month for the 100 sq ft space. His mainland Chinese wife, 27, remains in Guangdong province as she waits for a one-way permit to be in Hong Kong with him.

With unstable working hours and wages, Fong said he struggled to make ends meet. The cost of raising a child in one of the world’s most expensive cities is too heavy a burden to bear for now.

“If you bring a child into the world, you have to raise them. It’s not something to be taken lightly,” he said.

“It requires real commitment and a good environment for the child to grow up in.”

World.title: 39 pupils and staff fall ill after eating school lunches in Sha Tin
World.content:
Hong Kong health authorities are investigating an outbreak of suspected food poisoning that hit 39 pupils and staff members who ate lunch at a Sha Tin school earlier this week.

Twenty-three boys and 14 girls, aged between five and 11, from Baptist (Sha Tin Wai) Lui Ming Choi Primary School and two employees, aged 34 and 38, were affected.

They developed stomach pain and diarrhoea about eight to 22 hours after eating school lunches provided by a supplier on Wednesday.

A spokesman for the school, located at 8 Yuen Chau Kok Road in Sha Tin, could not be reached for comment on Saturday night.

The Centre for Health Protection did not name the supplier in a statement on Saturday.

“Initial investigations of the [centre] revealed that the affected persons consumed the same type of lunchboxes before the onset of symptoms, pointing to food poisoning likely related to the consumption of marinated chicken leg and penne provided by the lunch supplier,” it said.

Two pupils sought medical advice but did not require hospitalisation. They were in a stable condition.

World.title: Quality concerns prompt further tests on concrete used in 3 public housing blocks
World.content:
The quality of concrete used in three blocks of a public housing estate under construction in Tung Chung requires further testing and review, Hong Kong’s Housing Authority has revealed.

According to official documents, the main contractor on the project is Able Engineering. The same company is also involved in a scandal over defective lift installation work at an expansion project at Queen Mary Hospital in Pok Fu Lam.

The authority said on Saturday that regular checks had uncovered issues with the quality of concrete used in three blocks of the estate at Tung Chung Area 42 on Lantau Island between late August and early September.

“The Housing Authority’s engineering team discovered during routine concrete cube strength tests between late August and early September that the quality of concrete used in certain structural components of blocks 3, 4 and 5 at the Tung Chung Area 42 public housing estate required further review and testing,” a spokesman said.

The estate, with a total site area of about four hectares, comprises six residential blocks, providing more than 6,000 public housing flats for a planned population of 16,611. The project’s cost was estimated at about HK$5.4 billion in 2023.

The authority said it had instructed the contractor to extract additional concrete core samples for compressive strength testing in accordance with contract standards to assess whether the concrete strength met the design and contractual requirements.

World.title: A year after lawmakers veto equality bill, LGBTQ Hongkongers still hope for change
World.content:
When Hong Kong’s Legislative Council vetoed a government bill that would have granted limited recognition to the city’s same-sex couples, 51-year-old Isaac Yick said he was “disappointed but not surprised”.

Yick was born and raised in Hong Kong before moving to Canada, where he eventually met and married his husband. They returned to the city together in 2013.

He said there was initially a sense that things were changing for the LGBTQ community in the city, citing victories in court that conferred some rights for same-sex couples, including one landmark case from 2019 involving spousal benefits

“It would still have to go through all the courts, which was unnecessary, but once the decision was handed down, we saw the change,” he said.

So when the Court of Final Appeal ruled in 2023 that the government had a positive obligation to recognise same-sex partnerships in the city, there was reason for optimism.

But by the time the government’s bill made its way to Legco two years later, Yick had the feeling legal recognition was not going to happen. In the year since the bill was rejected, the pace of change had slowed considerably, he said.

World.title: Rescue operation launched after boat begins to sink at Hung Hom
World.content:
A rescue operation was launched in Hung Hom in Hong Kong on Saturday afternoon after a recreational vessel began taking on water and sinking.

Emergency services were alerted at around 1.36pm when a man fishing nearby spotted the pleasure boat gradually submerging off the Hung Hom Promenade.

Police and firefighters rushed to the scene, and fire service divers swept the vessel.

Following a search of the submerged hull, rescue personnel confirmed that no one was on board.

It is understood that the vessel had been anchored at the location for about a month.

It was not immediately clear why the vessel began to sink.

World.title: Hong Kong Police College becomes first government unit to roll out degree course
World.content:
The Hong Kong Police College has become the first government department to offer a bachelor’s degree programme, with the force set to roll out the course for rank-and-file officers by the end of this year.

Commissioner of Police Joe Chow Yat-ming announced the development on Saturday, after the Hong Kong Council for Accreditation of Academic and Vocational Qualifications approved the college’s Bachelor of Policing (Honours) (Security and Criminal Investigation) programme last month.

“We hope that the programme can start by the end of this year. Students will take around three to four years to complete it. With this bachelor’s degree, they can 

He said the programme, which is free, would target rank-and-file officers.

The curriculum will cover foundation and criminal investigation training, internships including frontline patrols, and language courses. Students will also be expected to complete a thematic report before graduating.

“The Police College has become an institution that can confer a bachelor’s degree, and it is also the first government department that is qualified to do so,” Chow said.

World.title: Elderly couple found dead in Ma On Shan flat after foul odour reported
World.content:
Hong Kong police are investigating the deaths of a couple in their seventies after their bodies were discovered inside their home in Ma On Shan.

Police said officers were alerted at around 8pm on Friday to a strange odour emanating from a flat in Heng Yat House at Heng On Estate.

Firefighters forced entry to the flat, discovering a 72-year-old man and his 74-year-old wife lying in the living room, police said, adding the couple were pronounced dead at the scene.

No suicide note was found, and the cause of death is pending autopsies, the force said.

A source said on Saturday that the couple had a good relationship, and had one daughter and two sons, who lived separately after getting married.

The couple suffered from high blood pressure, diabetes and hyperlipidemia, while the wife had also been living with dementia for five years, the source added. Both required regular medical appointments at Prince of Wales Hospital in Sha Tin.

World.title: Hong Kong’s ethnic minority groups can play key role in belt and road, summit hears
World.content:
Hong Kong’s ethnic minority communities can leverage their multicultural backgrounds and language skills to play an “important role” in the city’s efforts to build ties with belt and road countries, the labour minister has said.

Other speakers at the Zubin Foundation’s Ethnically Diverse Youth Leadership Summit on Saturday also highlighted the advantages these historically marginalised communities possessed in helping mainland Chinese companies go global.

In his opening remarks, Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han told an audience of about 300 young people from ethnic minority backgrounds that they had a role to play as the city pursued deeper ties with countries under the Belt and Road Initiative

“When looking ahead, we are building and forging much closer collaboration with countries from the belt and road,” Sun said.

“Here in Hong Kong … we have a locally grown talent [pool]. They speak the language, they know the culture … while they know so much about Hong Kong.

“So I think you do have a very important role to play in the years to come.”

World.title: Frog Gone: China’s Beloved Traveling Game Is Going Offline
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019013/Frog Gone: China’s Beloved Traveling Game Is Going Offline
World.content:
A mobile game beloved by millions of Chinese users about a traveling frog is set to shut down after the game operator and the IP holder failed to reach a licensing agreement.

Announced Tuesday by its official account on microblogging platform Weibo, the game, Travel Frog: China Journey, will discontinue on Dec. 8.

“This time, the little frog is going on a long journey, with no set date of return,” the announcement read. “But that quiet companionship will always remain in our hearts.”

A video game insider told domestic media that the IP holder, Japanese gaming studio Hit-Point, sought harsher terms from domestic operator Lingxi Games, including stripping it of its right to collaborate with other companies and sell game-related merchandise. After multiple rounds of negotiations, the companies could not reach an agreement, though the insider disclosed that they are in a final round of talks.

Travel Frog, released in 2017, is an idle game, meaning gameplay progresses with little player input. Chinese users began downloading the Japanese version before tech giant Alibaba secured authorization to publish it exclusively in the Chinese mainland under its gaming division, Lingxi Games, a year later. By then, the original version was already popular, with iOS downloads in China alone exceeding 30 million.

At its peak, the game was more popular than the domestic, Tencent-produced game Honour of Kings, topping the domestic App Store free chart. Lingxi Games was acquired by the private equity firm Trustar Capital in August this year.

In Travel Frog: China Journey, the protagonist, a frog who lives alone in a cave, passes its days reading, writing in its diary, eating, and whittling wood. It also travels around China, such as to the Great Wall in Beijing and West Lake in the eastern city of Hangzhou. While on the road, it meets fellow animal travelers, brings back local specialties, and sends home postcards, which devoted users post on WeChat.

After learning that the game would be discontinued, a graduate student in Shanghai surnamed Fang spent a day trying to redownload it. She had played since her first year of university but hadn’t reinstalled the game after changing phones, not thinking it would shut down permanently.

“(I will have to) think of it as a child growing up and setting off on a new journey — a solo trip where the parents don’t need to worry anymore,” Fang said. “I really loved my frog … It felt like a real little baby.”

Another player, surnamed Wang, in the southern city of Guangzhou, first tried the game’s Japanese version in 2018. The frog’s ability to travel, rest, and meet friends whenever it wanted — moved her, as she said that adult life is all about KPIs, responsibilities, and pressure.

When she learned the game would be taken offline, Wang told Sixth Tone that she was devastated. “This isn’t just a game,” she said. “It’s a second life.”

Online, some called the move the “tears of an era,” a Chinese internet slang term referring to something that evokes a strong sense of nostalgia. Others lamented that their “youth is over,” or said they could not bear to delete the game, hoping it might one day be restored.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A screenshot from Travel Frog: China Journey. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018994/She Preserved the Memory of the Mogao Grottoes. Now It’s All She Remembers.
World.title: She Preserved the Memory of the Mogao Grottoes. Now It’s All She Remembers.
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018994/She Preserved the Memory of the Mogao Grottoes. Now It’s All She Remembers.
World.content:
Chang Shana, one of China’s most treasured artists, is sitting on her living room sofa in Beijing, her eyes fixed on a TV documentary about Dunhuang, the northwestern oasis city where she spent much of her childhood. When a familiar face appears on screen, the 95-year-old breaks into a broad smile.

“That’s my father,” she says, pointing out Chang Shuhong, an accomplished painter best known for his research on the ancient Buddhist murals at the Mogao Grottoes.

Alzheimer’s disease, the most common cause of dementia, has robbed Chang Shana of most memories, yet her face still lights up the moment anyone mentions Dunhuang.

“Apart from Dunhuang, her family, and the caregivers who attend to her day and night, my mother has largely forgotten the people and things outside her immediate world,” says her son, Cui Donghui.

Gone are her memories of studying under world-renowned masters, of her mother walking out on the family, of helping design state gifts and landmark buildings like Beijing’s Great Hall of the People and the Cultural Palace of Nationalities, of losing her beloved husband, and of her tenure as the longest-serving president of the Central Academy of Arts and Design, now Tsinghua University’s Academy of Arts and Design.

On a desk in her bedroom is “Clothing Patterns of China Dunhuang Mural,” which compiles 328 color illustrations of cave murals and sculptures from various periods. “I drew this book. It’s all decorative motifs,” says Chang, standing up. After catching her breath, she points out another book: “This one, ‘Dunhuang! My Father’s Call,’ was written by my father, but I contributed many of the illustrations and written materials.”

Would she like to return to Dunhuang one day? “Yes,” she replies in a soft voice, without hesitation. Then, she slowly wanders back to the sofa to continue watching her documentary.

Life on the move

Chang Shana was born in Lyon, France, in 1931. Her father was among China’s first generation of French-trained artists, and both her parents went on to attend the prestigious Beaux-Arts de Paris school.

After being moved by a photobook about the Mogao Grottoes that he discovered in a secondhand book stall beside the Seine, Chang’s father returned to China alone in 1936 to head the fine arts department at the National Art School in Beiping, predecessor of Beijing’s Central Academy of Fine Arts.

However, as invading Japanese troops advanced toward Beijing, he was forced to flee, eventually moving with the academy to Nanjing in the eastern Jiangsu province — where he was joined by his wife, Chen Zhixiu, and daughter — and then to the southwestern city of Chongqing, which served as the nation’s wartime capital during the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression. In 1943, the family relocated again to Dunhuang in the northwestern Gansu province, where Chang Shuhong was appointed director of the National Dunhuang Art Research Institute.

Chang Shana found it difficult adjusting to their austere life among the arid dunes. In her 2013 memoir, “Yellow Sands and Blue Sky,” the artist recalls that first winter night, eating cold noodles with only salt and vinegar, and her father promising, “Things will get better.”

Yet despite the lack of material comforts, she instantly found an abundance of inspiration at the Mogao Grottoes. On days without school, she would walk the dirt roads, past the shimmering poplars, and climb into the grottoes to copy the murals. “I loved going into the caves to draw. I was always eager to do it. My parents never had to tell me to go,” she wrote. She would also chat with the many visiting artists and scholars, laying a strong foundation for her artistic development.

Previously, students had typically copied the murals with tracing paper, which they secured to the walls with thumbtacks, leaving tiny holes. Chang Shuhong prohibited this practice to prevent further damage to the relics, meaning his daughter had to recreate the originals stroke by stroke through observation alone. Although laborious, it helped her develop extraordinary levels of precision.

But the desert took as much as it gave. Under the strain of his responsibilities, Chang Shuhong was often irritable, and his relationship with his wife became fractious. She eventually left him and moved back east in 1945.

Chang Shana was 14. She dropped out of school and stayed home to help with the housework and to knit sweaters for her 4-year-old brother.

That same year, the Nationalist government ordered the Dunhuang Art Research Institute to close. As funding dwindled and workers left, Chang Shuhong traveled extensively to enlist fresh support, eventually recruiting a group of teachers and students from art academies in Chongqing and Chengdu, capital of the neighboring Sichuan province.

With the institute’s future secured, he instructed his daughter to make copies of representative murals covering various Chinese dynasties. In her memoir, Chang recalls her work to recreate the figures of warriors from the Western Wei dynasty (535–556): “The lines followed my feelings; my brushwork was especially free and expressive.”

Finding faith

When Chang turned 17, a Canadian friend of the family sponsored her to study in the United States at what is today Tufts University’s School of the Museum of Fine Arts. There, she took classes in drawing, anatomy, art history, perspective, color, painting, and design.

Although confident in French, she initially struggled with some of the highly specialized English terminology. What baffled her most, though, was the painting course. With abstract expressionism on the rise, her professors required students to create work without recognizable forms or subjects. In a letter to her father, she wrote, “Perhaps I just don’t understand.”

According to her son, Chang’s diary entries from the early 1940s are filled with confusion and unease. She occupied her time with sketching and knitting, often questioning the meaning behind such pursuits. Yet her letters home in 1950 reveal “a completely different person,” he says.

In one, she wrote about “finally finding faith,” and expounded on her belief that art should be accessible and serve the people. In other letters, she displayed a weariness with life overseas. “Staying here, depending on others for everything, life feels so empty,” she wrote. “I have a perpetual sense that something is missing, like I owe a debt.”

Chang returned to China in December 1950 without completing her degree. She immediately began helping her father organize an exhibition of Dunhuang cultural relics in Beijing, featuring copies of murals she and several art researchers had made.

The following year, she was introduced to the influential architects Liang Sicheng and Lin Huiyin, who agreed to recommend her for a teaching assistant position at Tsinghua University’s School of Architecture. Under Lin’s guidance, she and two other students applied traditional cloisonné enamelwork techniques and motifs to everyday items such as table lamps, cigarette cases, and plates.

With a growing portfolio, Chang was commissioned to design themed gifts for the 1952 Asia and Pacific Rim Peace Conference, held in Beijing. She created a silk headscarf and large cloisonné plate with peace dove motifs, inspired by Dunhuang cave paintings from the Sui dynasty (581–618).

When China began reforming its university system in the early 1950s, she transferred to the Department of Applied Arts at the Central Academy of Fine Arts before ultimately joining the Central Academy of Arts and Design in 1956.

Gone too soon

Chang met her first husband while studying in the U.S. The couple married in China in 1953 but divorced after just a few years. The artist barely mentions this time in her memoir, not even naming him.

Her second husband, Cui Taishan, was a Japanese-language interpreter. They met while part of a Chinese cultural delegation to Japan in 1961 and were married two years later, spending 26 years together until Cui’s death in 1989.

The artist’s friend, Huang Xuanzi, recalls that Chang often talked to her late husband’s photo before she developed dementia. “She’d grumble at him for leaving her too soon, then turn to me and say, ‘Look at him, always smiling at me like that,’” she says, adding that Chang still sometimes recognizes him in photographs. “One day, she suddenly smiled and said to me, ‘Cui Taishan was very handsome.’”

Huang recalls a thick stack of flower studies Chang had painted when she was pregnant, each accompanied by a short poem handwritten by her husband. “They were never published, so almost no one outside the family knows about them,” she explains. “You can clearly feel the depth of their affection in those paintings and poems.”

In 1983, Chang was appointed president of the Central Academy of Arts and Design, leaving her less time for family. Around the same time, Cui was diagnosed with diabetes and then liver cancer. Even during his final days, she was unable to stay with him full time, yet he would always reassure her, “You go ahead with your work. I’m fine.” He was just 62 when he died.

The artist struggled to cope with the combination of grief and work stress. “There were photos of her husband everywhere in the house,” says her sister-in-law, Wang Fulan. “She would always say, ‘He left us too soon. He was so young.’ She felt that she had devoted herself entirely to her work and left household matters to her husband, and that was what had worn him down.”

In later years, Chang told a friend: “I have done right by everyone and everything in my life. My father Chang Shuhong wanted me to carry on the cultural legacy of Dunhuang, and I spent my life doing so. Lin Huiyin mentored me to become a designer, and I devoted myself to that career. The only person I failed was my husband, Cui Taishan.”

Forever home

Shortly after losing her husband, Chang’s father was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s. His condition remained largely stable until he took a serious fall at age 92. After that, his memory began deteriorating rapidly, and he passed away two years later in 1994.

Huang says Chang Shana was also healthy and mentally sharp until her early 90s. She might forget small things, but a little prompting was enough to bring her back.

During the pandemic, her son Cui Donghui couldn’t visit in person; he could see her only through the security camera installed at her home. When he checked late at night, he often saw her lying alone on the sofa watching television. When he was finally able to return, she opened the door, looked at him, and said, “Who are you?”

Leafing through his mother’s book, “Clothing Patterns of China Dunhuang Mural,” he proudly remarks, “This is her life’s work. She systematically cataloged the motifs from different periods and defined their evolutionary progression. This foundational body of work is still essential today, whether for research or for the development of cultural products.”

All the detailed illustrations inside were completed during a special trip Chang took to the Mogao Grottoes in 1959 with two colleagues. For the artist, it was a joyous return to the place she once called home.

“We were young then,” she wrote in her memoir. “We rode horses and camels, climbed the Singing Sand Dunes barefoot, and had an absolutely wonderful time.”

At 95, the journey to Dunhuang is impossible. Yet smiling at that flickering TV screen, she is already back among the caves. The memories are gone, but the patterns remain.
