World.title: Bolick redeems self, Ahanmisi catches fire as Gilas Pilipinas rips Kazakhstan in Asian Games
World.content:
Robert Bolick and Jerrick Ahanmisi spearhead Gilas Pilipinas' scoring spree from three-point range as the defending champions earn their first win in the Asian Games and boost their chances of advancing to the quarterfinals

MANILA, Philippines – Robert Bolick rebounded from a scoreless outing, while Jerrick Ahanmisi shot the lights out as Gilas Pilipinas claimed its first win in the Asian Games, dealing Kazakhstan a 109-78 beating at the Aichi International Arena in Nagoya, Japan, on Saturday, September 12.

Held scoreless in a narrow 89-85 loss to Bahrain the day prior, Bolick fired 20 points in just a little over 15 minutes to help the defending champion Philippines improve to an even 1-1 record in Group C and boost its chances of advancing to the quarterfinals.

Ahanmisi, meanwhile, erupted for a game-high 22 points on a 7-of-11 clip from beyond the arc, torching the Kazakhs in a fourth-quarter scoring spree that allowed the Filipinos to break the game wide open.

Gilas Pilipinas held a slim 18-15 lead at the end of the opening period before Bolick took charge and scattered 13 points in the second frame as it mounted a 50-37 halftime advantage.

Ahanmisi then picked up where Bolick left off, knocking down five three-pointers in the fourth quarter and singlehandedly outscoring the entire Kazakhstan team, which managed just 12 points in the final period of the 31-point blowout.

Calvin Oftana, who erupted for 31 points in the loss to the Bahrainis, still made his presence felt with 12 points, while Sedrick Barefield contributed 11 points, 5 assists, and 4 rebounds as he redeemed himself after going scoreless last game.

Zavier Lucero also delivered a near double-double outing of 10 points and 9 rebounds in the win, which saw the Filipinos sink 16 of their 29 attempts from long range for a healthy 55% shooting.

Bolick and Barefield, who both went 0-of-5 from three-point land against Bahrain, made 4 and 3 triples, respectively, this time around.

One of the few bright spots last game before he tweaked his right ankle late in the fourth quarter, Adrian Nocum played just a little under 16 minutes against the Kazakhs, contributing 4 points and 3 assists.

Anton Bykov produced 15 points and 10 rebounds to show the way for Kazakhstan, which fell to 0-2 after also absorbing a 38-point drubbing from China.

Given a one-day break, the Philippines turns its attention to unbeaten China in its last game of the group stage on Monday, September 14, with a win sending the Filipinos to the quarterfinals.

Only the top two teams from each of the three groups and the two best third-place teams will reach the knockout rounds.

The Scores

Philippines 109 – Ahanmisi 22, Bolick 20, Oftana 12, Barefield 11, Lucero 10, Baltazar 6, Arana 6, Abarrientos 6, Trollano 5, Nocum 4, Ganuelas-Rosser 4, Bates 3.

Kazakhstan 78 – Bykov 15, Marat 12, Maydekin 12, Neff 11, Rabchenyuk 9, Murzagaliyev 8, Fedchenko 7, Ivanov 2, Sakhipov 2, Severgin 0, Marchuk 0, Kuanov 0.

Quarters: 18-15, 50-37, 82-66, 109-78.

– Rappler.com

World.title: Multi-sport athlete Chino Sy finds Olympic calling in judo
World.content:
DREAMS. Filipino judoka Chino Sy hopes to make it to the grandest stage in sports: the Olympics.

Also a standout athlete in sambo and wrestling, Chino Sy has shifted his focus to judo as he pursues an Olympic berth that would fulfill not only his dream, but also that of his family

MANILA, Philippines – Filipino judoka Chino Sy learned at an early age to make the most of every opportunity.

Hailing from Davao City, Sy developed a sense of responsibility to perform whenever he and his family traveled to Manila for combat sports competitions, knowing that they invested not only time and effort, but also money, just to be there.

As he embarks on his biggest challenge yet to make the Olympics, Sy is taking that same approach.

“I feel like those experiences shaped how I compete today and my mentality towards sports. Even when we were young, we were told that we couldn’t come home with a loss. For one, we already spent money on plane tickets. We also paid entry fees and covered all other expenses,” said Sy in a mix of Filipino and English.

Sy, 25, grew up immersed in combat disciplines.

His father, Paolo Tancontian, represented the Philippines in judo, winning medals in international competitions including the Southeast Asian Games and the Arafura Games, and now serves as the president of the Pilipinas Sambo Federation.

Sy’s older sister, Sydney, is currently the fifth-ranked sambo athlete in the world in the women’s +80kg division and has won medals in the last three Asia and Oceania Sambo Championships, including gold in 2025.

With martial arts deeply rooted in his family, it comes as little surprise that Sy found success in the field that he captured medals in three different sports in the SEA Games.

At 18 years old, Sy delivered a sambo gold when the country hosted the biennial showpiece in 2019. Four years later, he earned a wrestling silver in the 2023 edition in Cambodia.

But Sy has shifted his focus on judo, the sport in which he dominated the UAAP by winning gold medals in four seasons at UST and earning two MVP awards, as he sets his sights on qualifying for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

And he showed promise in that pursuit by striking a judo gold in the men’s -100kg division in the 2025 SEA Games in Thailand.

“Every athlete’s dream is the highest stage, the Olympics,” said Sy. “I feel like I’m at the peak of my career as an athlete. I’ll grab this opportunity and I’ll do everything I can to make it to the Olympics.”

Sy is not pursuing the Olympic dream for himself alone, but also for his family, revealing that his father once dreamed of competing in the 2000 Sydney Olympics — hence his sister’s name.

“This is not just my dream, it’s also my family’s dream. Papa may not have made it to the Olympics, but he’s doing everything he can to help me achieve our dream,” said Sy.

“If all goes well, this will truly be a milestone for our family.”

And with an Olympic dream in sight, Sy knows his belief in himself has to match his ambition as he eyes a rare judo medal in the upcoming Asian Games, which will be hosted in Nagoya, Japan, from September 19 to October 4.

The Philippines has won only one judo medal in Asian Games history courtesy of Kiyomi Watanabe, who bagged the women’s 63kg silver in the 2018 edition in Indonesia.

“My target is to win. I know it will be difficult, but I’m doing everything I can in training and preparation,” said Sy.

Sy also looks to Watanabe, who represented the Philippines in the 2020 Tokyo and 2024 Paris Games, for inspiration, hoping to learn from someone with Olympic experience as they team up in the Asian Games.

“[Kiyomi] has been competing for a long time and I’m looking forward to seeing how an Olympian thinks, how she prepares, and how she approaches every match,” Sy said.

And just as he did in his early years, Sy is determined to live up to the trust placed in him — this time, not only by his family but the entire country.

“I never want to let our country down, myself, or everyone who has put their trust in me,” said Sy. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kilyab’s Karl Ramirez turns Bicol pop into call for good governance
World.content:
By putting Bicol music at the center of his work, this musician inspires a new generation of artists to celebrate their roots and use their craft to push for change

ALBAY, Philippines – From the dimly lit corners of local bars and cafes in Naga City, Karl Ramirez and his band, Kilyab, quietly listen to the stories of their community. They transform these local narratives, heritage, and aspirations to reinvent Bicol pop — giving voice to the region’s call for change.

Now, the movement is helping the younger generation of musicians to do the same.

Ramirez, a music industry veteran, returned to Bicol during the pandemic. As a founding member of Musika Publiko, a nationwide network of artists dedicated to advance socially relevant music, he sought to localize the group’s advocacy.

KILYAB. Karl Ramirez and his band perform at Pista Nin Teatro 2026, introducing the Bicol pop movement to a nationwide audience. Photo courtesy of The Mariners Collegian

Starting without financial backing in an unfamiliar base, Ramirez and his band brought together local musicians from across Camarines Sur to create a platform for original Bicol music. Initially, they had to persuade reluctant bar and cafe owners to grant them a stage to perform. Soon, those same venues were inviting them back, fueling the community’s rapid growth and popularity.

“We were surprised when more and more bars and cafes opened their doors to Bicol pop. It was challenging at first because every venue has its own specific brand, but through their support, our movement grew larger and reached more listeners,” Ramirez said.

By rooting their songs in community struggles, the movement transformed Bicol pop into a platform for local causes. To sustain this momentum, the organization eventually formed Pagsibol, an initiative that trains aspiring musicians, particularly the youth, to write songs about their local experiences in their native language while using music as a driver for social advocacy.

“We decided to form Pagsibol to expand our reach and prepare younger musicians to lead and advance the movement. We realized we needed to grow our ranks,” Ramirez said.

He explained that the organization not only expanded its footprint, but also created a more open environment for continuous growth: “We wanted to encourage the youth to create fresh work that directly serves their communities and generation.”

Pagsibol now functions as a structured platform for training enthusiasts in songwriting and music production. Beyond developing artists, the group focuses on empowering broader communities through local skills training.

PAGSIBOL. Aspiring young musicians participate in a Pagsibol songwriting workshop aimed at advancing socially relevant original Bicol music. Contributed photo/Verna Abalyan-Velasco

Local support

In Naga City, the group has leveraged music to reinforce good governance, placing “active listening” at its core. Partnering with the local government, they have reached more students while advancing advocacy for Musikong Nagueño, a collective pushing for local government support and funding for community musicians and cultural workers.

“We invited Mayor Leni Robredo to a concert held in 2024 at the Jesse M. Robredo Coliseum, where we presented her with a Bicol pop roadmap and policy proposals for the Naga City music industry,” Ramirez recalled.

“Following her election, our movement established a collaborative partnership with the local government, placing active listening at the center of the city’s good governance agenda.”

He noted that if such a partnership can thrive in Naga, there is immense potential for other local government units to provide genuine backing for artists working to preserve and promote their local heritage.

HERITAGE. The cast of ‘Ibalong Z: A New Bikol Musical’ performs 17 original songs composed by Karl Ramirez in collaboration with the local theater collective Sining Banwa. Reinnard Balonzo/Rappler

In August 2026, Ramirez also served as the lead composer and music producer for Ibalong Z: A New Bikol Musical, writing and producing 17 original songs in just 17 days. The production was funded by the City Government of Legazpi.

“With this play, the original Bicol music we produced, and state support, we proved that local artists and collectives deserve greater investment if we want to advance regional talent and heritage,” Ramirez said. “Ibalong Z stands as a testament that with proper support, local artists can rival mainstream productions.”

Hyperlocal to mainstream

Speaking on the shift to mainstream media, Ramirez said that Pagsibol students are fully supported if they choose to pursue mainstream careers. For him, Bicol pop serves as a springboard — helping emerging artists introduce their work to broader audiences and share regional stories with the national music scene.

“We encourage our musicians to seize opportunities to go mainstream and bring Bicol pop to more listeners. Our hope is that wherever their success takes them, they carry the movement with them,” Ramirez said.

ARTISTIC SUPPORT. In partnership with the City Government of Naga, Bicol pop launched its SongLab initiative for Pagsibol students. Contributed photo/Verna Abalyan-Velasco

Through this hyperlocal music movement, artists gain a solid community to rely on a network that offers support wherever their careers lead. Ultimately, the movement aims to empower budding musicians by giving them greater leverage in their creative expression and stronger control over their career trajectories.

“What we teach the youth goes beyond writing lyrics. We focus on how we, as a community, can support one another in artistic growth and management while advocating for artists’ rights and welfare,” Ramirez shared. “We also guide them as they navigate the music industry and hone their talent.”

For now, Ramirez and Kilyab continue to mentor Pagsibol’s emerging artists by immersing them in local communities. This hands-on approach ensures that every lyric accurately reflects the real issues, places, and people they write and sing about. – Rappler.com

World.title: What the settlement left out: Meta can still collect data from kids
World.content:
ZUCKERBERG. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg attends the annual Allen and Co. Sun Valley Media and Technology Conference at the Sun Valley Resort in Sun Valley, Idaho, U.S., July 9, 2026

In August 2026, Meta agreed to one of the largest consumer protection settlements in American history. The settlement resolves claims from 47 states alleging that Meta intentionally designed its Facebook and Instagram platforms to be addictive to young users and harmful to youth mental health.

As part of the settlement, Meta agreed to pay up to US$17.1 billion — approximately 20% of Meta’s 2025 pretax profits — in penalties over the next 10 years. Meta also agreed to implement changes to its platforms for young users, including daily time limits, access restrictions during school hours and late nights, and “productivity breaks” that interrupt scrolling every 60 minutes.

The $17.1 billion penalty and promised changes to the platforms have grabbed the headlines. But, as a law professor who studies social media regulation, I believe that what the settlement does not include will prove more important to youth safety in the long run. The settlement does not restrict Meta from continuing to collect data from young users, from using that data to sell its targeted ads, or from serving those targeted ads to young users.

In short, while Meta agreed to some limited changes to safeguard young users, it also succeeded in protecting its surveillance-based business model.

How Meta makes money

Meta’s core business is advertising. It is the world’s second-largest digital advertising company by revenue and will soon overtake Google to claim first place. Last year, Meta generated over $200 billion in revenue, up 22% over the prior year.

Meta’s growing revenue comes from delivering more ads to platform users and charging advertisers more for those ads. For Meta, maximizing the amount of time that users spend on its platforms is critical to revenue growth. The more time users spend on Meta’s platforms, the more ads Meta can serve to those users and, consequently, the more money Meta makes.

Meta’s ad business operates on a surveillance model that gives advertisers the ability to serve personalized ads to the users who are most likely to purchase the advertiser’s goods or services. Meta does this by collecting a large amount of data about platform users. This data includes users’ friends, followers and other connections; the websites they visit, the apps they use, the games they play and the purchases they make; their demographics, including education level; the ads they see and how they interact with them; and how they use third parties’ products and services, online or in person.

The more time a user spends on Meta’s platforms, the more Meta learns about that user and the more effective its targeted ads become. This means Meta has a strong incentive to keep users scrolling on its platforms and to collect as much data as possible from those users. The recent settlement does not change that incentive structure.

A history of breached settlements

This is not the first time that Meta has settled with the government and agreed to change its platforms to improve user safety. In 2012, Meta, then Facebook, Inc., settled with the Federal Trade Commission to resolve claims that it deceptively designed its privacy settings and collected data from users without their knowledge.

Then, in 2019, the FTC again sued Facebook, alleging that it violated the terms of the 2012 agreement by continuing to collect user data without consent. Again, the company settled, agreeing to pay a $5 billion penalty and again promising to stop its deceptive data collection practices.

Based on Meta’s prior conduct violating the terms of its settlements, many observers questioned whether the $5 billion penalty would deter Meta from continuing its data collection practices. It did not take long to get an answer.

In 2023, the FTC brought yet another action against Meta, alleging that it had violated the terms of the 2019 settlement. As a result of this violation, the FTC sought to restrict Meta from collecting and monetizing the data of young users.

Meta responded by challenging the FTC’s authority to impose those restrictions. Litigation in that case is ongoing.

Meta’s incentives remain the same

In 2026, Meta has again settled with the government, again paid a penalty and again promised changes. And again, those promises do not restrict it from collecting data and monetizing young users, nor does the settlement restrict Meta from continuing to serve young users targeted ads.

Youth safety advocates and legislators have long fought to stop social media platforms from collecting data from young users and targeting ads to them. They have argued that doing so would remove social media companies’ incentive to design platforms that addict young people. By not including data collection and targeting restrictions in the settlement, I believe that the states missed an opportunity to change this incentive structure.

Repeatedly violating the terms of its settlements with the government seems to be an effective strategy for Meta. The company has learned that penalties for doing so are small in comparison with the profits gained through its conduct. This recent settlement looks like more of the same. With this pattern in mind, it is fair to ask whether the settlement will provide meaningful protection for young social media users or just allow Meta to continue with business as usual.

As former FTC Commissioner Rohit Chopra stated when dissenting from the FTC’s 2019 settlement, “When companies can violate the law, pay big penalties and still turn a profit while keeping their business model intact, enforcement agencies cannot claim victory.”

I believe this most recent settlement repeats the patterns of the past and continues to leave young users vulnerable on Meta’s platforms. – Rappler.com

This article originally appeared on The Conversation.

Randolph A Robinson II, Associate Professor of Law, University of Illinois Chicago

World.title: P17.6-M allegedly smuggled cigarettes seized in Pangasinan
World.content:
CALASIAO, Pangasinan — Police seized an estimated P17.65 million worth of allegedly smuggled cigarettes from a van intercepted in Agno, Pangasinan on Thursday, authorities said.

In a report on Saturday, the Pangasinan Police Provincial Office (PPO) said an inspection of the van led to the discovery of 278 boxes of Red Modern cigarettes containing a total of 139,000 packs.

The two men aboard the vehicle—a 31-year-old married driver from Bataan and a 47-year-old substitute driver from Sorsogon—failed to present valid documents authorizing the possession and transport of the cigarette products, according to the police.

Article continues after this 

Based on data from the Department of Agriculture (DA) Region 1, the cigarettes have a prevailing market price of P127 per pack.

The suspects, vehicle and cargo were brought to the Agno Municipal Police Station for documentation, inventory and verification.

The Bureau of Customs and Bureau of Internal Revenue also conducted on-site inventory and verification.

Police said the evidence was submitted to the Department of Justice (DOJ) for the filing of a case for alleged violation of Republic Act No. 12022, or the Anti-Agricultural Economic Sabotage Act.

The case was subsequently referred to the DOJ Prosecutor General.

Article continues after this 

The two suspects remained in the custody of the Agno police pending the DOJ’s evaluation.

Police Col. Dennis L. De Leon, officer-in-charge of the Pangasinan PPO, commended the Agno police, led by Police Maj. Noeralyn R. Tamayo, for their vigilance and prompt action in intercepting the shipment.

Article continues after this 

The Pangasinan PPO said the operation supports the directive of PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio C. Nartatez Jr. to curb the proliferation of illicit cigarettes and hold those involved in illegal activities accountable under the law.

World.title: Maguindanao Sur officials turn over loose guns yielded by constituents
World.content:
Ampatuan Mayor Rasul Sangki, Shariff Aguak Mayor Akmad Ampatuan, Sultan sa Barongis Mayor Allandatu Angas Sr., 6thID commander Brig. Gen. Ricky Bunayog, and 601stIB commander Brig. Gen. Gremel Brual pose with the high-powered firearms that local officials turned over to the military in Maguindanao del Sur on Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026. (Photo from 601st Infantry Brigade)

COTABATO CITY —Three town mayors in Maguindanao del Sur have surrendered six high-powered firearms, including a caliber .50 machine gun, yielded by their constituents, officials said.

Brig. Gen. Ricky Bunayog, acting commander of the Army’s 6th Infantry Division (ID), received the loose firearms collected from the municipalities of Shariff Aguak, Ampatuan and Sultan sa Barongis on Saturday, as part of continuing efforts to maintain peace and security in the province.

Shariff Aguak Mayor Akmad Ampatuan, Ampatuan Mayor Datu Rasul Sangki, and Sultan sa Barongis Mayor Allandatu M. Angas Sr. went to the headquarters of the 601st Infantry Brigade in Barangay Kamasi, Ampatuan town to formally turn over the firearms to Bunayog.

Article continues after this 

The surrender of the weapons was a result of the intensified campaign against loose firearms by Brig. Gen. Gremel Brual, 601st Infantry Brigade (IB) commander, with the help of local government officials.

Brual said the firearms were collected by the local officials from their constituents in support of the government’s campaign against loose firearms.

Bunayog welcomed the local officials’ efforts to hand over the firearms to authorities ahead of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao parliamentary elections on Monday, Sept. 14.

“Such joint efforts help strengthen public trust and security and contribute to a safer, more peaceful and progressive Bangsamoro,” Bunayog said.

World.title: Ombudsman Remulla: France trip to get info on Co, Legarda
World.content:
Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla —Inquirer file photo

MANILA, Philippines — There is no assurance that Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla would be able to successfully facilitate the return of former House lawmaker Zaldy Co and Sen. Loren Legarda, both of whom are reportedly in France.

Remulla said his trip to France with other officials would only “lay the groundwork” for flying them back to the Philippines to face their respective criminal liabilities in compliance with European Union rules.

“There will be an exchange of information first,” he said in his weekly radio show “Executive Session” on dzRH.

Article continues after this 

Asked on whether the trip would result in capturing Co or Legarda, Remulla said: “No, what is needed there is to prepare… prepare for the different questions you want to ask (authorities).”

READ: PNP ready to coordinate with France to locate Zaldy Co

Co, who previously chaired the House committee on appropriations, is charged with graft and malversation for his alleged role in an irregular flood control project worth P299.4 million in Naujan, Oriental Mindoro.

‘Asylum’In April, Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida initiated efforts to expedite the return of Co after President Marcos Jr. announced that the former Ako Bicol party list lawmaker was accosted at the border of Germany and Czech Republic.

READ: DILG chief to visit France for red notice bid vs Zaldy Co

Article continues after this 

Co was later released by Czech authorities as there was no standing international arrest warrant or red notice from the International Criminal Police Organization against him. He, however, is now believed to have been staying in France, where he supposedly applied for asylum.

On the other hand, Legarda and son Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste left the country on Aug. 2 for Hong Kong, with France as their final destination. They departed days after the Office of the Ombudsman announced that the two lawmakers were being investigated for plunder and graft in connection with “ghost electricity” projects.

Article continues after this 

The projects allegedly cost the government more than P10.4 billion in unpaid financial obligations.

FATF meeting eyed

Remulla said he intends to meet with the Paris-based Financial Action Task Force to raise possible money laundering issues, as well as with EU officials since Co and Legarda may easily move between the border-free Schengen area.

Remulla said he wants to relay to the EU representatives that the bloc should not be a haven for money laundering, citing rumors about the acquisition of properties by public officials.

He added that the absence of an extradition treaty between the Philippines and France should not stop the government from exhausting legal means to bring Co or Legarda home.

‘No gov’t money was stolen’

Also on Saturday, Legarda’s spokesperson, lawyer Tony La Viña, criticized as a “waste of prosecution resources” the investigation into the plunder and graft complaint filed against her and her son, Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste, particularly over the latter’s solar companies.

The Ombudsman is conducting a preliminary investigation into the complaint filed in connection with alleged irregularities involving Leviste’s Solar Para sa Bayan (SPBC) and Solar Philippines Power Project Holdings Inc.

This also stems from the more than 30 service contracts granted to Leviste which the Ombudsman said created a “monopoly” of solar projects.

In an interview with DWIZ, La Viña maintained that “no government money [was] used, no government money was stolen,” as he previously explained that service contracts and franchises acquired by Leviste are not allotted government funds and used only private funds.

He said further the fines on these contracts were even paid by Leviste.

“There is no so-called [P]24 billion or [P]10 billion. Not a single document asking him to pay for that,” La Viña said.

No influence

He said Legarda did not help her son secure a solar franchise when she headed the Senate committee on finance as the votes were unanimous.

“It seems absurd, doesn’t it? That just because you’re a senator and have a son, it’s automatically assumed you used your power to secure franchises or contracts for him?” the lawyer said.

He acknowledged, however, that 90 percent of Leviste’s renewable energy initiatives failed, while only 10 percent delivered.

Yet he also noted that the “most successful renewable energy project” of the administration was among Leviste’s projects.

“That’s the nature of the business, is what I’m saying. Leandro is only one of several players in the business. But again, what Senator Legarda has nothing to do with that,” La Viña said. —With a report from Holly Bacay

World.title: Grim task begins as authorities identify ferry fire victims
World.content:
Rescuers carry the remains of victims of the recent fire on the MV June Aster ferry as they arrive on board a Philippine Coast Guard vessel at the Borac port in Coron, Palawan province, western Philippines, Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026. —AP photo/Aaron Favila

PUERTO PRINCESA CITY, PALAWAN, Philippines — Families of passengers who remain missing after the MV June Aster fire are facing another agonizing wait as authorities struggle to identify the bodies recovered from the charred vessel.

The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) warned on Saturday that the death toll of 35 could grow as some relatives who rushed to the island continued to hope that their loved ones survived the tragedy.

The ferry sailed from Manila, and was off the village of Turda some 39 kilometers from the Port of Coron, when a fire tore through it “in seconds.” At least 30 bodies have already been recovered from the ship’s economy accommodation as of Friday. Of the 132 people on board, 43 survivors have been accounted for, while 54 people remain missing.

Article continues after this 

READ: Palawan ferry fire death toll climbs to 76 as identification process begins

The charred remains were transferred to the PCG vessel BRP Cape Engaño and brought to the Port of Borac in Coron on Saturday morning, PCG spokesperson Commodore Noemi Cayabyab said at a press conference in Manila.

She added that the remains have been turned over to the Philippine National Police Scene of the Crime Operatives (PNP-Soco) for proper handling and identification.

For now, Cayabyab said, the agency’s priority remains the recovery of bodies from the ill-fated vessel.

“Currently, we are focused on the retrieval, and after that, we will proceed with the investigation,” she said.

Article continues after this 

Missing captain

Search and rescue teams were able to finally enter the vessel on Friday, about 40 hours after the incident. But they had yet to access other sections, particularly the cargo hold where the fire reportedly started following an explosion.

“As coordinated with the incident commander, the cargo deck is still somewhat flooded. We will later determine the possible factors because, as we mentioned, the initial statements from survivors indicated that a strong explosion came from the cargo deck,” Cayabyab said.

Article continues after this 

The PCG said it was trying to locate the captain, identified as Roel Sarmiento by Atienza Interisland Ferries Inc., the company that owns and operates the ferry.

Sarmiento was not included on the list of 43 survivors provided to authorities despite reports that he was alive, she said.

According to records from the emergency operations center in the area, the 43 survivors included 30 passengers and 13 crew members.

Cayabyab said the PCG had remained in constant communication with the shipping company but had yet to receive confirmation on the captain’s whereabouts or status.

“The captain is at large because all of the survivors are listed, but the name of the captain is not on the list, although I heard some information that he is alive. But as we speak, we have not received any statement or communication as to the status of the captain of the vessel,” Cayabyab said.

The PCG, she added, was exerting efforts to locate the captain because his account would be crucial to the investigation.

“Definitely the captain has a responsibility and a liability,” she said. “It is very important for him to come forward and shed light on what really happened, what he did, and what instructions he gave after receiving the report of the fire.”

‘Contributing factor’

The PCG has activated its Maritime Safety Investigation and Maritime Crime Investigation units to determine the cause of the Sept. 9 incident and establish possible liabilities.

Cayabyab said the initial phase of the investigation focused on statements from survivors, particularly their accounts of an explosion followed by the rapid spread of smoke and fire.

She said survivors recounted the incident happened quickly, with no time to get life jackets. A tarpaulin that shielded the open areas of the ship from the rain “may be a possible contributing factor but we can’t determine now if they were trapped inside,” Cayabyab added.

Arnulfo Nokki Villanueva, a survivor who recounted the chaos inside the ferry after the fire quickly spread, told a local news outlet that he couldn’t get a life jacket as people were in a panic and stepping on him.

Lira Daco, whose 20-year-old daughter is missing, said she was pained by the thought that her daughter could have burned alive, and at the difficulty of identifying her among the charred remains found in the ship.

Two of the survivors were tourists from Chile, according to Rachel Conserman, a staffer of the ship’s owner. The PCG said the foreigners have left Coron and authorities have coordinated with their embassy.

Fishermen to the rescue

Investigators will also check if fire emergency procedures were followed, including if the captain sounded an alarm or gave a warning and instructions, and if the crew assisted the passengers.

Images provided earlier by the coast guard showed the charred interior of the ship and what appeared to be human remains, ashes and burnt metal, including a car.

Among the first rescuers were fishermen Jun Razote, 55, and son, Manuel, 22, from Barangay Turda.

Razote said he received a call from a fisherman friend from Mindoro around 6:30 p.m. on Wednesday about a ship on fire off Coron.

“As soon as I turned to look at the sea, I saw the boat already ablaze,” he said, adding that he immediately ran to inform the local coast guard.

He and his son then headed to the burning ferry and rescued two females and six males, all of them with burn injuries.

They then brought the eight to Turda where the villagers gave them first aid and other assistance.

“We immediately went back to the boat, but we didn’t find any more survivors,” he said.

Another fisherman, Roman Macoy, 58, was alone fishing when a coast guard team on a speed boat told him to follow them to the burning ferry. They rescued five men who were transferred to his boat and brought to Turda.

World.title: Gatchalian proposes localized class suspensions
World.content:
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian —Inquirer photo/Niño Jesus Orbeta

MANILA, Philippines — Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Saturday called for more localized learning measures amid the prolonged suspension of in-person classes due to the recent weather disturbances.

“This is concerning. While we know that class suspensions seek to ensure the safety of learners and teachers, widespread disruption of classes can aggravate learning loss,” he said in a statement.

His Senate Bill No. 53, or the proposed 21st Century School Boards, seeks to delegate to the local school boards the “timely, organized and localized interventions” in delivering basic education, amid the continuing calamities brought by the monsoon rains and other emergencies.

Article continues after this 

READ: WALANG PASOK: Class suspensions on Friday, Sept. 11 amid habagat rains

Apart from the rains throughout much of August, at least 20 weekdays of in-person classes across the country have been suspended this month alone, due to the severe effects of the recent typhoons as well as the southwest monsoon or habagat.

Even areas unaffected by inclement weather were affected because of the system-wide implementation of class suspensions, Gatchalian said.

“While we ensure the welfare of our students during calamities, we must also ensure that education continues in safe locations,” he said.

Within the last two years, an average of 30 to 50 class days out of the 180-day school calendar have been lost due to class suspensions, Gatchalian said, citing a study by the Second Congressional Commission on Education.—Holly Bacay

World.title: Manibela to go on strike Sept. 14-15 over fuel price increases
World.content:
Manibela chair Mar Valbuena —Manibela/FB

MANILA, Philippines — Transport group Manibela will hold a two-day nationwide strike on Sept. 14 and Sept. 15 to protest the expected increase in fuel prices next week.

Manibela chair Mar Valbuena announced the planned strike in a social media post, noting the price trend of fuel already reaching as high as P100 per liter.

“Next week, the prices of petroleum products will increase again, and you’re once again using the war in the Middle East as the reason,” Valbuena said.

Article continues after this 

Diesel prices may increase by P2 to P2.50 per liter, while gasoline prices may jump by P4.50 to P5 per liter. This would be the second consecutive week of fuel price increases.

READ: Another fuel price hike seen next week

Tax, subsidy

Fuel price watchers have noted escalating hostilities in the Middle East conflict and their impact on the flow of oil supplies from the region.

READ: Airfares to rise anew as fuel surcharge hits Level 14

Valbuena called anew for the suspension of the excise and the value-added tax on petroleum products to ease the impact of the price hikes.

Article continues after this 

“We cannot get the excise tax and value-added tax on petroleum products removed,” he said.

He also expressed concern over the government’s P12-per-liter fuel subsidy, saying drivers were still being charged by gas stations.

Article continues after this 

“The P12-per-liter assistance or fuel subsidy at gas stations … we’re the ones being charged by the gas stations because, they say, LandBank is not paying the subsidy being provided to drivers,” Valbuena said. /cb

World.title: PGH vows ‘objective,’ ‘professional’ examination of ex-Speaker
World.content:
An ambulance carrying former House Speaker and Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez arrives at the Philippine General Hospital (PGH) in Manila from Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City on Saturday, September 12, 2026. —Inquirer photo/Grig C. Montegrande

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine General Hospital (PGH) said it had formed a team of specialists to check the health of former Speaker Martin Romualdez, who has asked the Sandiganbayan to let him stay in a medical facility following his recent arrest on plunder charges.

Its doctors will remain “objective” and “professional,” PGH said in a statement issued Saturday shortly after Romualdez was transferred to the government hospital in Manila from Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City.

Their findings “will be the basis of PGH’s recommendation on whether the continued stay of Congressman Romualdez in the hospital is necessary,” it added.

Article continues after this 

READ: Romualdez to stay in PGH indefinitely starting Sept. 12

The Sandiganbayan’s Third Division on Friday ordered the Leyte lawmaker’s transfer to PGH, citing the need for an “independent examination” of Romualdez to “verify” the one reported in court by his doctors at Cardinal Santos.

Jail transfer on hold

Shortly after being placed under arrest while already confined at Cardinal Santos on Sept. 7, Romualdez and his lawyers filed a motion seeking his extended stay in the hospital.

The pending motion prevented the immediate implementation of a court order transferring him to New Quezon City Jail under the custody of the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP).

PGH said it would release no details of Romualdez’s condition to the public, other than those that will be presented in court.

Article continues after this 

PGH director Dr. Gerardo Legaspi or an authorized representative is expected to testify on Monday morning regarding the findings and on whether there is an “imperative need” to extend the hospital stay of the accused.

Type 2 diabetes

The former Speaker is expected to remain at PGH until further orders from the court.

Article continues after this 

Romualdez and former Ako Bicol Rep. Zaldy Co, who remains at large, along with two other individuals were charged by the Office of the Ombudsman with the nonbailable offense of plunder for allegedly receiving more than P7 billion in kickbacks from government projects from 2022 to 2025.

According to his motion for continued hospital stay, Romualdez, a cousin of President Marcos, was suffering from Type 2 diabetes, hypertension, primary hypothyroidism and other illnesses. —Gillian Villanueva

World.title: Impeach court spox: 11 votes can scrap ‘16-vote’ conviction threshold
World.content:
On its 23rd day of proceedings at the Senate in Pasay City on Tuesday, Sept. 8, 2026, the impeachment court continues its evaluation of Article I, which focuses on allegations surrounding Vice President Sara Duterte’s misuse of confidential funds. —Inquirer photo/Niño Jesus Orbeta

MANILA, Philippines — The spokesperson of the Senate impeachment court holding the trial of Vice President Sara Duterte clarified that at least 11 votes, including that of the presiding officer, are needed to nullify an earlier ruling that set the threshold for conviction at 16 votes.

That is, if the court will continue to see the absence of four senators—two of them detained due to criminal cases, one a fugitive facing arrest, and another on medical leave since Aug. 3—and maintain the total number of participating senator-judges at 20.

Court spokesperson Reginald Tongol on Saturday said the presiding officer, Sen. Francis “Chiz” Escudero, had sent word that he intended to cast his vote on the matter—contrary to Tongol’s earlier statement that Escudero would no longer vote.

Article continues after this 

READ: 4 retired SC justices giving views on ‘2/3’ conviction vote

This would bring the total number of senator-judges able to vote at 20 in the absence of four senators, pegging the majority vote at 11, Tongol said in an interview on dwIZ.

Guidance from ex-justices

The four senators unable to attend are Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, who has been in hiding since the issuance of an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court; Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta, who are both facing the nonbailable charge of plunder before the Sandiganbayan; and Loren Legarda, who has been abroad on extended medical leave.

“I was informed by our presiding officer and the clerk of court that, based on their assessment, the presiding officer would also be voting on the matter,” Tongol said, adding:

“In the ordinary course of Senate proceedings, the Senate President typically does not vote; the other members are the ones who cast their votes. [But] the presiding officer discussed this at length … And he decided to take this direction by voting on the question (of threshold).”

Article continues after this 

The court on Thursday asked four retired Supreme Court justices to serve as amicus curiae, or “friends of the court,” to share their views on the constitutional provision stating that conviction in an impeachment trial requires the vote of at least the two-thirds of “all senators.”

Expected to attend the court session on Sept. 16 are retired Chief Justices Artemio Panganiban, Reynato Puno, as well as retired Associate Justice Rodolfo Azcuna. Retired Chief Justice Hilario Davide, Jr., however, may able to attend only through videoconference.

Article continues after this 

Another session set for Sept. 23 will hear the oral arguments of the House prosecution team and Duterte’s defense lawyers. /cb

World.title: Foreign Digital Firms Pay Kazakhstan Nearly $390 Million in Tax Since 2022
World.content:
ASTANA – Foreign digital companies have paid Kazakhstan 178.8 billion tenge ($390.2 million) in value-added tax since 2022, with annual collections rising more than fivefold over three years under the country’s so-called Google tax.

The figures show the growing fiscal contribution of international platforms serving consumers in Kazakhstan. They do not, however, directly measure the country’s total digital consumption or cross-border e-commerce, because the mechanism covers both digital services and goods sold through online platforms.

Kazakhstan introduced VAT rules for foreign internet companies, commonly known as the Google tax, in 2022. The mechanism requires international companies providing digital services or selling goods online directly to consumers in Kazakhstan to register and pay VAT.

Taxpayers include companies providing software, entertainment, gaming, education and other digital services, alongside businesses selling goods through online platforms.

How much did companies pay

As of Aug. 1, 133 foreign companies were registered as taxpayers, according to the State Revenue Committee of the Ministry of Finance, as reported by Kazinform.

Annual collections increased substantially through 2025. Foreign companies paid 10.4 billion tenge (US$22.7 million) in VAT in 2022, the first year of the mechanism. Payments increased to 24.3 billion tenge (US$53 million) in 2023 and 35 billion tenge (US$76.4 million) in 2024.

In 2025, the figure reached 57.6 billion tenge (US$125.7 million), more than five times the amount collected in 2022. Foreign companies paid 51.5 billion tenge ($112.4 million) during the first seven months of 2026, nearly 90% of the full-year amount collected in 2025.

Who are the largest taxpayers

The largest taxpayers illustrate the range of activities covered by the mechanism. The list spans physical goods, gaming, entertainment, software, communications and online education, underscoring that the mechanism extends well beyond online shopping.

In 2025, Singapore-registered Elementary Innovation Pte. Ltd., associated with the Temu marketplace, paid 13.3 billion tenge (US$29 million) in VAT. Apple paid 11.2 billion tenge (US$24.4 million), while Valve Corporation, the company behind the Steam gaming platform, paid 10.3 billion tenge (US$22.5 million).

Google contributed 7.3 billion tenge (US$15.9 million) and iHerb paid 4.9 billion tenge (US$10.7 million).

Netflix paid 353.9 million tenge (US$772,333), Spotify paid 293.1 million tenge (US$639,646), Zoom paid 183.2 million tenge (US$399,806) and Coursera paid 33.2 million tenge (US$72,454).

Expanding e-commerce market

The trend comes as Kazakhstan’s e-commerce sector continues to expand. Retail e-commerce reached nearly 3.8 trillion tenge (US$8 billion) in 2025, with marketplaces accounting for 86% of online retail sales, according to the Bureau of National Statistics. Together, these developments point to a broader shift in how Kazakh citizens purchase goods and access services, with both domestic and international digital platforms playing an increasingly important role.

The expansion of e-commerce has coincided with the widespread adoption of digital payments. Cashless payments account for 98% of transactions by number and 87% by value.

The tax receipts do not represent the total value of Kazakhstan’s digital consumption or measure cross-border e-commerce alone. Taken together with rising online retail sales, however, they indicate the growing presence of foreign platforms in the country’s consumer economy.

World.title: Almaty Museum of Arts Opens Exhibition Tracing Seven Decades of Kazakh Sculpture
World.content:
ASTANA – The Almaty Museum of Arts has opened a major exhibition exploring the development of Kazakh sculpture over seven decades.

The exhibition, titled “Müsinder: Sculpture in Kazakhstan from the 1950s to the Present Day,” opened on Sept. 8 in the museum’s Saryarka Hall and brings together more than 50 works by several generations of Kazakh artists, reported the museum’s press office. The project is curated by art historian Aliya Tiesenhausen and is part of the museum’s first-anniversary programme.

Among the artists represented are Kha­kimzhan Nauryzbayev, Isaac Itkind, Erkin Mergenov, Madina Zholdybek, Rysbek Akhmetov, Moldaqul Narymbetov, Yerbossyn Meldibekov and Aruzhan Zhumabek.

Rather than presenting a strictly chronological history, the exhibition examines how the language of sculpture has changed from the Soviet period to contemporary Kazakhstan. The works explore themes including the human body, memory, family, identity and social change.

The title refers to the Kazakh word “musin,” which can mean both “sculpture” and “human figure.” The human body therefore becomes a central element of the exhibition, allowing artists from different periods to reflect on society and personal experience.

The exhibition is divided into four thematic sections. One of them, “Game of Opposites?”, focuses on sculpture from the late 1950s through the early 1990s and examines the tension between officially accepted artistic practices and more individual approaches developed by artists in their studios. Works by Isaac Itkind and Erkin Mergenov demonstrate the emergence of more personal forms of sculptural expression during the Soviet period.

Later sections turn to contemporary approaches to the human body and its relationship with politics, culture, gender and personal experience. The exhibition thus connects works created under very different historical circumstances, highlighting changes in artistic materials, techniques and interpretations of the human figure.

According to curator Aliya Tiesenhausen, the exhibition presents sculpture as a “living artistic process” rather than simply a historical record. Soviet-era academic works are placed in dialogue with contemporary pieces to show how both artistic language and perceptions of sculpture have evolved.

“The history of sculpture is at the same time a history of society, memory, and the human being,” said Tiesenhausen.

The exhibition will run from Sept. 8 through May 2027. An illustrated catalogue accompanying the exhibition will be published in Kazakh, Russian and English, featuring scholarly texts by Tiesenhausen and art historians Valeria Ibrayeva and Alexandra Tsai.

The exhibition is also part of the Almaty Museum of Arts’ broader effort to study and present Kazakhstan’s artistic heritage. The museum, which opened in September 2025, was established as a major platform for Kazakh, Central Asian and international contemporary art.

In an earlier interview with The Astana Times, the museum’s artistic director Meruert Kaliyeva described its mission as combining the study and preservation of regional art with greater public access to international contemporary art. The museum was featured in an episode of The Astana Times exploring Almaty’s major cultural landmarks.

World.title: Kazakhstan Sets Out Priorities Ahead of BRICS Summit in India
World.content:
NEW DELHI – Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev is expected to participate in the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on Sept. 12-13, with Kazakhstan seeking to advance cooperation in energy, critical minerals, transport connectivity and global water security.

India is hosting the summit under the theme Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability. BRICS is a group of eleven major emerging markets and developing countries of the world. They include Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates, representing almost half of the world’s population and 40% of the global GDP.

Priorities of Kazakhstan, which joined the group as a partner country in 2025, were presented by Kazakh Ambassador to India Azamat Eskarayev at the BRICS Energy Partnerships for Progress and Prosperity diplomatic dialogue in New Delhi on Sept. 3.

Energy security was among the central topics of the meeting. Participants discussed traditional and renewable energy, new technologies, infrastructure, investment and critical minerals. Particular attention was given to resilient supply chains and emerging energy and transport corridors.

For Kazakhstan, the agenda closely aligns with its efforts to strengthen its role in Eurasian transport and energy connectivity. Eskarayev emphasized the country’s potential in traditional energy, renewable energy and critical minerals.

The discussion was not focused on a single project or agreement but on areas Kazakhstan intends to promote through the BRICS partnership.

Water initiative adds another dimension

Separately, Yeskarayev highlighted Tokayev’s initiative to establish an International Water Organization under the auspices of the United Nations.

The initiative calls for stronger international coordination on water resources and seeks to bring greater political attention to global water security. Kazakhstan has previously presented the proposal in other international forums, including the United Nations.

According to Aidar Kurmashev, head of the Asian Studies Department at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies under the President of Kazakhstan (KazISS), the initiative could gain practical value if it is accompanied by cooperation on water technologies and management.

He suggested that Kazakhstan could develop pilot projects for arid regions involving satellite monitoring of water resources, digital irrigation management, wastewater reuse and specialist training.

“Kazakhstan could offer its territory for pilot projects involving Indian, Chinese and Emirati companies. Then the idea of an international water organization will gain a practical dimension, and potential partners will see specific facilities, technology needs and a possible financing model,” Kurmashev told The Astana Times.

From critical minerals to concrete projects

Kurmashev noted that in critical minerals, Kazakhstan should promote projects focused on domestic processing, component manufacturing and modern exploration technologies, Kurmashev said.

He emphasized that projects should have a clearly defined resource base, site, energy and water requirements, technology partner, potential buyer and financing model. The same approach should apply to transport and digital projects.

“Tokayev’s participation in the summit could help present Kazakhstan as an independent Eurasian participant with a practical agenda covering transport, energy, water and food security and technology,” Kurmashev said.

“The Indian context is also important. India’s chairmanship makes South Asia, sustainable supply chains and technological cooperation issues more prominent,” he added.

However, he noted that the value of Kazakhstan’s participation should ultimately be measured by what follows the summit.

“Political presence should be assessed by the continuation: whether there are bilateral agreements, responsible operators and projects with certain deadlines after the summit,” Kurmashev said.

BRICS as a tool for economic diversification

For Kazakhstan, BRICS can provide an additional platform for expanding economic ties beyond its traditional partners, particularly with major economies in Asia, the Middle East, Africa and South America.

The grouping was established in 2006 by Brazil, Russia, India and China, with South Africa joining in 2011. Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Indonesia have since joined as members.

Kazakhstan is not a BRICS member but became one of the group’s partner countries in 2025. It participated in the 2025 BRICS Summit in Brazil as a partner country.

According to Kurmashev, the partner-country format gives Kazakhstan flexibility to advance its interests without making BRICS an exclusive foreign policy platform.

“Kazakhstan has a dense network of bilateral and multilateral channels with Russia and China. These are the Eurasian Economic Union and the the Commonwealth of Independent States with Russia, the the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and Confidence Building Measures in Asia, the Central Asia-China format and regular high-level meetings,” Kurmashev said.

“Therefore, the additional value of BRICS lies primarily in reaching a wider audience. On the same platform, Kazakhstan gets access to the leadership and business circles of India, Brazil, South Africa, the United Arab Emirates, Indonesia, Egypt and other countries with which the intensity of economic contacts still varies,” he said.

Kurmashev emphasized that BRICS membership or partnership does not automatically increase trade. The grouping is not a customs union and does not create a common market or uniform tariffs.

Its practical value lies in bringing governments, companies and development institutions closer together, helping them identify partners and address barriers.

For Kazakhstan, the success of economic diversification should therefore be measured not simply by total trade with BRICS countries, but by increased trade with countries such as India, Brazil, Indonesia, the UAE, Egypt and South Africa, the emergence of new export categories and a broader investor base.

Kurmashev suggested that government agencies along with QazTrade, a state-owned agency aimed at promoting trade, develop individual country strategies, organize trade missions and support companies through the contracting process.

Can BRICS strengthen transport links with India?

Transport connectivity is another area where Kazakhstan sees potential for BRICS cooperation, although the grouping itself does not manage transport corridors.

The Trans-Caspian International Transport Route links Kazakhstan through the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Türkiye with European markets. For connections with India, the International North-South Transport Corridor, Iranian ports such as Chabahar, and the Kazakhstan-Turkmenistan-Iran railway offer potential links.

According to Kurmashev, a possible long-term route could connect India, Iran, Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan, with onward access through the Kazakh ports of Aktau and Kuryk to the Trans-Caspian route.

However, he noted that political declarations alone would not make such a route commercially viable. Stable cargo volumes would be needed to support regular container trains and shipping services, reduce empty runs and distribute fixed costs.

“At the BRICS Summit, Kazakhstan could propose preparing a pilot container shipment involving Indian, Iranian, Turkmen and Kazakh operators. Such a project could help identify actual transit times, tariffs and bottlenecks at each stage of the route,” he said.

At the same time, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Türkiye remain essential to the Trans-Caspian route, meaning key decisions on its operation would need to be coordinated outside the BRICS framework.

“Payments, insurance, sanctions risks around Iran and the number of transshipment points will remain important constraints. Therefore, BRICS can bring together interested parties, but the commercial viability of the route must ultimately be confirmed by carriers and shippers,” Kurmashev said.

World.title: Foreign Media on Kazakhstan’s Economic Transformation, AIFC and Rybakina’s Rise to World No. 1
World.content:
ASTANA — The Astana Times has selected articles from global media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest highlights the country’s economic and financial development, sovereign wealth strategy and global ambitions, alongside Elena Rybakina’s historic rise to world No. 1.

Elena Rybakina becomes world No. 1 for first time after U.S. Open win over Zheng Qinwen

Women’s tennis has a new world No. 1. Elena Rybakina took the top spot from Aryna Sabalenka on Wednesday at the U.S. Open with a quarterfinal win over China’s Zheng Qinwen, 3-6, 6-1, 6-4. It is her first time at the summit of women’s tennis, reported The New York Times on Sept. 9.

“It’s a great achievement, and I feel like you will appreciate and think about it even more when you finish your career,” Rybakina said in a news conference, when asked about the milestone.

Kazakhstan’s AIFC says other countries are seeking to replicate its model

Kazakhstan’s financial hub says its model is attracting interest abroad as competition between financial centres intensifies, while limited market liquidity remains a key challenge, reported Euronews on Sept. 9.

For two days, Astana Finance Days 2026 brought together representatives of global financial institutions that collectively manage more than $26 trillion in assets, as Kazakhstan seeks to strengthen its position in the global competition for capital.

How Kazakhstan’s economic reforms have turned the tenge into the best-performing currency in Europe and Asia

EU Reporter published an article on Sept. 7 examining the tenge’s strong performance in 2026 and highlights Kazakhstan’s accelerating economic transformation, driven by foreign investment, diversification, digitalization, infrastructure development, and the expansion of its financial and technology sectors.

“The Kazakhstani tenge has become the best-performing currency in Asia and Europe in 2026, according to the Financial Times. Since the beginning of the year, it has appreciated by nearly 10% against the US dollar, outperforming all other currencies worldwide except for several currencies of Latin American and African countries. This performance has been underpinned by economic growth driven by the transformation of Kazakhstan’s economic model. The country is rapidly evolving from a commodity-based economy into a financial and technology hub for Central Asia, amid growing inflows of foreign capital,” reads the article.

Erlan Karin’s appointment links reform and national identity

The Times of Central Asia published an article on Sept. 1 about Erlan Karin’s appointment as Vice President of Kazakhstan.

“When President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev put forward Erlan Karin for vice president on Aug. 31, he called him ‘a genuine patriot’ with long experience in government. He also stressed Karin’s part in implementing major reforms, his grasp of long-term state strategy and his understanding of Kazakhstan’s prospects for socioeconomic development.

Karin has spent seven years in senior posts under Tokayev. He also has a sustained interest in a question that runs through the president’s agenda — how Kazakhstan can modernize while remaining connected to its own history and national identity,” reads the article.

From oil reserves to infrastructure: How Kazakhstan invests in future generations

EU Reporter released an article on Sept. 8 examining how Kazakhstan can transform part of its sovereign wealth from financial savings into long-term national capital by investing in infrastructure, healthcare, education, and other assets that can generate lasting economic and social benefits for future generations.

“Savings from the National Fund are already being utilized directly in the interests of future generations. Since 2024, Kazakhstan has operated the National Fund for Children program: every young citizen of Kazakhstan is annually allocated a portion of the fund’s investment income, and upon reaching 18 years of age, the accumulated funds can be used for education or housing improvement. This program has already entered the phase of practical asset utilization. Between February 2024 and Aug. 1, payouts were received by more than 338,000 young Kazakhstanis, totaling approximately $67.8 million. Meanwhile, the funds belonging to minors remain within the National Fund’s assets and continue to be invested until they reach adulthood,” reads the article.

Almaty and Astana set to retain Central Asia’s economic lead

Almaty and Astana are likely to retain their position as Central Asia’s leading economic centers, even as Tashkent and Bishkek record rapid growth and invest heavily in their future expansion. Kazakhstan’s two largest cities benefit from an economic scale, financial infrastructure and established business ecosystems that have been built up over decades, reported the Times of Central Asia on Sept. 7.

“Almaty and Astana benefit from an economic scale unmatched elsewhere in Central Asia. Kazakhstan alone accounts for more than half of the region’s GDP and roughly two-thirds of its inward FDI stock, according to TCA’s Central Asia Balance Sheet. That scale helps generate the fiscal resources needed to build and maintain the municipal infrastructure that supports business activity,” reads the article.

World.title: Kazakhstan Looks to New Players and Products to Drive Next Phase of Digital Finance, NBK Governor Says
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan has built the core digital infrastructure for its financial sector and is now entering a new stage focused on developing new products, attracting new market participants and creating innovative business models, National Bank Governor Timur Suleimenov said at the Central Asia Fintech Summit 2026 in Almaty on Sept. 11.

Speaking at the opening of the third annual summit, Suleimenov said Kazakhstan’s financial sector has already reached a high level of digitalization, with more than 90% of payments made without cash and most basic banking and government services available through digital platforms.

The summit, held on Sept. 11, brings together regulators, financial institutions, technology companies and experts to discuss the future of financial markets, digital currencies, artificial intelligence, digital assets, cybersecurity and other areas of fintech.

Suleimenov said the National Bank’s approach has evolved from simply digitizing its own operations to actively encouraging innovation across the financial market.

“We decided to change the approach altogether – instead of being the one who is pushed, to become the one who pushes the market,” he said, describing the regulator’s role as creating a “push” for the market and encouraging participants to move faster.

Kazakhstan builds digital financial infrastructure

Kazakhstan has established a national digital financial infrastructure. It includes biometric identification, interbank payments, the digital tenge and mechanisms designed to protect citizens and businesses from financial fraud.

The infrastructure has been expanded through successive stages, with the digital tenge entering industrial use in 2023, the National Anti-Fraud Center launched in 2024 and new interbank and QR payment infrastructure introduced subsequently.

The digital tenge is gradually being integrated into government financial processes, including public procurement, budget planning and the management of state funds. Suleimenov said the National Bank, together with the government, intends to increase the volume of digital-tenge operations to 2 trillion tenge (US$4.4 billion) over the next 12 months.

Suleimenov pointed to the interbank mobile payment system launched this year as one of the latest developments. The system includes transfers by phone number and a unified QR code. Since its launch on July 19, it has processed more than 20 million transactions worth around 400 billion tenge (US$888 million), according to the National Bank.

He described the high level of digitalization as a major achievement, noting that in many countries reaching 50–60% of non-cash turnover remains a challenge.

From infrastructure to products

The next challenge, Suleimenov said, is no longer primarily about building the technological “rails” of the financial system but about using them to create products that meet the needs of businesses and consumers.

During the opening plenary, moderator Vitaliy Volyanyuk, co-founder and CEO of Digital Business, asked Suleimenov to assess what the measures introduced by the NBK and other regulators had actually delivered and how Kazakhstan’s financial sector looks today.

Suleimenov described the sector as bank-centered but increasingly diverse, with the domestic financial system, the Astana International Financial Center and emerging digital-finance initiatives creating complementary opportunities.

“Briefly, the system is strong, highly capitalized and digitalized, and it has a huge future,” he said.

But Suleimenov stressed that infrastructure alone would not be enough.

“The second step is, of course, financial infrastructure, on which these solutions have to run. We are also creating that. But now, probably, the main step is creating products,” he said.

“We cannot and will not create the products ourselves,” he added, calling on banks, traditional financial institutions and new financial companies to work both together and in competition to develop new products and business models. The objective, he said, is to make access to financing, payments and cross-border transactions easier for both businesses and individuals.

Digital maturity remains uneven

The transformation, however, is not taking place at the same pace across the entire financial sector, Chair of the Agency for Regulation and Development of the Financial Market Madina Abylkassymova said during the summit.

Volyanyuk also asked about the readiness of smaller banks, insurance companies and other financial institutions for digital and AI transformation, rather than focusing only on the largest banks with significant technological and financial resources.

Abylkassymova said the agency had assessed the digital readiness of 94 financial organizations this year, examining process digitalization, data quality, infrastructure, cybersecurity, AI use and employee competencies.

“Banks remain the leaders, with almost 75% already using artificial intelligence. However, a gap remains between banks and other parts of the financial sector, particularly insurance and microfinance,” she said, stressing that digital transformation is not simply about introducing technology.

“It is also about the competencies of employees,” Abylkassymova added, arguing that digital and AI tools need to be embedded into the actual processes of financial organizations.

According to her, the agency is now developing a strategy for large-scale digitalization and further AI adoption across the financial sector. It has identified 1,200 specific measures and prepared individual development plans for the 94 organizations assessed.

Kazakhstan looks to export financial services

Suleimenov identified exporting Kazakhstan’s financial industry as another strategic priority. This includes helping domestic financial companies enter foreign markets and attracting international players that can serve global customers through Kazakhstan’s jurisdiction and financial infrastructure.

He said the country has a strong domestic financial jurisdiction alongside the Astana International Financial Center, which he described as an additional driver of competition and investment.

The next stage, however, will depend on whether market participants can turn the established infrastructure and regulatory framework into products that can compete both domestically and internationally.

“We have a strong foundation, but now we need the market to become more active – with new products, partnerships and business models that will allow us to fully use these opportunities,” Suleimenov said.

The Central Asia Fintech Summit 2026 brings together more than 120 speakers and experts. It focuses on the development of digital finance, including payments, digital assets, AI, cybersecurity, tokenization and anti-fraud technologies.

World.title: Kazakhstan Highlights Middle Corridor Growth and Digitalization at Batumi Forum
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan highlighted the rapid growth of the Middle Corridor and the need to accelerate its digitalization at the Georgian International Maritime Forum in Batumi on Sept. 7-8.

Kazakhstan Deputy Minister of Transport Zhanibek Taizhanov said freight volumes along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR) rose 22% in January-August, while East-West transit increased 55%.

Digitalization drives seamless transit

Speaking at the panel session From Seas to Corridors: The New Geography of Global Trade, Taizhanov stressed the importance of integrating maritime, rail and port infrastructure to make international supply chains more efficient and resilient, the ministry’s press service reported.

He also presented President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s initiative to develop a digital map of transport routes, providing an integrated view of transport infrastructure, logistics chains and cargo flows along international corridors.

The Middle Corridor currently has a capacity of 6 million tons, including 182,000 TEUs. Measures to streamline logistics have reduced cargo delivery times from 38 days to 13-17 days, with a target of 10-12 days from China to ports in Georgia and Türkiye.

Kazakhstan is also advancing the Digital Trade Corridor, which enables online cargo tracking and single-window contracting. Its Tez Customs module has reduced transit customs processing from eight hours to 30 minutes, the ministry told The Astana Times.

Infrastructure expansion

The forum brought together government officials, maritime administrations, international organizations, port operators, logistics companies and industry experts.

Discussions covered port infrastructure, maritime cooperation, digital transformation, navigation and shipping safety, and applying the single-window principle in the maritime sector.

Discussions on the Middle Corridor also highlighted the need for further infrastructure investment. Speaking at the 5th International Forum on Freight Transport in the Black and Caspian Regions 2026 in Baku, World Bank Senior Transport and Logistics Specialist Luis Blancas said a new comprehensive report on the Middle Corridor is scheduled for publication on Sept. 27, Trend reported.

The report covers all nine participating countries and identifies 16 critical investment priorities worth around US$25 billion. More than three-quarters of the required investment is already underway, Blancas said.

The report is expected to provide a broader assessment of infrastructure needs as cargo flows between Asia and Europe continue to grow.
