World.title: Tokayev to Outline Kazakhstan’s Goals and Priorities in October Address
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev will deliver a state-of-the-nation address in October, outlining Kazakhstan’s goals and priorities for the upcoming period, he said during a Sept. 11 ceremony honoring winners and medalists of the sixth World Nomad Games in Astana.

President Tokayev made the announcement at a ceremony at the Palace of Independence, where he congratulated Kazakhstan’s athletes and coaches on their performances at the World Nomad Games, praising the national team for demonstrating strong skills and strengthening Kazakhstan’s standing in traditional sports.

“Today, the authority of Kazakh sport is higher than ever, and the whole world recognizes this. Our athletes are always among the best,” he said.

Tokayev also highlighted sport’s broader role in strengthening public health and human capital, pointing to work underway to advance these principles enshrined in the Constitution. He said Kazakhstan is moving forward as a nation focused on the future, with ambitious goals and clear plans.

Tokayev also highlighted Kazakhstan’s growing role as a host of major international sporting events. Next year, the capital will host seven world championships, while Almaty is set to host the 10th Asian Winter Games in 2029.

“We have a huge amount of work ahead, but all these international events are extremely important for strengthening the authority and prestige of our country,” Tokayev said.

World.title: “Arresting a person in Georgia over their views on a 34-year-old war is a legal absurdity” – opinion
World.content:
Opinion on Giorgi Baramidze’s arrest

“Arresting someone over an opinion expressed in a historical programme about a 34-year-old war — especially when he has since apologised for the statement — is a legal absurdity,” said Tamta Mikeladze, director of the Social Justice Center, commenting on the arrest of Georgian opposition leader and former defence minister Giorgi Baramidze.

On 11 September, Giorgi Baramidze was arrested on charges of treason against the state, specifically sabotage. His arrest followed an interview on the programme “Birth of Georgia”, in which he said that at the beginning of the 1992–93 Georgian-Abkhaz war, the Georgian side had no prisoners because they were “shot”.

Tamta Mikeladze: “Arresting someone over an opinion expressed in a historical programme about a 34-year-old war — especially when he has since apologised for the statement — is a legal absurdity.

The prosecutor’s argument that the statement damaged Georgia’s international standing and image, offended the honour of war veterans and so on has no basis in criminal law. If specific individuals believed Baramidze had defamed them, they could have taken him to court in a civil case.

Claims that the statement could be used in international legal proceedings are also unfounded. There are no international legal proceedings concerning the war in Abkhazia, and Baramidze was not a decision-maker at the time. His words therefore could not carry the kind of weight that would affect any legal consequences.

Arresting someone for expressing an opinion – even if that opinion is unfounded, foolish, offensive or unacceptable – is therefore an unimaginable departure from the rule of law.”

Mikeladze also examines the alleged offence in detail and points to a mismatch between the charge and the statement, arguing that no remarks of this kind can legally constitute sabotage.

News in Georgia

World.title: One of Georgia’s opposition leaders, Giorgi Baramidze, detained on “treason and sabotage” charges
World.content:
Opposition figure Baramidze arrested in Georgia

Giorgi Baramidze, one of the leaders of the opposition United National Movement and Georgian former defence and interior minister, has been detained in Georgia.

Prosecutors searched his home before handcuffing him.

The detention stems from an interview Baramidze gave on the programme “Birth of Georgia”, in which he said that at the beginning of the 1992–93 Georgian-Abkhaz war, the Georgian side had no prisoners of war because they were “shot”.

On 7 August, the prosecutor’s office said it had opened an investigation into “treason against the state and sabotage” over the statement.

As of today, five former Georgian defence ministers are (!) in prison, while a sixth is facing criminal charges.

Giorgi Baramidze is now the seventh on the list.

What the prosecutor’s office says

Deputy Prosecutor General Amiran Guluashvili confirmed that Giorgi Baramidze was detained on charges of treason against the state, specifically sabotage. The charge carries a prison sentence of up to four years.

Giorgi Baramidze, one of the leaders of the opposition United National Movement and Georgian former defence and interior minister

The prosecutor’s office says its investigation found no evidence that prisoners of war were executed by Georgian armed forces or other participants in the conflict. It therefore described Baramidze’s claim as “baseless and fabricated” and said it was part of a targeted information campaign.

According to the prosecutor’s office, Baramidze’s statement could damage Georgia’s international image, the reputation of its defence forces and the dignity of those who took part in the war. It could also undermine efforts to reconcile with communities affected by the conflict and rebuild trust.

The prosecutor’s office says Baramidze’s remarks harmed Georgia’s peace and de-occupation policy and obstructed the work of state agencies, including the Office of the State Minister for Reconciliation and Civic Equality, which is working to restore trust and cooperation.

The prosecutor’s office will ask the court to remand Baramidze in custody. The investigation is ongoing.

What Giorgi Baramidze said

During the programme “Birth of Georgia”, Giorgi Baramidze recalled the exchange of prisoners during the Georgian-Abkhaz war and said: “We had no prisoners. Our side did not take prisoners — they were shot.”

Baramidze’s statement drew a strong reaction from government officials. He later explained several times what he had meant.

He said he was referring to the very beginning of the war, when the Georgian side still had no regular, organised army and some fighters, driven by grief after losing loved ones in the fighting, sometimes did not take enemy combatants prisoner.

“During the first period, this was the situation: people whose mothers, fathers or other loved ones had been killed were so consumed by anger that they did not take prisoners during fighting and killed them instead. They had been driven to despair. This is the bitter truth about the early stage of the war, which I know because I was personally involved in prisoner exchanges,” Baramidze explained.

He said the situation later changed, with the Georgian side beginning to take prisoners, making prisoner exchanges possible.

Baramidze also says he was personally involved in the process, which ultimately helped secure the return of around 200 Georgian prisoners.

News in Georgia

World.title: Live from Gyumri, Armenia, in photos and videos
World.content:
Gyumri, Armenia, photos and video

Gyumri is the second-largest city in Armenia after Yerevan. The video was filmed during a journey from Georgia to Armenia, and the story follows this route.

As soon as you cross the Georgian border and enter Armenia, the road becomes mountainous. The plains and forest-covered mountains gradually give way to rocky slopes.

The road runs across the Ashotzk Plateau along the Akhuryan River gorge and around the Shirak Range. This is where Gyumri lies, at an altitude of more than 1,500 metres above sea level.

The air is noticeably cooler here, which is why both tourists and residents of the capital come here in summer.

Locals are particularly proud of their drinking water. It comes from mountain springs and is exceptionally cold and delicious.

Small drinking fountains can be found throughout the city. Locals call them “pulpulak”. They attract attention partly because of their distinctive designs, with no two fountains looking quite alike.

They are usually built from local stone — tuff or basalt — and decorated with national ornaments, crosses and various symbols.

There is also a tradition of building pulpulaks in memory of deceased loved ones.

A defining feature of Gyumri is its black stone. Almost all the city’s old buildings are made from local volcanic tuff.

Drinking fountain in Gyumri, Armenia. JAMnews photo.

In the city centre lies Vardanants Square. It was named in memory of the battle between the Armenian army, led by commander Vardan Mamikonian, and the Persian army in 450–451.

Vardanants Square in Gyumri, Armenia. JAMnews photo.

Churches of Gyumri

On either side of the square stand two churches: the Church of the Holy Mother of God, also known as the Church of the “Seven Wounds”, and the Church of the Holy Saviour.

The Church of the Holy Mother of God holds a special place in Gyumri’s history. During the Soviet period, when most churches in the city were closed and converted into warehouses or museums, the “Seven Wounds” Church remained one of the few still operating. It became a centre that preserved church traditions and a symbol of believers’ resistance.

Symbolically, the church courtyard contains a brass cross riddled with bullet holes. It commemorates the clergy who continued their service and supported believers during Stalin’s anti-religious campaign. Dozens of members of the Shirak Diocese clergy were arrested and executed.

Today, the bullet holes in the cross are clearly visible even from a distance. The names of clergy members who died during those years are engraved on its lower section.

On 7 December 1988, an earthquake almost destroyed the city in just 30 seconds.

The entire northern part of Armenia was affected. More than 27,000 people died, and 750,000 were left homeless.

A huge fragment of stone broke off the Church of the Holy Saviour in Gyumri during the earthquake. They left it lying beside the church. According to local residents, it serves as a reminder of that terrible day.

A bronze memorial, “To the Innocent Victims, the Compassionate Hearts”, was built nearby. The inscription appears on the monument in three languages: Armenian, Russian and English.

It depicts figures emerging from the rubble and helping one another.

The scale of the destruction clearly showed the difference in quality between older buildings and structures from the Soviet period.

Low-rise buildings in Gyumri made from traditional black tuff. JAMnews photo.

One- and two-storey buildings dating from before the Soviet era proved more resilient, while high-rise buildings constructed in the 1970s and 1980s were completely destroyed.

The tragedy fundamentally changed the city’s future development strategy. Based on the findings of seismologists and architects, Gyumri banned the construction of high-rise residential buildings.

The city returned to its historic style: low-rise, sturdy buildings made from local black and orange tuff.

Tourists often explore the city in these horse-drawn carriages, which are popular in Gyumri. JAMnews photo.

Gyumri, Armenia, photos and video

World.title: Armenian citizenship to become harder and five times more expensive under Interior Ministry draft
World.content:
New requirements for obtaining Armenian citizenship

The procedure for obtaining Armenian citizenship could change. If parliament approves the draft, obtaining citizenship will become not only more difficult but also more expensive.

The Interior Ministry proposes increasing the state fee for obtaining Armenian citizenship fivefold and the fee for renouncing it tenfold. Applicants will have to pay 250,000 drams ($690) to obtain Armenian citizenship and 1.5 million drams ($4,143) to renounce it.

The ministry has already published its draft on the electronic platform where legal acts are made available for public discussion.

The authorities justify the proposed changes by the need to “rethink” the institution of citizenship:

“In recent years, the number of people without a sufficient factual connection to Armenia has increased. These are people who have never visited the country or lived there for a significant period, but obtained Armenian citizenship for practical benefits, including when planning trips.”

The package of amendments includes not only changes to the state fees but also procedural changes. The government expects the amendments to take effect on 1 January 2028.

Between 1 January 2021 and 31 August 2026, 110,219 people obtained Armenian citizenship. Over the past 15 years, 250,000 people have obtained Armenian citizenship. Most of the new citizens did not live in the country permanently.

Those who renounce Armenian citizenship will not be able to regain it for five years

Applications to obtain or renounce Armenian citizenship will be submitted electronically. If necessary, applicants will then be able to schedule an appointment and submit their documents in person.

Under the new procedure, applicants must have legally resided in Armenia for the past five years to qualify for citizenship. They must also have spent at least 915 days in the country during that period.

Ethnic Armenians will face less stringent requirements. They will need to have legally resided in Armenia for the past two years and spent at least 366 days in the country.

A special commission within the Interior Ministry will verify ethnic background. Applicants will have to provide the relevant documents and archival records. The commission may also request certificates from religious or community organisations.

“People who have previously renounced their citizenship may apply to restore it only after five years have passed. They must also have lived in Armenia for at least 366 days during the two years preceding their application,” the draft’s explanatory note says.

Under the current legislation, people who have renounced Armenian citizenship can restore it without observing a minimum waiting period.

A presidential decree granting citizenship will take effect within one year of the applicant signing the oath. From now on, applicants will be able to take the oath only on the territory of Armenia.

If the authorities deny citizenship on grounds related to threats to national security or public order, the president’s decision cannot be challenged or changed through administrative or judicial proceedings.

The project aims to strengthen the standing and stability of the institution of citizenship

The authors of the bill say they have identified numerous applications to restore citizenship shortly after applicants renounced it. They cite the example of a parent who renounces citizenship to terminate their sons’ Armenian citizenship, allowing them to avoid compulsory military service.

The same person may then seek to restore their citizenship and regain the relevant rights and privileges. The amendments would make this impossible.

The authors justify the five-year restriction by arguing that the restoration of citizenship must not become a “situational mechanism”:

“Citizenship is not merely a formal legal status, but a long-term legal and political bond between the state and the individual.”

According to the drafters, the five-year restriction will promote:

“the stability of the institution of citizenship;

preventing its use for opportunistic purposes;

viewing citizenship as a long-term bond with the state”.

They stress that restrictions on restoring citizenship also apply in the Scandinavian countries, as well as in Germany, France and the United Kingdom.

Specialised commission to verify Armenian ancestry

The draft says that the system for making decisions on citizenship matters will also change. In particular, the interagency commission that reviews applications for the granting or termination of citizenship will be abolished.

The Interior Ministry considers that the commission’s work provides little practical benefit. It has almost never reviewed negative decisions or changed the administrative body’s preliminary position.

A specialised commission will be established in its place. Its task will be to verify applicants’ ethnicity, including their Armenian ancestry.

Until now, the authorities have based the verification of ethnicity solely on the availability of certain documents.

However, the Interior Ministry has concluded that applicants’ documents do not always provide a reliable basis for confirming Armenian ancestry. There have been cases in which people submitted forged or altered documents to take advantage of the simplified citizenship procedure available to ethnic Armenians.

According to the ministry, more than 70 such cases were identified between 2023 and 2026. The number of such incidents has also tended to increase each year.

“There were five such cases in 2023, 21 in 2024, 26 in 2025, and 19 in the first half of 2026 alone,” the Interior Ministry reports.

New requirements for obtaining Armenian citizenship

World.title: EPRC: Wildberries expansion poses significant risks for Georgia
World.content:
According to the Economic Policy Research Center (EPRC), the expansion of the Russian online platform Wildberries in Georgia poses significant risks for the country.

The centre makes this assessment in a new report examining the threats that Wildberries-related activities could pose to Georgian brands represented on the platform, consumers, Georgian banks and Georgia’s economic and financial system as a whole.

Wildberries is an online marketplace often described as “Russia’s Amazon”.

According to EPRC, at least eight Wildberries warehouses were put out of operation by Ukrainian strikes in late August 2026, while more than 20 facilities were damaged. During the same period, part of the company’s financial ecosystem, Wildberries Bank, was placed under international sanctions.

The centre says that, while Wildberries’ warehouse infrastructure in Russia became a target for Ukrainian drones and the company’s banking arm was placed on a sanctions list, Wildberries used Georgia and other neighbouring countries to expand its trading network and logistics capabilities.

EPRC predicts that, as a result, Georgia could become part of a regional infrastructure helping a company linked to the Kremlin and sanctioned Russian businesses reduce losses caused by the war and sanctions.

The report notes that Wildberries’ official infrastructure in Georgia includes warehouses, sorting centres and collection points. According to the company’s instructions, updated on 4 June 2026, Georgian sellers can choose a warehouse or sorting centre and review the conditions for accepting products, logistics rates, sorting times and delivery times to consumers.

According to EPRC, this indicates that the company’s activities in Georgia are no longer limited to collection points. Local infrastructure is also being used to receive, sort and subsequently deliver products. However, open sources do not currently confirm the existence of a large logistics centre in Georgia. A similar situation exists in Azerbaijan.

According to the report, information spread in September 2025 that local businesses had been given the opportunity to sell their products directly through the Wildberries platform.

EPRC also publishes what it believes is an incomplete list of Georgian brands available on the platform. The centre explains that finding a complete list is difficult because Wildberries does not allow users to search for brands by country of origin.

At this stage, the list of Georgian products and brands on the platform is believed to include Borjomi, Nabeghlavi, Natakhtari, Zedazeni, Gurieli, Kula, Badagoni, Chateau Mukhrani, Askaneli, Sarajishvili, MACH & MACH, ANOUKI and Aleksandre Akhalkatsishvili.

EPRC stresses that Wildberries operates as a marketplace. The presence of a particular product on the platform does not automatically mean that the manufacturer or an official brand representative is selling it directly. The product may be listed either by the manufacturer or by an independent reseller.

According to the centre, if an independent retailer sells the product, the brand may restrict those sales by protecting its intellectual property or using contractual mechanisms.

In EPRC’s assessment, Wildberries’ expansion in Georgia is no longer solely a matter of developing online trade. The centre identifies several major risks.

In particular, the report says Wildberries is linked to Russia’s trading and financial system, and its ties to the Kremlin have also been confirmed. The company’s financial arm, Wildberries Bank, has been placed under UK and EU sanctions. According to EPRC, the sanctions are linked to the bank’s role in financially supporting the military and the Russian authorities’ aggressive interests.

The centre also says the Wildberries platform is used to purchase goods needed by the Russian military, including military equipment and dual-use goods. According to EPRC, independent journalistic investigations have also confirmed this.

Against this backdrop, the report’s authors question the effectiveness of controls over the trade and export of such products in Georgia. In their assessment, this increases the risk that sanctioned goods or dual-use items could enter or be re-exported through the country.

EPRC pays particular attention to the development of Wildberries’ logistics capabilities in Georgia. The centre believes that, after a significant part of the company’s warehouse network in Russia was damaged, infrastructure outside Russia has become even more important to Wildberries. Georgia could therefore become part of the company’s regional diversification network.

The report also describes the growing integration of Georgian businesses into the Wildberries system. Products from Georgian brands are already sold on the platform, and Georgian entrepreneurs can join it as direct sellers. EPRC believes this creates both reputational and potential financial risks for companies in the future.

According to the centre, Georgia’s financial sector is also at risk. Wildberries Bank came under UK and EU sanctions in 2026, while 5% of the bank is also owned by the sanctioned Russian bank VTB.

EPRC says that the fact that customers in Georgia pay for purchases on Wildberries using Georgian bank cards means that the local banking sector must comply with the sanctions regime and carry out additional transaction checks. According to the centre, after sanctions were imposed on Wildberries Bank, the National Bank of Georgia shifted responsibility to individual financial institutions, explaining that each bank must assess the risks of violating or circumventing sanctions independently.

In EPRC’s assessment, given these circumstances, the development in Georgia of infrastructure linked to a sanctioned financial institution, a business close to the Kremlin and a platform used to supply the Russian military cannot simply be viewed as foreign investment or the expansion of retail trade.

The centre suggests that if Wildberries continues to expand in Georgia without state oversight or proper customs and financial monitoring, and Georgian companies and banks deepen their cooperation with the platform, the country could become part of an economic and logistics network that helps Russian businesses continue operating amid war and international sanctions.

EPRC believes that such a process could have long-term economic and reputational consequences for Georgia.

EPRC on the risks posed by Wildberries in Georgia

World.title: Georgian Legion commander on former prosecutor general: ‘He is following directives from Russian intelligence services’
World.content:
According to a statement by Mamuka Mamulashvili, commander of the pro-Ukrainian Georgian Legion, former Georgian prosecutor general Otar Partskhaladze, who recently took command of a unit fighting on Russia’s side, is following directives from Russian intelligence services. Mamulashvili also said Partskhaladze’s value as a military figure was zero.

The Georgian Legion is a volunteer formation established in 2014 after Russia invaded eastern Ukraine. In 2016, the Georgian Legion officially joined Ukraine’s 25th Motorised Infantry Battalion. It is now subordinate to the Main Directorate of Intelligence of Ukraine’s Defence Ministry. The unit includes Georgian volunteers as well as fighters of other nationalities. It currently has around 2,000 members. In 2023, Russia’s Interior Ministry added Georgian Legion commander Mamuka Mamulashvili to its wanted list.

According to Mamulashvili, Otar Partskhaladze will try to draw ethnic Georgians living in Russia into his adventure — the war against Ukraine. However, his chances of success are doubtful, as very few Georgians fighting on Russia’s side are seen on the front line, and most of them have already been killed.

Former Georgian prosecutor general Otar Romanov-Partskhaladze, who is fighting on Russia’s side, told Russian pro-Kremlin media that members of the Georgian Legion are “war criminals” and will face prosecution under Russian law. Earlier, on 7 September, it became known that Partskhaladze would lead the international “St George” unit, which was created to take part in the war against Ukraine.

Mamuka Mamulashvili: “Partskhaladze will get a response. He will realise that he made a serious mistake by launching a campaign against the Georgian Legion.

No unit, not even Ukrainian ones, has faced the kind of pressure the Georgian Legion has endured. We are one of the oldest units, even compared with Ukrainian volunteer formations. Russia does not like the fact that so many Georgians are fighting on Ukraine’s side. That is why Russia has been fighting us for more than 12 years, both informationally and physically.

Since they failed to destroy the Georgian Legion physically, they have now tried to create a counterweight by forming another Georgian unit that supposedly will fight on Russia’s side. In reality, this is an attempt to discredit Georgia and bring it under the same sanctions that Russia faces. To do this, they are using people with Georgian surnames who live in Russia and who make all sorts of absurd claims that the Georgian Legion should be tried under Russian law.

In 2022, Russia designated the Georgian Legion as a terrorist organisation. This is hardly surprising, as the Georgian Legion has inflicted enormous damage on the Russian Federation. We can see that their disinformation machine has become much more active. Attempts to kill us physically and attacks have also increased. I have personally been attacked seven times and have survived three attempts to poison me.

Partskhaladze is following directives from Russian intelligence services because his own value as a military figure is zero. I doubt that this man knows which end of a weapon fires. Most likely, he was ordered to finance and create another battalion. He will then try to draw people with Georgian surnames who live in Russia into this adventure. I do not know how successful he will be, because over these 12 years I have encountered very few Georgians on the front line — and those I did encounter were already dead.

The battalion will most likely consist of Russians, with a few Georgian-speaking people who will claim that the unit is mainly made up of Georgians.”

Commander of the Georgian Legion on former prosecutor general

World.title: Mzia Amaglobeli: ‘All it takes to avoid asking the regime for pardon is self-respect’
World.content:
“I don’t need advice to avoid apologising to an aggressor or asking the regime for a pardon. A sense of self-respect is enough,” political prisoner Mzia Amaglobeli writes in response to a statement by Shalva Papuashvili, speaker of the parliament of Georgia. At a briefing on 9 September, Papuashvili called prisoners of conscience “prisoners of Brussels’ shamelessness”.

The publication Batumelebi published Amaglobeli’s letter.

Mzia Amaglobeli: “The briefing in parliament was a display of shamelessness and nothing else. The regime has no morals. They do not even want to take responsibility for the unjust verdict that, in the name of Georgia, sent us to prison and branded us dangerous criminals.

They point the finger at Brussels and European diplomats. Shame on them. I don’t need advice to avoid apologising to an aggressor or asking the regime for a pardon. A sense of self-respect is enough.

If two years in prison is not humiliating enough, it will not be difficult for you to come up with something else if you want to keep me behind bars.

Power and state institutions are in your hands.

As for me, I will wait for international justice. I will wait for the day when the European Court of Human Rights examines the legality of the charges against me and the sentence imposed on me for slapping someone.

And you wait too, Mr Papuashvili. The European Court will examine the fairness and legitimacy of the repressive laws you have adopted, as well as their compliance with the Constitution and democratic processes.”

What Shalva Papuashvili said

On 9 September, commenting on the situation of political prisoners and prisoners of conscience, Shalva Papuashvili said they were “prisoners of Brussels’ shamelessness”. Papuashvili also spoke specifically about convicted journalist Mzia Amaglobeli, claiming that the court had given her the lightest possible sentence.

“Under Georgia’s Criminal Procedure Code, a lesser sentence is possible only through a plea agreement. That is what both the law and practice provide. A plea agreement was offered to her. It required only one thing: for Mzia Amaglobeli to acknowledge that what she had done was a crime and that her conduct had been wrong.

Mzia Amaglobeli is a prisoner of the shamelessness of those ambassadors who sat in court, looked her in the eye and effectively told her: ‘Do not plead guilty. Stay in prison.’ It is also the fault of those who awarded her completely unjustified prizes, including the European Parliament, thereby encouraging her not to admit that attacking a police officer is a crime,” Papuashvili said.

Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the well-known publications Batumelebi and Netgazeti, is the first female journalist in Georgia to become a prisoner of conscience.

Authorities arrested her in January 2025 in the city of Batumi during a protest after she slapped the head of the local police, Irakli Dgebuadze. The incident followed a confrontation between protesters and police, which the officers had provoked.

On 6 August 2025, Batumi City Court sentenced Mzia Amaglobeli to two years in prison. The court rejected her lawyer’s request to change her pre-trial measure.

Mzia Amaglobeli responds to the speaker of parliament

World.title: Armenia’s Anti-Corruption Commission did not open proceedings against Pashinyan
World.content:
Commission rejects case against Pashinyan

The Corruption Prevention Commission refused to open administrative proceedings against Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan. Commission members said the complaint contained no “obvious signs of violations of the code of conduct”.

Semyon Babayan, head of the human rights NGO Public Informant, had asked the commission to assess the prime minister’s alleged “violations of the code of conduct”.

“Pashinyan’s public rhetoric and the wording he often uses grossly violate the legally established integrity system and the ethical standards that public officials must follow,” the applicant said.

He presented the commission with 11 such examples. One of them was the word “immoral”, which the prime minister used to describe the Catholicos of All Armenians.

According to the human rights activist, “it insults the feelings of believers and violates the requirement for religious neutrality”.

However, the commission found that the wording remained within the permissible limits of freedom of expression.

For a long time, Nikol Pashinyan has demanded that Catholicos of All Armenians Garegin II step down. He claims that the Catholicos has broken his vow of celibacy and has a daughter. The prime minister also believes that the Catholicos has links to foreign intelligence services and follows their orders. On 24 August, Nikol Pashinyan called the Catholicos “immoral” while speaking in parliament. He also referred to the Patriarch by his secular name, Ktrich Nersisyan. He has used this name for him since launching his campaign to reform the Church. In protest, opposition MPs banged on their desks every time the Catholicos’s name was mentioned. “Your Catholicos is immoral. If you are not bothered by the fact that the man who heads the Mother See is sexually active, then keep banging your desks as much as you like. There is no other way to have a child — even in the Church. There is only one way to have a child: sexual intercourse,” Pashinyan said.

Commission says the word “immoral” falls within the bounds of political speech

The commission commented on the use of the word “immoral” against the Catholicos, citing case law from the European Court of Human Rights. It stressed that political speech enjoys a broader scope of protection.

Commission members assessed the prime minister’s wording as falling within what is permissible in the context of political debate:

“The use of exaggeration, generalisations and even shocking or striking expressions is characteristic of political speech during political debates — in this case, a speech delivered from the parliamentary rostrum.”

They also noted that, according to the European Court of Human Rights, freedom of expression covers not only positive and favourable statements, but also those that may “offend, shock or disturb”.

The Corruption Prevention Commission therefore concluded that the prime minister’s statement should be considered in the broader context of political debate.

The decision also gives the meaning of the Armenian word “պիղծ”, which Pashinyan used, citing academician Eduard Aghayan’s Explanatory Dictionary of the Modern Armenian Language. It notes that the word primarily means “unclean, immoral, vicious”, while in a religious context it means “heretical, unacceptable, ungodly”.

As for the statement “your Patriarch is immoral”, commission members found no attack on the faith or a religious group. In their view, Pashinyan made an “assessment of the alleged conduct” of a specific member of the clergy:

“Pashinyan’s statement sought to criticise not the person, but a specific phenomenon — namely, the alleged violation of the vow of celibacy.”

The commission also stressed that the word “immoral” carries a negative connotation but “does not cross the line into vulgarity or profanity”. Its members also found no calls for violence or threats in Pashinyan’s speech.

According to the decision, the prime minister’s speech was “predominantly critical in nature, as is characteristic of political debate”.

What other violations did the human rights activist identify?

Semyon Babayan also told the commission about 10 other “serious violations” that he believes the prime minister had committed:

“Violation of the principle of separation of powers: a public statement that ‘there is no judge who would not do what I tell them to do’, which directly undermines the independence of the judiciary and trust in democratic institutions.

Use of offensive language: using crude, street-level rhetoric in public against opponents or citizens — conduct that is clearly incompatible with the ethics expected of a senior public official.

Unsubstantiated assessments and ‘back-of-the-envelope estimates’: arbitrarily citing percentages related to corruption and bribery, such as 70% or 100%, without referring to official or verified factual data.

Erosion of public trust: using threats and divisive rhetoric from a high state platform, which contributes to the spread of intolerance.

Threats to ‘smear [people] across the asphalt’: publicly calling for the use of force in a personalised and punitive manner, outside the framework of legal procedures.

The phrase ‘whimpering judges’: humiliating members of the judiciary and systematically discrediting the institution.

Statements that citizens would be ‘brought to their knees’ because of their political views: entrenching a culture of communication based on force and a commanding tone that is unbecoming of a statesman.

Segregation of fellow citizens by labelling them ‘persons of Armenian origin’: violating the principle of national unity and artificially dividing society.

Showing preferential treatment towards members of his own team: violating the principle of equal integrity standards for the sake of political expediency.

Erosion of the integrity and image of a public official: maintaining a marginal, sarcastic and aggressive tone in public debate, undermining the duty of a public official to set an example of appropriate conduct.”

The commission found no signs of an obvious violation in any of the examples cited.

Commission rejects case against Pashinyan

World.title: Azerbaijani representative reaches final of Sea Breeze 2026 Beach Polo tournament (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 12. The finalists of the “Sea Breeze 2026” international beach polo tournament, being held in Azerbaijan for the first time, have been determined, Trend correspondent reports.

In the semifinal match between representatives of Azerbaijan and the United Kingdom, Elit polo club emerged victorious.

The Azerbaijani club defeated Red Star 9–7 to advance to the tournament final.

In the other semifinal, Switzerland’s Sankt Moritz proved stronger than Russia’s Moscow polo club. The Swiss team defeated its opponent 6–4.

Thus, Azerbaijani and Swiss clubs will meet in the final of Sea Breeze 2026. Red Star and Moscow polo club will face each other in the bronze medal match.

The final and the third-place match will be held tomorrow.

The event is officially organized by the Equestrian Federation of Azerbaijan and Sea Breeze.

Four teams representing Azerbaijan, the UK, Switzerland, and Russia will participate in the tournament. A total of 12 polo players will compete in the event.

The team rosters include athletes representing Azerbaijan, the UK, Switzerland, Russia, Argentina, and South Africa.

Two polo matches will be held daily at 16:00 (GMT +4) on September 11, 12, and 13. The match schedule—determining which teams face each other and on which day—will be decided by a draw held the day before the games.

In the beach polo format, each match consists of four periods, known as "chukkas." Each chukka lasts approximately seven minutes. Including intervals, the total duration of a match is around 30 to 40 minutes. Adjustments to the match duration and schedule may be made depending on weather conditions and temperature.

The tournament final will take place on September 13 at 16:00. Following the final match, an awards ceremony will be held to honor the winners and present the trophy.

In addition to the sporting program, the event will feature a DJ set and entertainment activities for the audience.

Admission to the tournament will be by ticket, and a total of approximately 500 spectators are expected to attend over the three-day event.

The tournament matches will be broadcast live on Idman TV. Furthermore, the online channel Polo Line, which caters to an international polo audience, will cover the event, contributing to media coverage and sharing the tournament with the global polo community. The Sea Breeze 2026 Beach Polo event is envisioned as a significant occasion for presenting Azerbaijani equestrian sport in a new and dynamic format, expanding ties with the international polo community, promoting the country's polo and equestrian culture, and showcasing Azerbaijan's potential for hosting international sporting events.
