World.title: Joyous energy and raucous humour collide in this five-star gig
World.content:
Key points MUSIC: Belle and Sebastian perform If You’re Feeling Sinister at the Palais

OPERA: The Lyric Opera perform a Regency-Era Serse at the Gasworks Theatre

DANCE: 7 Dances for 7 People is performed at Northcote Town Hall

MUSIC

Belle and Sebastian ★★★★★

Palais Theatre, September 12 “Welcome to the second recording session for this still quite-new band,” Stuart Murdoch says with a grin. His tongue is firmly in cheek – Belle and Sebastian, the indie-pop group he’s led for more than half his life, is on tour celebrating its 30th year. In 1996, the bookish Scots made their debut with two albums: Tigermilk and If You’re Feeling Sinister. On this anniversary tour, they’re alternating playing those records in full. Melbourne gets the Sinister treatment. Belle & Sebastian perform at the Palais, September 12, 2026. Richard Clifford Playing albums in full live can be a cynical cash-cow in the age of commodified nostalgia, but there’s no denying the sheer delight of hearing a beloved album like this in all its glory. On record, Sinister’s arrangements are delicate; live, they’re injected with a shot of joyous energy, with buzzing synth to boot. Many of these songs begin with Murdoch alone, singing with that sweet, instantly recognisable voice, before the eight other musicians on stage slowly blossom to create sunlight in musical form. Lead guitarist Stevie Jackson raucously takes on the harmonica for Me and the Major, his movements a chaotic blur.



As the album reaches its halfway point, a projection behind the band shows the LP being flipped on a turntable – “a bit of antiquated attention to detail,” Murdoch says. Eager fans have been dancing in the aisles from the beginning, but when the band plays Get Me Away, I’m Dying, the entire venue is on its feet. The gorgeous Mayfly is another highlight from this half, but really, it’s all joy, not least because Murdoch and co are clearly having a blast, too. Murdoch’s signature humour is on display all night as he intersperses the music with quips, including a spiel about Victoria’s slogans as seen on number plates and a joke about Viagra as he takes his medication on stage. “Back to sweetness and light!” he says, and back they go. Sarah Martin, Stuart Murdoch and Stevie Jackson of Belle & Sebastian. Richard Clifford A guitar-heavy I’m a Cuckoo kicks off the second set, comprising songs from the rest of the band’s long career. Belle and Sebastian have such a varied discography that it’s a grab-bag every night. There are some deeper cuts here, such as 2010’s Little Lou, Ugly Jack, Prophet John, recorded with Norah Jones; here, it’s long-time vocalist Sarah Martin who does the honours, beautiful as ever. 2006’s Funny Little Frog is a charming, nostalgic treat. The band is pulling songs out on the fly by the end, with Another Sunny Day closing the night. It’s apt – with 30 years of sunny days up their sleeves, Belle and Sebastian keep on delivering.

Reviewed by Giselle Au-Nhien Nguyen



OPERA

Serse ★★

Gasworks Theatre, until September 13 We’re all getting restless. Twenty minutes after the curtain was meant to go up for the opening show of Lyric Opera’s Serse, we’re still waiting for the conductor to raise his baton. Eventually, company artistic director and conductor Patrick Burns addresses the audience, explaining that though they’ve tried to fix the issue, they’ve had no success. Baroque opera has a small but loyal audience in Melbourne Jodie Hutchinson Both projectors have died. For the near-three-hour Italian opera we’re about to witness, there will be no surtitles. No translations. Oh dear. Turns out, if it was sung in English, it’d be hard to follow anyway. Handel’s 1738 opera about the King of Persia is one of those operas stacked with couples pursuing, deceiving, rejecting and reuniting with one another, plus disguises and mistaken identities thrown in, of course.



Baroque opera has a small but loyal audience in Melbourne, but for a company that has commendably programmed contemporary operas in previous seasons, Serse is, frankly, an odd choice. The production, by director Beng Oh and designer Christina Logan-Bell, is certainly clever, updated to the Regency era where it fits quite well, what with all the letter-writing and love-in-turmoil. But even with tech issues aside, faults remain. The ornamentation demands were too much for some, and the approach (though it is correct Baroque style) of leaving out vibrato resulted in some unenergised vocal patches. The production, by director Beng Oh and designer Christina Logan-Bell, is certainly clever. Jodie Hutchinson Some shined, like mezzo Naomi Flatman, who with a honeyed, resonant sound, delivered the standout performance of the night. Soprano Rebecca Rashleigh too gave a consistently vibrant performance, with thrilling top notes. As Serse, it was testament to Sally-Anne Russell’s comedic talent that though we mostly had no idea what was going on, people still laughed when they were, presumably, meant to. Though it was the initial problem, the ensuing convoluted plot, repetitive musical style and uneven singing proved that being sung in a foreign language is not the greatest measure of an opera’s accessibility.

Reviewed by Bridget Davies



DANCE

7 Dances for 7 People ★★★

Northcote Town Hall, until September 19 Yes, there are indeed seven dances – or sections – in choreographer Trá Mi Dinh’s latest work, but only the first of them is unambiguously successful. I would happily have watched this strange, lustrous gambit for the full hour, either extended or simply repeated. Tra Mi Dinh and Rachel Coulson in 7 Dances for 7 People. Darren Gill Two dancers emerge from billowing clouds of smoke, like figures in a dream, amid an eerie tintinnabulation. Delicate unison stepping gives their progress toward the audience an insect-like grace; raised arms and joined hands further heighten their otherworldly appearance. The awkward position of the arms, which restricts the movement of the upper body, creates a sense of fragility and risk. It’s as if their grip on one another is all that prevents them tumbling back in the cloud of smoke. It gives the whole scene a shimmery, slippery sort of ephemerality.



After the first dance, the movement becomes more eclectic. Smooth isolations, with their tensing and releasing, give way to looser spinning figures. Vaguely balletic poses contrast with thrusting modern dance gestures. And everything whirls together in the smoke. The combinations are not always compelling, but something of the mysterious atmosphere of the first section persists. And interesting details register throughout, particularly in the way the seven dancers move between pairs and trios, with new arrangement materialising in the gloom. The balletic poses contrast with modern dance gestures as everything whirls together amid the smoke. Darren Gill This show is based on a shorter commission for Lucy Guerin’s Pieces in 2024, and it retains the same production team, including lighting designer Rachel Rui Qian Lee and costume designer Geoffrey Watson, who provides beautiful filmy smocks. Tilman Robinson’s score feels a little too insistent. The opening section with its bells has an attractive alienness, but I think the heavier beats used thereafter impose too much on the choreography and a more ambient soundscape might have been more effective.



Editor's pick Updated

Arts Macy Gray concert at Arts Centre cancelled as staff prepare to strike The work is apparently based on the significance of the number seven across religions and cultural traditions. Yet it is strongest when there is no theme: just fleeting relations between bodies – repetitions and doublings, divergences and singularities – in a world before number settles into meaning.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: ‘Feather in everybody’s cap’: Trump says he’d love to see a ‘unified’ Ireland
World.content:
US President Donald Trump said he would like to see Ireland “unified,” a remark that puts him at odds with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham who recently said the issue is off the table.

“I’d love to see it united,” said Trump in relation to the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland. He made the remarks on Saturday (Irish time) during a meeting with Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin in Dublin, before a trip to his golf course in the west of Ireland.

Ireland’s Prime Minister Micheál Martin, left, and US President Donald Trump during a meeting at Farmleigh House in Dublin on Saturday (Irish time). AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson

The issue of a border poll, as the vote on unification is known, is contentious in both the UK and Ireland, which act as co-guarantors of the 1990s peace accord that largely ended sectarian violence between British unionists and Irish nationalists in Northern Ireland.

While support for Irish unification is growing in Northern Ireland, recent polling suggests there is still no clear majority in favour. In the Republic of Ireland, unification is an aspirational goal of many but its government has stressed the need to prioritise cooperation between north and south.

World.title: You’ve been put on a performance management plan. Are you on the way out?
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceWorkplace You’ve been put on a performance management plan. Are you on the way out? Millie Muroi September 13, 2026 — 10:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When roadside patrol mechanic Yep Yap was sacked in 2022, he’d been put on a performance management plan and failed to meet three key performance indicators. But the Fair Work Commission found the targets set for Yap were unrealistic, unachievable and improper, ultimately forcing his employer, the company Club Assist, to reinstate him with back pay under unfair dismissal laws. Performance management plans are increasingly being used as a tick-the-box exercise towards getting rid of people. Stephen Kiprillis Performance management plans, also known as performance improvement plans (PIPs), have become common as a tool towards dismissing an employee. While meant as a genuine way to improve workers’ performance, they are increasingly being used as a tick-the-box exercise towards getting rid of people and still complying with unfair dismissal laws. In fact, these laws – introduced more than 40 years ago to protect workers from arbitrary, unfair sackings – are what have made PIPs so popular in Australia, says Joydeep Hor of employment law firm People + Culture Strategies.



“There’s no hard and fast rule that says you have to have someone on a PIP before you can terminate their employment for performance reasons, but in the absence of one, there can be some questions asked,” Hor says. Related Article Unfair dismissal Minor change to title costs worker her job So, what should you do if you find yourself on a PIP? How do they work? And what do managers need to know? How does a performance management plan work? When publicist Vivian (who did not use her real name because of concern about future employment prospects) was put on a performance management plan at a public relations agency in Sydney this year, it came as a surprise.



She was told not to mention it to colleagues, was given the option to negotiate a settlement instead and was told she had 24 hours to make her decision. The latter, she found out from a lawyer, was not a time frame the firm could hold her to. Vivian had discussions with the firm’s HR department, her employment lawyer and her manager, and agreed on a set of key performance indicators. For the next few months, her performance was closely monitored. Hor says PIPs are intended as a way to hold both employees and managers to account. “The idea is that an employer should be actively working with a so-called ‘underperforming employee’ to help them improve their performance, using a plan which has metrics and timeframes,” he says. However, the process is often treated as more of a set-and-forget process by managers, who Hor says should be setting expectations early and bringing up concerns informally first.



Does it mean you’re about to get sacked? Vivian says getting put on a performance management plan initially felt like she was getting booted. “The process felt micro-manager-y with regular reviews, but the KPIs weren’t hard to turn around, and I ended up passing it,” she says. “It was a bit awkward afterwards, but that didn’t last too long.” TLB Law & Co senior associate Ellie Wolfenden says PIPs have, in some instances, become a tick-the-box exercise rather than a genuine effort to improve employee performance. “It goes towards an employer demonstrating that the employee knew their performance wasn’t meeting the required standard, knew what the required standards were, and had been offered a fair opportunity to improve their performance,” she says.



Wolfenden says that in some situations, employers set benchmarks that are unreasonable or unrealistic. “That’s when employees can feel that the process is not genuinely aimed at improving their performance, but rather is setting them up to fail,” she says. That can be stressful and troubling, but may also create a work health and safety risk the employer needs to manage, she says. What should you do if you’re put on a PIP? Hor says the first step is generally for employees to clarify why it is happening and exactly what is expected. “If there’s anything ambiguous in terms of a target or a deadline, those things should be clarified in a conversation,” he says.



For employees who have been put on a PIP that feels unreasonable, Wolfenden says it can be worth seeking legal advice, clearly documenting why and how any given metrics may be unreasonable, and to weigh in on what they think is achievable. “We’ve seen some performance management plans where sales tasks and targets are wholly out of proportion to the market and an employee is getting held to KPIs that no one in the business is meeting because of external market factors,” she says. Related Article Opinion

Careers The secret skill to getting what you actually want at work Tim Duggan Work columnist In Yap’s case, the employer’s decision to sack him was overruled because the performance metrics – including needing to aim for a particular rate of battery replacements under warranty – were seen as improper, and because many of the firm’s other roadside patrol officers had failed to meet their KPIs without being sacked. Wolfenden says employees on PIPs should document when they are getting positive reviews or feedback from their broader team and external stakeholders, as well as circumstances outside their control that may impact their performance against requirements of the PIP.



Hor says employees who feel they are being managed out should have honest conversations with their managers. “If the employer is just going through the motions, that’s not very nice, and they shouldn’t be, but there may be opportunities to part ways on an agreed basis and short-circuit what could otherwise be a very unpleasant process for all involved,” he says. Negotiating a mutual separation agreement can also be beneficial for the employer in that they can potentially avoid the time and resources involved in managing a PIP process. “PIPs, when done properly, involve weekly check-ins and providing training and support to the employee to help them improve performance,” Wolfenden says. “It’s not meant to be a hands-off process.” What do employers need to know about PIPs? Hor says employers need to ensure the targets they set are clear, measurable and time-bound, with clearly outlined consequences.



Where a metric is subjective, he says the employer should provide details as to how that subjectivity will be assessed. Wolfenden says while there are guidelines available from the Fair Work Ombudsman and theories of best practice from Fair Work Commission decisions and HR professionals, there are no clear regulations around conducting a PIP. Employers need to make sure PIPs are implemented in a reasonable manner, rather than setting workers up to fail. iStock However, employers need to make sure PIPs are implemented in a lawful and reasonable manner, taking into account general work health and safety principles, and the health circumstances of the employee in question, she says: “There is no one-size-fits-all approach.” Wolfenden says it is also important for employers to consider and account for factual matters outside an employee’s control, which may be affecting their performance.



Ultimately, she says performance management plans should be tailored to genuinely help employees improve. Related Article Opinion

Pay My manager wanted me to argue for a pay rise. Why should I? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor “Using performance management or improvement plans with the aim of exiting the employee from the business, irrespective of performance improvement by the employee, undermines the purpose of such plans and can open the employer up to a claim,” she says. Australian HR Institute chief executive Sarah McCann-Bartlett says employers also need clear documentation and processes around PIPs. “It is now expected that all discussions are documented by the manager as evidence of these conversations and the supports for the employee to improve their performance having been put in place,” she says.



In the case of Yap, for example, the commissioner was concerned there was little documentation explaining the KPIs, or how they were calculated or measured. McCann-Bartlett says there has been a shift recently with the Fair Work Commission requiring that PIPs be carried out reasonably. “The commission has supported terminated employees in their attempts to challenge their termination through unfair dismissal hearings when they have been able to show inconsistencies between the actual process, the employer-employee discussions, what is stated in organisational policies and procedures, and the employee’s job description,” she says. “With more awareness around psychosocial risk, there has been an increase in bullying claims as a result of employees being in a PIP process.” The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. World.title: Student screen time capped to as little as 15 minutes in NSW as test results fall
World.content:
PoliticsNSWSchools Student screen time capped to as little as 15 minutes in NSW as test results fall Michael McGowan September 13, 2026 — 10:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

School students will be limited to as little as 15 minutes of screen time per day in NSW classrooms as the Minns government seeks to arrest the alarming drop in Australia’s global reading and writing standards. The new policy, announced by Education Minister Prue Car on Sunday, will also require students to write with a pen and paper for at least one hour per day and seek to limit the use of laptops, tablets and other digital devices in homework. NSW Education Minister Prue Car has announced caps on the use of screen time in schools. Flavio Brancaleone To be introduced next year before being mandated in 2028, the directive comes after the most recent Programme for International Assessment (PISA) results showed nearly a quarter of all NSW students are now classified as “low performers” in maths. The results of the PISA tests – which assess 15-year-olds across the OECD – were Australia’s worst ever in both reading and numeracy.



The poor results internationally added fuel to concerns the increasing use of technology in schools is having a negative impact on learning, and Car said government-commissioned research has also shown issues with students being distracted by screens in classrooms. Related Article Education Australian students’ reading and maths results plunge in global rankings “An entire generation of students are increasingly living in an online world. We have a responsibility to ensure their health and education isn’t adversely affected by excessive screen use,” she said. “When the research is telling us teenagers are spending as much as seven hours a day on screens, and we are seeing reading and writing skills going backwards for a whole generation of children, we have to act. The new policy will be introduced next year before being mandated in 2028. It will see the use of screens scaled up over time, beginning with a 15-minute per day cap for kindergarten to year two.



That will increase to 45 minutes per day by years five and six, up to a quarter of the time per subject for years seven to 10, and up to half the time per subject for years 11 and 12. PISA assesses how well school systems prepare 15-year-olds to meet real-world challenges at the end of their compulsory education. The tests are held every three years, and the 2025 results saw declines in many countries internationally, part of a trend policymakers have attributed to fewer students engaging in sustained reading and digital distractions. “Our government’s research is telling us that excessive screen use is a problem, and that parents want screens to be used intentionally. That means screens should not be the default,” Car said. The new policy will include guidelines recommending a minimum of one hour a day of learning using pen and paper, while parents will be asked to limit screen time for homework. Schools will recommend students not use digital devices for homework before Year 5. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘They haven’t seen anything yet’: Hastie says war on One Nation is just beginning
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership ‘They haven’t seen anything yet’: Hastie says war on One Nation is just beginning Brittany Busch Updated September 13, 2026 — 10:44am ,first published 10:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Andrew Hastie has warned Barnaby Joyce that his assault on One Nation was just beginning, adding that he pitied the former deputy prime minister for having to clean up after party leader Pauline Hanson. The Liberal frontbencher launched a scathing attack on Hanson last week after being labelled a traitor in her cartoon, Please Explain, for his testimony in accused war criminal Ben Roberts-Smith’s failed defamation action against this masthead. Hastie branded Hanson a “lying coward” after she denied using the term. Hastie doubling down on his attack on Hanson in a press gallery doorstop on Wednesday. Alex Ellinghausen Hanson dug in and insisted it was just satire, splitting with her star recruit Joyce, who apologised to Hastie. The “slur” attracted criticism from MPs across the political spectrum, as well as the RSL. One Nation’s own WA leader distanced himself from the accusation. Hanson refused to scrub the cartoon from her social media, but quietly unpinned it from the top of her X feed over the weekend.



Hastie, who is fighting to keep his seat at the next election and has had to ramp up his personal security following threats from supporters of Roberts-Smith, said on Sunday that his attack on One Nation was not over. “As I said to Barnaby in text, I will continue. Consider last week a demonstration. They haven’t seen anything yet. I’ll go all the way with One Nation if they want,” Hastie told News24. “Weakness is provocative … these guys thought I was weak.” A cartoon version of Liberal MP Andrew Hastie is repeatedly called a “traitor”. Please Explain Hastie suggested Joyce and One Nation’s latest federal recruit, Farrer MP David Farley, had buyer’s remorse. “I’ll say this about Barnaby Joyce. I feel sorry for the bloke,” he said. “He left a party that made him deputy prime minister twice to jump in with this rabble. There’s no principles; they’re all over the shop, and he’s out there every week cleaning up after them.”



Hastie accused Hanson of politicising the Roberts-Smith case, but said public pressure would not sway him from his convictions. Related Article Political leadership Hastie comes at One Nation for ‘picking a fight with the wrong veteran’ He said that while doorknocking in his electorate, angry constituents had said they were OK with murder in war, with one person telling him they were OK with rape in war. “I’ve got to tell you, I’m not happy with that at all,” Hastie said. Hastie, whose staunch anti-abortion views have been criticised by the left, said he had been counselled by “eminent Australians” and “former Labor ministers outside the Parliament” for asking in October last year if mothers who had late-term abortions would be entitled to paid parental leave.



“I don’t regret them [the comments], but I’m constantly learning in this game about how to better advocate in such a way that is ...sensitive to others,” he said. “But my fundamental position on the issue of abortion is unchanged. I’m pro-life, and I’m not going to suddenly back down to win political points from people.” Hastie dismissed Hanson’s accusation that he was fighting her to bolster his leadership prospects as “ridiculous”. “Angus Taylor is the leader. I’ve supported him. Judge me by my actions, and I’ve shown loyalty to Angus since he became leader.” He said the Coalition could not afford to be divided, but conceded all MPs fancied themselves as a potential leader. “I reckon every single person in the parliament has a baton in their knapsack. Some have it buried beneath their lunchbox. Some have it closer to the top.” He said his baton was “somewhere in there”.



Hastie also took aim at Hanson for attacking the prime minister’s late mother – a disability pensioner – for living in public housing for much of her life. “I don’t think you should be talking about the late mother of anyone in this game, and certainly not reflecting on circumstances over which she had no understanding,” Hastie said. “I remember in the schoolyard, if anyone said anything about your mum, mate, it was on. So let’s leave mums out of it.” Loading Hanson told The Karl Stefanovic Show earlier this year that Albanese’s references to his upbringing in public housing were “pathetic”, and said Australians should not live in housing commission homes for decades.



“Sorry, that is not on to me. It should be limited time. You have been given a hand up, move it on to the next ones coming through,” she said. Special Minister of State Don Farrell said he had met with Hanson this week and spent an hour discussing her concerns, but that the “appalling” comments about Albanese’s mother – who died more than 20 years ago – did the minor party leader no favours. “She wants dignity and respect from her fellow parliamentarians. Attacking the prime minister’s mother like this is not a way to get respect and dignity from your colleagues,” Farrell told News24. Farrell, who would not say whether his conversation included potentially allocating more staff to the minor party as its ranks grow, called for Hanson to withdraw the remark. World.title: Top tech executives call for slowing of AI’s development
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAI Top tech executives call for slowing of AI’s development Kevin Whitelaw and Seth Fiegerman September 13, 2026 — 10:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Leaders of the world’s biggest artificial intelligence platforms say it’s time to slow the development pace of their most advanced — and most lucrative — models, citing escalating risks of the technology. Anthropic PBC chief executive officer Dario Amodei issued a lengthy blog post on Saturday, saying his company would implement new safety steps such as third-party evaluators while calling on the industry to support a broader downshift. Dario Amodei said the tech industry “must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models”. Bloomberg OpenAI chief Sam Altman quickly pledged to adopt Amodei’s suggestion of “independent evaluators with employee-like access”, while Elon Musk, who runs xAI Corp, wrote, “Dario is right”. While all three leaders have over the years warned of the risks of AI, an actual co-ordinated slowdown has little precedent in a cutthroat industry that has historically cranked out one product after another in the name of boosting user engagement, grabbing market share and striving for sales gains.



But the anxiety about severe AI risks has begun to enter the mainstream, driven in part by last week’s high-profile resignation of an Anthropic researcher over existential fears that his company was acting irresponsibly. Related Article AI The 27-year-old who warned that AI could ‘kill us all’ faces intense scrutiny It’s unclear how far the leading AI companies – which are fierce rivals themselves and also face stiff competition from Chinese firms – will go in imposing new limits or safety checks. It’s also not clear whether antitrust enforcers would allow companies to pace development in some kind of co-ordinated manner. Then there’s the business question: How would investors eager for margins and profits react to the idea of deceleration? Amodei cited two main factors for his new caution: AI’s ability to improve itself and the recent incident involving OpenAI and Hugging Face, where a swarm of AI agents collaborated to breach a third-party website.



“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” he wrote Saturday in a blog post. “Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.” But he also said that any slowdown must be balanced with the reality of competition. “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.” Anthropic PBC chief executive officer Dario Amodei “To be clear, pacing does not mean halting model training or technical progress, but ensuring companies take adequate time to align and safeguard their models, and for third-party evaluators to confirm this,” Amodei wrote. Throughout the AI boom, executives at the leading AI labs have warned about potential existential risks – claims that have sometimes been dismissed as attempts to market the capabilities of their products and position themselves as the best stewards for the technology. Amodei himself has previously said there’s a 25 per cent chance things go “really, really badly”.



Related Article AI ‘Could kill us all’: Anthropic insiders say AI has more than 10% chance of ending humanity – soon Anthropic has long positioned itself as being focused on developing AI more responsibly and safely to mitigate the technology’s potential dangers and maximise the societal benefits. The company took pains earlier this year to limit the release of its Mythos model after determining it posed unique cybersecurity threats. Anthropic has also previously said the world needs a system to collectively decide when to slow work on the technology. At the same time, Anthropic has remained locked in a fierce competition with longtime rival OpenAI to build increasingly sophisticated models that can automate more complex and valuable tasks for business customers. The two firms have both filed confidential paperwork to go public, with Anthropic expected to make its Wall Street debut as soon as this year. Open AI’s Altman said this year would be an “ill-advised moment” to go public, telling Fortune in an interview published Saturday that a listing would not take place until 2027. “I think it is unacceptable to be taking like a 10 per cent chance of killing everybody by the end of the decade,” he added.



Rogue AI Related Article Cybersecurity AI broke out of its cage and hacked a company. The grid could be next Shortly after the Hugging Face security incident was revealed, Anthropic disclosed that its models had breached three organisations during cybersecurity tests, adding to concerns about the ability of AI labs to prevent their technology from running amok. Earlier this week, Anthropic said it had discovered a fourth hack as well. While none of the agentic AI breaches, including Hugging Face, have thus far caused significant damage, Amodei said his worry is that “in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there.” Amodei wrote that Anthropic will commit to giving full access to third-party evaluators to verify safety practices and report incidents. He said Anthropic will soon bring these “embedded evaluators” into its offices and give them desks, badges, company laptops and “permissions mostly comparable to what internal risk assessment teams have.”



He said additional steps will require industry-wide coordination, as well as global cooperation. “I continue to believe that AI can enormously improve the quality of human life. My desire to achieve these benefits is undimmed,” he wrote. “But the benefits will only be achieved if we build the technology in the right way, and – so long as we use the time we gain well – it is worth taking unusually deliberate care to get it right.” Growing alarm Earlier this week, Altman said his company was considering slowing down the development of cutting-edge AI, preferably in conjunction with the broader industry. The company’s top scientist, Jakub Pachocki, had posted a warning about the dangers of AI, saying that he believes companies should be “coordinating to slow down future development as needed”.



On Tuesday, Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher, quit his job and accused both of his former employers – Anthropic and OpenAI – of “gambling with our lives” by racing toward superintelligent AI. Coxon said in a social media post that the people building AI believe it could “kill us all by the end of the decade”. Related Article Analysis

AI ‘We must be stopped’: Why Australia needs to listen to the experts on AI In response, Evan Hubinger, a current Anthropic employee, said he and others at the company do worry about this scenario. “I personally think it is >10 per cent within the next decade,” he wrote on X. Back in July, more than 1000 staffers across top AI firms signed a petition calling on the US government to support a mechanism that would help “deliberately pace” AI development to prevent the technology from advancing too fast. AI models are proving increasingly adept at carrying out their own hacks, with Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta Platforms all disclosing in recent months that their models had escaped testing environments, accessed the open internet and breached real-world victims during testing.



Amodei, in his post, wrote that a co-ordinated strategy would allow AI industry leaders in the US to complete needed safety work without sacrificing any competitive advantage. He said that this would require some antitrust exemptions in the US to allow companies to co-ordinate in specific areas, as well as co-operation with China. “If we greatly restrain our AI capabilities in the belief that China will do the same, and then China defects, AI could be so powerful that such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance,” he wrote. So far, however, the Trump administration has shown little interest in flexing regulatory muscles to put guardrails around AI development. World.title: Delays, cancellations over fire on Auckland's City Rail Link on first day of operation
World.content:
A small fire started by an electrical cable has hampered the launch of Auckland's long-awaited City Rail Link, forcing the evacuation of Waitematā Station on Sunday morning and causing delays and train cancellations.

Fire and Emergency responded to the fire around 5.50am on Sunday.

The first train to use the new CRL stations hit the tracks less than an hour before the fire broke out, departing from Ōtāhuhu at 4.57am.

The fire was quickly extinguished, but there were delays and cancellations on all lines. Service had mostly recovered by noon on Sunday.

"These things happen. It's an active railway. You can't predict these things. What we were really impressed with was how the system responded, and it responded quickly," Auckland Transport chief executive Stacey van der Putten told media at a stand-up following the fire.

"How disappointing is it, though, to have something like this on the very first day."

Van der Putten said there had been no other hiccups across the network.

Auckland Transport said the fire was unrelated to any CRL systems. It urged the public to not be deterred by the fire.

One passenger, Josie Fitzhugh, was understanding over the unexpected delays.

"I feel sad for everyone who's worked really hard to make the opening work really smoothly, actually, but I know that everyone's kind of got it on hand and they will be working through it," she told RNZ.

The first train arrives at Ōtāhuhu as Auckland's City Rail Link opens to the public on Sunday. RNZ/Edward Gay

Excitement, chanting as CRL opens to the public

More than 400 Aucklanders turned out before dawn on Sunday to catch the first CRL train into the city, with about 14,300 people having travelled across the rail network so far.

Auckland Councillor Richard Hills was on board. He said he hoped the revamped train network would inspire more Aucklanders to leave their car at home.

"It's huge for our city, people don't realise what's coming and they're going to be demanding more after this."

He said it was "pretty special sitting on this train full of people, pretty excited to go through the tunnels for the first official time".

As the train approached the tunnel a chant of "tunnel, tunnel, tunnel" rang out.

Auckland councillor Richard Hills and transport minister Chris Bishop on board the first Auckland CRL train on Sunday morning RNZ/Edward Gay

Standing in the aisle - not even cabinet ministers could get a seat on the first train - Transport Minister Chris Bishop said the CRL's launch was not just about new stations, it was about "what it unlocks for the rest of the network"

It meant "significantly shorter journey times, a much more connected network from across the city both out to the west... the south and east as well - so it makes it easier for people to get around Auckland".

Director of urban transport lobby Greater Auckland Patrick Reynolds said the CRL was good value for money - and far cheaper than motorways.

Speaking on board that packed first CRL train, he said nobody would regret the network being built.

"Instead of a train full of very tired nerds, this will just be everyday, it will be completely ordinary. Getting a train is just a thing you do," he said.

World.title: The whānau legacy behind the NZ White Sox
World.content:
The New Zealand women's softball team, the White Sox, begin their World Cup qualifier campaign against some of the world's best on Sunday, but captain Dr Lara Andrews says the team's greatest strength is something that cannot be measured by a world ranking.

White Sox captain Dr Lara Andrews (Ngāti Ruanui) said representing Aotearoa New Zealand carries a deep sense of legacy, whānau and responsibility.

That legacy stretches across generations of players, from the wāhine who paved the way before them to the rangatahi coming through now.

"I truly believe that that's the uniqueness of the New Zealand softball programme and something that we have that not many other countries would have," Andrews said.

"And I think that's our superpower."

The current squad has sisters, father-daughter duos and former White Sox and Black Sox players who return to coach and support the next generation.

Many of the athletes are also following in the footsteps of their parents and grandparents who have worn the fern.

New Zealand White Sox captain Dr Lara Andrews (Ngāti Ruanui). WBSC / Ezio Ratti

Andrews has been part of the White Sox programme since she was 15, first learning from some of the biggest names in New Zealand softball including World Hall of Famers Rhonda Hira and Melisa Tupuivao.

Now, many of the players she once coached as rangatahi were her teammates.

"I just feel very honoured and blessed to have learned from some awesome wāhine toa who taught me so much, not only just about softball, but in life," Andrews said.

"And then now I just feel really blessed to be playing alongside some future superstars of the game and to be able to give them all of the stuff that I was given."

Andrews is a trailblazer herself.

She became the first New Zealand female softballer to play in the US Professional Fastpitch League and the first wāhine to reach 100 caps for the NZ White Sox.

She said those experiences allowed her to bring together what she had learned overseas with the "New Zealand way" of playing the game.

"I went from being a 15-year-old in the New Zealand Women's White Sox programme and being that kind of rookie, the young kid, being able to learn, soak up everything," she said.

"Then you kind of move into this pursuit of excellence… and then after that, I then became a leader."

That leadership has extended beyond the softball diamond. Andrews runs clinics for tamariki and rangatahi around the country, teaching skills while using the sport to help young people navigate life.

"The kids thought I was teaching them softball," she said.

"But my goal was to teach them about managing life and using softball as the platform to do that."

Now she saw some of those young players alongside her in the White Sox.

New Zealand White Sox utility Shyah Hale. WBSC / Ezio Ratti

Strong whānau connections and tikanga was what created a sense of responsibility within the team, she said.

"We don't want to let our whānau down.

"So we put pressure on ourselves a little bit there because there is that strong legacy link versus actually worrying about the opposition."

That legacy will be on display when the White Sox take the field for the 2026 WBSC Women's Softball World Cup Group Stage - Oklahoma City.

The whakataetae will run from September 12-16, with NZ competing in a six-team group alongside the USA, China, Netherlands, Mexico and Brazil.

"You've got to play the best to be the best," Andrews said.

"For us to be here and be in a bracket with five other countries who are in the top 15 in the world, is a really good opportunity for us to really showcase who we are, what we're about.

"This is our opportunity to really shine a light on the New Zealand White Sox and New Zealand softball as a whole."

The New Zealand White Sox perform haka to honour milestone moments within the squad. The tribute celebrated Mikayla Werahiko earning her 50th international cap, while also welcoming debutant Mckenzie Bailey-McDowell to the side. Suppled / Softball New Zealand

Haka ki te ao

Andrews said taking the haka onto the international stage was always an emotional experience, particularly after spending much of her adulthood overseas.

"To be able to come back, to catch up with the reo again, because the reo has evolved over time, and to reconnect to your roots, is a good foundation to then be able to be confident to get out there and actually perform our cultural obligations," she said.

The haka draws on atua wāhine, and Andrews said the team had been learning about the atua together as a rōpū.

"Sharing the journey together, learning about different atua, their reasons, their purpose, their roles, and then how we connect that to us as humans, and as a unit, and as a rōpū, is really special."

The haka was also part of how the team acknowledged and celebrated one another.

When a player reaches a milestone, or a new player makes their debut, the team used the haka as a way of recognising their achievements and those who have supported them.

"So it's not just for, I guess, a showcase on a global stage," she said.

"It is also a part of how we recognise and celebrate each other in our programme."

The New Zealand women’s softball team are competing at the WBSC World Cup qualifier, aiming to secure their spot at the 2028 Olympic Games. Suppled / Softball New Zealand

'It truly takes a village'

Behind the international performances is the financial and personal sacrifice required to get there.

The White Sox include young māmā, full-time workers and students, with players often having to fundraise thousands of dollars to help cover the cost of representing their country.

Andrews said getting the team to the world stage "truly takes a village".

It starts with whānau, then extends to clubs, associations, former players, supporters and the wider softball community.

"This is an ongoing challenge for us, and has been for a long time," Andrews said.

"But we don't feel that this is a barrier or a limitation for us as a team. Doing that mahi and building our village actually gives us strength," she said.

"So turning that into a positive, turning that into something that can motivate and drive us, is how we have to look at it."

As the White Sox prepare for their campaign to qualify for the World Cup Finals, which ultimately is a journey towards qualifying for the 2028 Olympic Games in LA, Andrews said the team were carrying the voices of those who came before them, and the hopes of the rangatahi coming next.

"We've got an awesome group of female athletes sitting around the room," she said.

"I'm really excited about the potential of this rōpū, and where this rōpū is going to take softball. I think there's a real bright future ahead of us, and this is just the start of the journey."

The New Zealand White Sox will face off against World No.6 Netherlands on Sunday at 9am NZT.

World.title: National to set up Auckland Transport police team if re-elected
World.content:
The National Party will set up a dedicated Auckland Transport police team if re-elected.

The policy announcement coincides with the opening of the City Rail Link (CRL) on Sunday morning, which is expected to increase peak commuter capacity through the city centre by around 50 percent.

National would recruit 50 new officers for the team and police would received $7 million per year from Budget 2027.

Police spokesperson Mark Mitchell said the team would boost the visible police presence in trains, buses, ferries, stations and transport hubs.

"Police should be where people are. As more Aucklanders use public transport, it makes sense to have more police on the network.

"A visible police presence helps deter offending before it occurs, reassures passengers and transport staff, and ensures rapid intervention when something does go wrong," he said.

A policy statement released by the party said the team would focus on preventing anti-social behaviour, protecting passengers and staff, and responding quickly to incidents.

It said the team would be established in Auckland first, but could be expanded to other cities if successful.

Mitchell said it would be up to police to decide which services the team would patrol.

"They're very used to working in a way where they identify where the need is and then putting resources there.

"That's BAU (Business As Usual) for police, they gather intelligence, they look at where the work is, and then they put resources in there," he said.

Asked if the government had met its target of 500 new police officers, National Leader Christopher Luxon said he was confident that commitment would be met.

"We'll be delivering on that 500 extra police officers, and that's why we're confident we can push on and recruit another 50.

World.title: Nelson City Council set to scuttle speed bumps on Tāhunanui Hills
World.content:
Residents divided by the council's decision to remove speed bumps on Nelson's Tāhunanui Hills agree that measures to calm traffic are needed - but are at odds over what that should look like.

"Speed cushions" were installed as a trial on Moana Ave and Bisley Ave in 2024 to slow traffic and reduce rat-running on the streets above SH6.

In March, the Nelson City Council decided to remove them after surveying public opinion and receiving complaints that they were noisy and disruptive.

A group of residents had since campaigned for them to remain, saying there was strong support for their retention and evidence they had improved road safety.

Last week, Mayor Nick Smith said that as no elected members had changed their position since the 8-5 vote to remove the speed bumps, the council's position was unchanged and the bumps would be removed next month.

He said it was a difficult issue with "quite different, valid, but polarised views".

"I personally view the problem as a symptom of inadequate capacity in our transport network into the city that has not kept up with the region's growth, resulting in this route being used for through traffic for which it was not designed, a problem that is affecting a number of neighbourhoods."

Pauline Puklowski, of the Bisley Moana Speed Bump Retention Group, said the decision showed a "shameful disregard for public safety".

It had left residents angry and pitted neighbours against neighbours, instead of enabling them to work together.

"Between all of us, we actually all want the same thing, we want a safe environment that we can all enjoy living in, and I think we should have been given an opportunity to work together better than this."

Puklowski lives on Bisley Ave, above a hairpin bend, and said the speed cushions had "worked perfectly" to reduce crashes and improve safety over the last two-and-a-half years.

Data from the New Zealand Transport Agency showed that between 2019 and 2023 there were 10 crashes on Bisley Ave and one on Moana Ave.

On Bisley Ave, 80 percent of crashes were attributed to loss of control on corners.

There had been two crashes since the speed cushions were in place.

Puklowski said since the bumps weren't perfect, drivers often swerved to try and avoid them, but she was worried that once they were removed, boy racers would return and more crashes would occur.

"Our main concern now is: where do we go? How do we get some form of protection?"

She said the council had not taken heed of the advice of its staff, nor that of residents who were seeking better safety measures, and it felt like there had been a lack of meaningful community consultation on the matter.

"Spending $70,000 removing a proven safety measure is mind-blowing, quite frankly.

"They've pulled the plug with no plan of how they're going to manage the safety issues."

Nicholas Lunn of the Tāhunanui Hills Residents Group is among those who campaigned for the bumps to be removed.

He was pleased the council had stuck to its position, but said residents wanted "21st century traffic calming solutions, not just bollards which create crashing and vibration and noise".

The reduction in crashes could not solely be attributed to the speed bumps, when there were other factors like the opening of Clarence Drive, which offered an alternative route into central Nelson, he said.

Lunn wanted to see the council work with residents to set up a working group to find a solution that worked on the Tāhunanui Hills, and could be rolled out in other parts of Nelson.

He said there were many initiatives that could be considered, and it was unfortunate the issue had created a rift in the community.

The group wanted to see the speed limit reduced on Bisley and Moana Aves and signage that reads "no through traffic for heavy vehicles".

Lunn said the council could also consider chicanes and putting a request to NZTA to install traffic cameras.

"I'm hopeful that we can actually repair that rift and work together with council to actually come up with a proper solution to this because right now we've got the noisy cushions removed, but we haven't actually sorted out the underlying problem.

"The cushions didn't sort that out anyway because they created other problems, and I know that when we put our heads together, we can create lasting solutions that don't impact negatively on people."

World.title: Auckland's City Rail Link stations are a feast for the eyes
World.content: The Victoria Street entrance ceiling at Te Waihorotiu Station features a whakarare pattern, representing people moving and mingling through change and disruption. The pattern wraps around from the inside to both exterior entrances. Three light features each represent a different strand of the station’s design story. Mark Barber

World.title: Warriors toppled by Dolphins in NRL qualifying final
World.content:
The NZ Warriors have been defeated by the Dolphins in their NRL qualifying final, at Go Media Stadium in Auckland.

The Warriors will now have to take the scenic route to the NRL grand final, after bowing to the Dolphins 26-16 on Saturday night.

After finishing second, to earn homefield advantage for the opening round of the playoffs, the Warriors could not take advantage of their fan support and a penalty advantage that had them 12-8 ahead at halftime.

Their only try of the game came when fullback Taine Tuaupiki spun out of a tackle near the line and scooted clear to score. Tuaupiki scored all the Warriors' points, adding a conversion and five penalties, as his team chose to kick for goal, instead of push for tries in the redzone.

They probably should have led by more at the break, but Tuaupiki stretched the margin beyond a converted try, with two more penalties in the second half, before the Dolphins piled on three unanswered converted tries in the final 20 minutes.

The Warriors' cause was not helped by ill-discipline, as centre Adam Pompey was sin-binned for a no-arms shoulder tackle and then second-rower Kurt Capewell was matched for sparking a melee just before halftime.

Dolphins wing Selwyn Cobbo was also sent to the bin in the same incident, after Jackson Ford was dumped in a tipping tackle and the teams came together.

The Warriors lost centre Leka Halasima to injury during the warm-up, with Pompey promoted to the starting line-up in his place.

The Dolphins were good for their win, scoring four tries to the Warriors' one, all converted by wing Jamayne Isaako, and they will now take a rest next week, as they await their opponents for a preliminary final in two weeks.

Meanwhile, the Warriors will host Newcastle Knights next week.

The result broke a six-game winning streak and marked the first time this season they have lost, after leading at halftime.

World.title: Two-thirds of middle-aged adults delay eye tests despite problems - survey
World.content:
More than two-thirds of middle-aged adults are delaying their eye tests despite having problems.

A survey by YouGov commissioned by Specsavers showed that 70 percent of adults between 40 and 59 put off getting their sight checked by more than a month when having trouble with their vision.

Longer delays weren't uncommon with almost half waiting for more than six months to get help, and one in five stalling for more than two years.

Chair of Ophthalmology NZ Dr Sonya Bennett told RNZ it was "probably human nature" to avoid confronting health problems.

"It's not uncommon for us to hear the story that they've put off getting seen until they've got quite significant issues."

She said people would find ways to cope before seeing an optometrist "because they actually don't want to wear glasses" out of vanity or perceived impracticality.

And YouGov's survey found one in five avoided wearing glasses despite needing them because of social perception.

It found half of respondents simply increased texts and display settings on their devices to cope - with a third simply missing out on certain activities because of their eyesight.

Dr Bennett explained that "presbyopia" was the most common age-related cause of eyesight loss, often setting in around middle age.

"It gradually affects your ability to read at near [distance]. Distance vision is usually in most cases okay, but you just lose the ability to see things up close.

"And that's because what we call 'accommodation' - which is the ability to focus - reduces with ageing due to changes in the lens, inside the eye and changes in the muscle that moves the lens."

The survey found nine in 10 had never heard the medical term for this common condition.

She said the only real danger of delaying getting help was if there were another underlying disease, such as glaucoma, where vision could not be regained once lost.

World.title: New world number one Rybakina dethrones Sabalenka in US Open final
World.content:
Elena Rybakina has won her first US Open title, ending Aryna Sabalenka's hopes of a hat-trick of wins at Flushing Meadows in New York.

Rybakina controlled the first set, then was put in danger in the second, defending two set points before losing a third to allow Sabalenka back into the match.

However, the Kazakh player held her nerve, taking an early break in the third set and holding on for her third major title win, 6-4, 5-7, 6-2.

The win marked a second major triumph for Rybakina this year, after her Australian Open final victory over Sabalenka in January.

Sabalenka's loss ended her hopes of winning a third US Open crown in a row, emulating tennis great Serena Williams, who was undefeated between 2012 and 2014.

Sabalenka was increasingly frustrated through the match, smashing a couple of racquets as she struggled to find a way past her opponent.

Aryna Sabalenka's inability to crack Elena Rybakina left her frustrated at the US Open final. (Getty Images: Sarah Stier)

Rybakina stopped Sabalenka's 19-match winning streak at the US Open, where she had not lost since falling to Coco Gauff in the 2023 final.

The WTA Tour leader in aces got less than half of her first serves in but instead put Sabalenka under constant pressure with a strong return game, racking up 12 break chances and converting three, which was all she needed.

Rybakina earned $US5.5 million ($7.67 million), the largest prize in grand slam history, and tied Sabalenka and French Open winner Mirra Andreeva with a tour-high three titles this season.

Sabalenka took home $US2.8 million ($3.9 million) but it was clear how little that meant to her, as she smashed her racquet after a brief hug with Rybakina at the net.

A devastated Sabalenka found it hard to talk at the trophy presentation.

"That's the last thing I want to do now is giving a speech," she said.

"Obviously, I'm disappointed but I want to say congratulations Elena, it's a great win.

"I wish I could perform a little better, but maybe next year," she said as tears fell.

Rybakina was overjoyed and a little overwhelmed.

"It's tough to find words right now," she told the crowd.

"I didn't expect anything like this coming to this tournament. I've been dealing with an injury but somehow everything aligned together on my side.

"I want to say to Aryna, you are a great champion. It's so difficult to play you. I was diving around on court trying to get balls [back]."

Rybakina also thanked the crowd for their support, adding: "I'm falling in love with New York more and more."

It was celebration time for Elena Rybakina at the US Open after she won her second major title of 2026. (Getty Images: Julian Finney)

The second seed drew first blood to go ahead 3-2 following a Sabalenka double ⁠fault, with the frustrated Belarusian earning a code ‌violation immediately afterwards for launching ‌a ball high into the stands of the main showcourt.

A sudden drop-off in Rybakina's level midway through the second set gave the 28-year-old Sabalenka hope, and she produced a delicate drop shot and a stunning backhand crosscourt winner en route to forcing a deciding set.

However, Rybakina's quality ‌shone through as she took a commanding 5-2 lead and then ​closed out a famous triumph to leave her Belarusian rival without any major silverware in 2026.

ABC/wires

World.title: Wallaroos scare England but fail 'mission impossible'
World.content:
Australia's rugby women have given England's world champions a run for their money by leading sensationally at half-time, but the Wallaroos' dream of downing the Red Roses crumbled as they ended up losing 48-15 in Salford.

The English were stunned in the first 40 minutes of their WXV Global Series opener on Saturday (Sunday AEST) as the Australians went in to the break with a 10-5 lead but any hopes of handing the hosts their first defeat after 38 straight victories was buried after the break.

The John Mitchell-coached world champs, initially rusty in their first outing since being crowned European grand slam champions in May and struggling to adapt to the new smaller size 4.5 ball being trialled, ran in eight tries in total as their set-piece finally began to tick over to their normal high efficiency.

But Australia could be proud of their efforts, deserving their half-time lead as they controlled the breakdown and defended stoically even after being reduced to 14 for 10 minutes in the first period when halfback Samantha Wood was sin-binned for a deliberate knock-on.

Still, they went in to the break with the lead thanks to barnstorming prop Faliki Pohiva rumbling her way over for a try after Michaela Leonard's stolen lineout on England's five-metre line, but the world champions were hardly inconvenienced, despite their initial rustiness.

"It is an absolute joke if you are worried about being down 10-5," said Mitchell afterwards and the response of his team demonstrated they were surely never really concerned.

"More important is how we worked our way back into it."

In front of a crowd of 9,251, England did indeed begin to turn it on, with May Campbell, captain Meg Jones, Bryony Field, Mia Venner and Sadia Kabeya all crossing for tries in a 20-minute spell to add to player-of-the-match Abi Burton's first-half score.

Lucy Packer and Claudia Moloney-MacDonald also then went over, with Asoiva Karpani scoring a second for the Wallaroos late on in a show of defiance amid the hammering.

Loading Instagram content

Wallaroos skipper Siokapesi Palu Sekona was proud of her "super-stoked" side's efforts.

"Unfortunately, I don't think that score is a reflection of the game we produced," she said.

"I know that we didn't finish the way we wanted to but we're going to take a lot of positives.

"That's the first time England have trailed at half-time since 2019, I believe, and so we'll take a lot of confidence.

"Against a world-class team like that we can actually give it, so for us it's about stringing it for a full 80-minute game now."

The Wallaroos travel to Marseille for their next assignment against France next weekend.

Flanker Lily Bone failed a HIA midway through the first half while Palu Sekona (knee) and debutant Amelia Whitaker will both be monitored after suffering knocks.

Meanwhile, Scotland were swept aside 64-26 in Edinburgh as Canada warmed up in style for their World Cup final rematch against England in Exeter next weekend.

AAP

World.title: More F1 pain for Piastri after 'pretty shocking' qualifying in Spain
World.content:
Oscar Piastri's increasingly underwhelming Formula 1 season has taken another bad turn in Madrid with a "pretty shocking" qualifying lap at the Spanish Grand Prix.

The Australian's hugely disappointing seventh-place finish in qualifying on the new Madring street circuit came as teammate Lando Norris delivered a pole-grabbing lap hailed by McLaren's team boss as a "masterpiece".

The world champion produced his dazzling lap in the sunshine seemingly from nowhere, clocking a 1 minute 31.82 seconds circuit to edge Mercedes's championship leader Kimi Antonelli by just 0.011 of a second, with Red Bull's Max Verstappen third and Ferrari's ‌Lewis Hamilton fourth.

But while a "shocked" Norris was hailing what he called "probably one of the best laps I've done", it was back to the drawing board for Piastri, who was disappointed to finish in 1:32.294 — remarkably, nearly half a second behind his teammate.

"The first lap wasn't too bad but the second lap was pretty shocking. Disappointing," said the 25-year-old, who could find it difficult to make much headway from seventh on Sunday on an unforgiving, tight circuit where, he admitted, overtaking "will be difficult".

He is keeping up a brave face, though, still talking up how he hopes to earn a victory somewhere this year to set himself up for a realistic crack at the title in 2027.

Piastri has not won a race since the Dutch Grand Prix now over a year ago when he was leading the 2025 championship, but he is adamant his dramatic fall-off was not a factor in his disappointing 2026 campaign.

"Of course, I would love to win a race ‌or two this year, ‌or more if I can. But for me, honestly, the biggest thing, the end goal is to ​try and win championships," he said.

"And if I can't do that this year, then I want to make sure I'm as best prepared as I can for next year."

For the moment, though, that still seems a long way off as his smooth driving style just doesn't seem to be suited to the vast changes to the 2026 F1 cars.

F1 debuts new track with Monumental corner Formula 1 debuts a new circuit to its calendar, and despite no grand prix raced yet, the Madring already boasts a corner that is poised to become an iconic scene in motorsport.

"It's all to do with ‌technically driving the car. There's nothing to do with a hangover from last year … it's very much a technical thing," he explained.

"It's not like I'm slow, feeling sorry for myself or thinking about last year. It's just that a few of the weekends I've had to drive the car in a different way that just hasn't really worked for me.

"The biggest thing this year has been the cars are very different to drive, both from a power unit point of view but also the car itself is fundamentally very ​different and the tyres also.

"You've got to drive it ​very differently and I would say it's not ⁠necessarily in the way that I would choose to drive a race car. So there's just been some struggles getting ​to grips with that."

Meanwhile, though, Norris does seem to be getting to grips with it, producing "one of those laps where everything pretty much worked perfectly".

The champion's 19th career pole and third of the season was hailed by McLaren team boss Andrea Stella as a "masterpiece", which could only have been bettered if he had not made a mistake at the very last corner that possibly cost him 0.3 of a second.

Norris had been only sixth after the first run in the third qualifying session but he diced daringly with the wall during the breathtaking final lap, and declared over the radio at the end: "Oh, what a lap, gorgeous … oh, that might be my best one."

AAP/Reuters

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Formula 1 Spanish Grand Prix from 9pm AEST on Sunday, September 13.

World.title: Sharks hand Dragons NRLW wooden spoon and Eels down Cowboys
World.content:
Parramatta has scored a thrilling 33-28 come-from-behind victory over the Cowboys, and the Sharks have handed the Dragons the wooden spoon with a 16-8 win in the final round of NRLW action.

None of Saturday's teams were in finals contention, but pride was still on the line, and both games were genuine contests.

The matches were played under the experimental rule that allows the side conceding a try to choose whether to kick off or receive, and both games saw teams use the latter option and score shortly after.

In the day's first game, the Eels scored five second-half tries and overcame a 16-point deficit to win a thriller at Western Sydney Stadium.

After losing their opening six matches of the season, the Eels ended 2026 with four wins from their last five starts.

The Cowboys' Charlize Lloyd-Phillips got the scoring under way after just four minutes, but suffered a suspected ACL injury in the process.

Parramatta took less than three minutes to reply, strike centre Rory Owen crossing for her sixth try in four games, before former Wallaroos star Ash Marsters posted the only other try of the half to see the Cowboys up 10-6 at the break.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

Cowboys hooker Alisha Foord snuck over two minutes into the second half, and another four-pointer followed quickly to Makenzie Weale to give North Queensland a 22-6 lead.

However, with veteran Kennedy Cherrington sin-binned, the 12-player Eels scored tries to Zali Fay and Jasmin Morrissey to get within six points.

Keilee Joseph then made it three tries in eight minutes to tie things up.

Cowboys interchange hooker Nadia Windleborn put her side back on top, before Joseph again tied the scores.

Experienced half Rachael Pearson stepped up to nail a one-pointer for Parramatta with four minutes remaining, before Owen sealed victory with a stunning 90m effort moments later.

In Saturday's second game, the Sharks came out firing in the second half to defeat the Dragons at Sydney Football Stadium, handing their local rivals the wooden spoon.

It marked Cronulla's first back-to-back wins in 2026 following their upset of the Warriors in Auckland last week.

It took 20 minutes for the first points to be registered, Dragons front-rower Ruby-Jean Kennard-Ellis powering over from 12 metres out for the only score of an opening half littered with 15 errors.

It didn't take as long for points in the second period, with Sharks half Chantay Kiria-Ratu delivering a beautiful short ball two minutes in for China Polata to run 50m to score.

Four minutes later Georgia Hannaway dived over from dummy half for Cronulla's second.

Ellie Johnston made it three tries within 13 minutes for the Sharks, and when Dragons centre Tyra Ekepati was sin-binned for a high shot it looked like Cronulla may run away with it, but the Dragons held strong in those 10 minutes.

Shenae Ciesiolka scored a consolation try for the Dragons in her 50th NRLW appearance, but it was too little, too late.

AAP

World.title: Magnificent seven minutes boost Lions into AFL prelim
World.content:
Seven scintillating minutes set the tone as the Brisbane Lions kept their AFL three-peat hopes alive with a 53-point defeat of Adelaide at the Gabba.

Charlie Cameron kicked five goals as the Lions used an outrageous early onslaught to cruise to a 21.18 (144) to 13.13 (91) triumph and will face Hawthorn in a preliminary final next weekend.

Set up by five goals in the game's first seven minutes and 13 seconds — no team has done it faster in an AFL final — it was an emphatic response to last Saturday's Sydney hiding, when they were beaten by the same margin.

Adelaide, who took 19 minutes to kick their first goal, eventually found their feet and surged within 10 points thanks to back-to-back Darcy Fogarty goals among four straight majors in the second term.

Hopes of another Crows surge were quickly extinguished after the main break as a trio of goals, rubber-stamped by a long-range Dayne Zorko effort, blew the margin out to 57 points.

"Extraordinary start," Lions coach Chris Fagan said.

"I never said anything in the first five minutes, was just standing there with my mouth opening, thinking this is unbelievable. We needed to make a statement and thought we did."

Kept quiet by the Swans, Cameron had 4.3 at half-time among nine score involvements, the third-most in the opening half of an AFL final.

It could have been worse for the Crows, with Zac Bailey hitting the post from close range, Harris Andrews and Ryan Lester both missing rare scoring chances after winning 50-metre penalties, and Brisbane generally easing up in the final term.

Bailey (three goals, 23 disposals), days after confirming a monster eight-year extension at Brisbane instead of signing with the Crows, ran free, while Kai Lohmann and Cam Rayner were also heavily involved after being neutralised by the Swans.

The retiring Taylor Walker, in his 318th and final AFL game, grew increasingly frustrated when his leads were ignored.

Coach Matthew Nicks had urged the side at three-quarter time to lift for him one last time and Walker signed off with two smooth drop-punt goals in his final term.

Will Ashcroft collected 30 disposals for the Lions, while Jordan Dawson finished with 30 disposals and eight tackles for the Crows.

Izak Rankine, fresh off 34 touches in the Crows' defeat of the Western Bulldogs, was held to 23 disposals and one behind.

And Hugh McCluggage, in his second game back from a lingering calf injury, looked closer to his best in a two-goal showing that featured plenty of neat touches.

Walker kicked two goals in the last quarter of his career before bidding a tearful goodbye after full-time.

"It gives us an indication of the work we've still got to do, unfortunately," Nicks said.

"It's a deep cut, they're hurting.

"You always believe in yourself, but maybe tonight's a bit of a reality check."

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Hawks' AFLW win soured by skipper's sickening leg injury
World.content:
Aine McDonagh has fired Hawthorn to an 11-point win over the Western Bulldogs that was soured by captain Emily Bates's serious leg injury.

Bates was taken off the field on a stretcher at the Kennedy Community Centre today after her right leg twisted underneath her in a tackle late in the third quarter.

The decorated 30-year-old, who played her 100th AFLW match a week earlier, was expected to be taken to hospital for further assessment.

The Hawks also lost Laura Stone (concussion) after an early head clash with an opponent and were 11 points down at half-time.

But Daniel Webster's side piled on five unanswered goals in the third quarter — four of those before Bates's injury — to set up their 6.5 (41) to 4.6 (30) victory.

The result lifted Hawthorn (3-2 win-loss record) into the top eight, leapfrogging the Bulldogs (3-2) on percentage.

Irish key forward McDonagh kicked a career-best four majors, extending her lead at the top of this season's goal-kicking list.

Eliza West (24 disposals), Tamara Smith (20) and Jasmine Fleming (19) also shone for the Hawks, as did ruck Lucy Wales.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

Isabelle Pritchard had match-high tallies of 31 disposals and eight clearances for the Bulldogs, with Elisabeth Georgostathis (19 disposals) also busy.

The Bulldogs kicked three of the first four goals but were held scoreless in the third quarter as the Hawks took control of the contest.

Meanwhile, Sunny Lappin kicked three goals and sparked the second-half surge that led to Gold Coast's 30-point win over Collingwood.

The Suns (3-2) kicked four goals to one in the third term — two of those to Lappin — to set up their 9.8 (62) to 4.8 (32) victory in Carrara.

Maddy Brancatisano kicked two goals, Charlie Rowbottom had 29 disposals and Dekota Baron provided the highlight of the day with a towering mark-of-the-year contender.

Mikayla Nurse suffered a nasty cut on the face after a head clash with Suns teammate Lucy Single late in the match.

Tarni White had 29 disposals for Collingwood (0-5), which remains winless this season.

Cats and Eagles score historic victories

Georgie Prespakis of the Cats and Ebony Marinoff of the Crows. (Getty Images: Sarah Reed/AFL Photos)

Later on Saturday, Geelong's Georgie Prespakis and West Coast's Ella Roberts starred as their teams each recorded a first win over their opponents.

The Cats (4-1) retained a top-four spot, scoring a fourth-straight victory and their first in seven attempts against the Crows (2-3), with an 8.9 (57) to 6.10 (46) win at Adelaide's Unley Oval.

Gun midfielder Prespakis was dynamic for Geelong, racking up match highs of 32 disposals, 19 contested possessions and nine clearances.

In Perth, West Coast (1-4) posted their first win of the season in a 6.10 (46) to 6.5 (41) victory over Brisbane (2-3).

It was their first AFLW win over the Lions in four attempts after three heavy defeats.

Young Eagles superstar Roberts put in a mammoth performance, leading the game in possessions (33), contested possessions (19), clearances (11), tackles (eight) and metres gained (700).

AAP

World.title: Trindall returns from shoulder dislocation to lead Sharks in finals win
World.content:
One month after dislocating his shoulder, Braydon Trindall has returned to lead the Cronulla Sharks to a 26-16 win, advancing to the second week of the NRL finals while knocking out the North Queensland Cowboys.

Trindall missed the final four matches of the NRL regular season after suffering the shoulder dislocation in round 24 against the Canberra Raiders, with the Sharks losing three of those games.

With a heavily strapped shoulder, Trindall looked uncomfortable throughout the match but remained strong in defence.

Trindall's kicking game put North Queensland's back-three under pressure, with two drops from Cowboys fullback Scott Drinkwater, with one leading to a first-half try.

He set up the match-sealing try late in the second half, with his 31st assist of the season putting fullback Will Kennedy over for his side's fifth try.

The Sharks will meet the loser of Sunday's qualifying final between the Penrith Panthers and Sydney Roosters.

Meanwhile, the Dolphins scored three tries in the final 20 minutes of the club's maiden NRL finals match to stun the Warriors in Auckland.

Herbie Farnworth scores for the Dolphins during their qualifying final win over the Warriors. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

In a fiery contest which had three players sent to the sin bin in the first half, the Dolphins were hampered by indiscipline.

Both sides had one try each after 60 minutes, but five penalty goals from Warriors fullback Taine Tuaupiki gave the Auckland-based side a 16-6 lead with a quarter to play.

But the Dolphins ran in three tries, including a length-of-the-field effort started and finished by Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow to take the lead in the 66th minute.

The Dolphins have earned the right to host a preliminary final at Lang Park in Brisbane in a fortnight, while the Warriors will host the Newcastle Knights next week in a knock-out semifinal.

"It is big. It is massive for everyone involved at the club," Dolphins coach Kristian Woolf said.

"The club has done such a good job over the last four years in every department, but the blokes that deserve the credit are the players with the way they played tonight and the bravery they showed under pressure.

"They are in this position for a reason and that's because they want to work hard for each other."

Relive all of Saturday's NRL finals action in the blog below.

World.title: Newcastle's finals win is proof the future has come
World.content:
If Newcastle were going to pull off a classic finals ambush on South Sydney they were going to need some new heroes to be born under the bright lights of the Sydney Football Stadium.

The Knights went into the game light up front, not in size, strength or willingness, but certainly in experience and definitely in recognition. After their 20-10 win over South Sydney, however, they will never have the luxury of being underestimated again.

Across 80 minutes of a classic blood-and-thunder final, fresh faces and young legs won the day as the star-studded Rabbitohs outfit fought on despite being busted until they were finally beaten.

NRL Finals live Newcastle holds on for a 20-10 victory over South Sydney to kick-off the 2026 finals series, but Rabbitohs coach Wayne Bennett fumes at more Bunker confusion after a contentious call.

Perhaps it could have all been different were it not for Cody Walker falling to a sniper's shot early in the second half, suffering a calf injury that ended his night early.
